deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In supervision, a resident asks how Heinz Hartmann conceptualized the force that pushes ego development forward. According to Bienenfeld’s glossary, which process did Hartmann see as the driving force behind ego development?

options.text: Adaptation—coping with the environment to optimize physical and emotional survival
Conflict between id and superego resolved by repression
Mirroring of self-assertive ambitions by a selfobject
Separation-individuation beginning at about age 5 months
Optimal frustration within a shared selfobject matrix

answer_text: Adaptation—coping with the environment to optimize physical and emotional survival
answer_raw: A. Adaptation—coping with the environment to optimize physical and emotional survival
explanation_text: A is correct: adaptation is coping with the environment to optimize physical and emotional survival (alloplastic or autoplastic), and Hartmann saw it as the driving force behind ego development. B describes structural conflict/repression, not adaptation. C is Kohutian mirroring. D is Mahler’s separation-individuation. E is self-psychological optimal frustration. Teaching point: Hartmann’s ego psychology centers adaptation, not only drive conflict.
clinical_application: When conceptualizing ego growth, ask whether the patient’s solutions are alloplastic (changing circumstances) or autoplastic (changing the self)—both are forms of adaptation.
video_query: psychodynamic adaptation Hartmann alloplastic autoplastic
context: Appendix A glossary entry for adaptation; anchors Hartmann’s ego psychology.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: Adaptation may be alloplastic (changing the environment) or autoplastic (changing some part of the self). Heinz Hartmann saw adaptation as the driving force behind ego development.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: A resident reviewing Jungian theory is asked which glossary term denotes an inborn tendency to sense things in a certain way, organized around stereotypes such as mother and hero. Which term fits?

options.text: Collective unconscious
Archetype
Latent content
Primary process
False self

answer_text: Archetype
answer_raw: B. Archetype
explanation_text: B is correct: an archetype is an inborn tendency to sense things in a certain way, organized around stereotypes (e.g., mother and hero in Jung’s model). A is the collective unconscious (the shared storehouse), not the archetype itself. C is Freudian latent dream content. D is primary process thinking. E is Winnicott’s false self. Teaching point: archetypes are organizing templates; the collective unconscious is the shared storehouse.
clinical_application: If a patient organizes relationships around timeless figures (rescuer, devouring mother), consider Jung’s archetypes as one lens for the pattern’s cultural depth.

context: Appendix A glossary entry for archetype (Jung).

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: archetype—an inborn tendency to sense things in a certain way, organized around stereotypes. In Carl Jung's model, archetypes include such figures as mother and hero.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Which of the following best defines the collective unconscious in Bienenfeld’s glossary of psychodynamic terminology?

options.text: Mental content outside awareness but retrievable with effort
The underlying wish-fulfillment intent of a dream
An inborn collection of potentials that all humans share, inherited across cultures
The story and images perceived by the dreamer after dream work
Material repressed by ego that forms the id in Kernberg’s model

answer_text: An inborn collection of potentials that all humans share, inherited across cultures
answer_raw: C. An inborn collection of potentials that all humans share, inherited across cultures
explanation_text: C is correct: the collective unconscious is an inborn collection of potentials all humans share; central to Jung’s model, it is inherited across cultures and is the transpersonal element of the psyche. A defines the preconscious. B defines latent dream content. D defines manifest content. E states Kernberg’s claim about the id, not the collective unconscious. Teaching point: Jung’s collective unconscious is transpersonal and shared, not personal repression.
clinical_application: Distinguish personal unconscious material (history-specific) from Jungian collective themes that may appear across cultures without personal learning.
video_query: psychodynamic Jung collective unconscious
context: Appendix A glossary entry for collective unconscious.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: collective unconscious—an inborn collection of potentials that all humans share. Central to Jung's model, the collective unconscious is inherited across cultures and constitutes the transpersonal element of the human psyche.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In drive, ego, and object relations psychologies, which process does Bienenfeld’s glossary identify as propelling both normal development and psychopathology?

options.text: Empathy as vicarious introspection
Mirroring of goodness and wholeness by a selfobject
Holding environment provided by the mother
Conflict among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality
Secondary revision of dream reports after waking

answer_text: Conflict among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality
answer_raw: D. Conflict among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality
explanation_text: D is correct: conflict is struggle among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality, and in drive, ego, and object relations psychologies it propels both normal development and psychopathology. A is empathy/vicarious introspection. B is mirroring. C is the holding environment. E is secondary revision of dreams. Teaching point: conflict is generative—not only pathological—in classical and object relations models.
clinical_application: When charting a case, name the conflicting parties (wish vs defense, self vs object, ego vs reality) rather than treating conflict as a vague synonym for stress.
video_query: psychodynamic conflict development psychopathology
context: Appendix A glossary entry for conflict.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: conflict—struggle among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality. In drive, ego, and object relations psychologies, conflict propels both normal development and psychopathology.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: According to Bienenfeld, Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere includes which set of functions?

options.text: Repression, projection, and reaction formation
Libido, aggression, and wish fulfillment
Mirroring, idealizing, and twinship
Separation, individuation, and rapprochement
Locomotion, perception, and memory

answer_text: Locomotion, perception, and memory
answer_raw: E. Locomotion, perception, and memory
explanation_text: E is correct: Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere is development that proceeds of its own energy and includes functions such as locomotion, perception, and memory. A lists defense mechanisms, not conflict-free functions. B names drives/wish fulfillment, not autonomous ego functions. C lists selfobject transferences. D lists Mahler’s developmental sequence. Teaching point: not all ego functions arise from conflict; some are autonomously energized.
clinical_application: Intact conflict-free capacities (memory, perception, motor skills) can be therapeutic assets even when defensive and conflict-laden ego functions are impaired.
video_query: psychodynamic conflict-free sphere Hartmann
context: Appendix A glossary entry for conflict-free sphere.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: conflict-free sphere—the realm of development that proceeds of its own energy. In Hartmann's developmental scheme, this sphere includes such functions as locomotion, perception, and memory.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Bienenfeld defines defense as which of the following?

options.text: The ego’s attempt to protect against, or cope with, threats
The id’s pressure for immediate discharge of drive tension
The superego’s ideals and prohibitions internalized after the Oedipal crisis
Projection of hostile impulses onto objects in the first 3 months of life
Confirmation by a selfobject of one’s goodness and wholeness

answer_text: The ego’s attempt to protect against, or cope with, threats
answer_raw: A. The ego’s attempt to protect against, or cope with, threats
explanation_text: A is correct: defense is the ego’s attempt to protect against or cope with threats; defense mechanisms are the specific methods used against internal or external threats. B describes drive/primary-process discharge, not defense. C defines the superego. D defines the paranoid position. E defines mirroring. Teaching point: defense is ego activity; mechanisms are the named tactics.
clinical_application: Label the threat (internal wish, external reality, affect surge) before naming the defense mechanism—defenses answer a threat.
video_query: psychodynamic defense ego mechanisms
context: Appendix A glossary entry for defense.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: defense—ego's attempt to protect against, or cope with, threats. Defense mechanisms are the specific methods employed by the ego to cope with internal or external threats. (See Table 3-1.)

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: A PGY-2 asks how Melanie Klein’s depressive position differs from the paranoid position. Which statement matches Bienenfeld’s glossary definition of the depressive position?

options.text: Hostile impulses are projected onto objects with fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects in the first 3 months
An object relations configuration that accepts good and bad aspects of objects but still believes in the destructive power of aggressive impulses
Wish for union with the opposite-sex parent and destruction of the same-sex parent around ages 3 through 6
Loss of cohesion of the self under stress with breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion
Nontraumatic failure to gratify needs that fosters new learning and growth

answer_text: An object relations configuration that accepts good and bad aspects of objects but still believes in the destructive power of aggressive impulses
answer_raw: B. An object relations configuration that accepts good and bad aspects of objects but still believes in the destructive power of aggressive impulses
explanation_text: B is correct: Klein’s depressive position accepts good and bad aspects of objects while still believing in the destructive power of aggressive impulses; the child fears harming the libidinal object; it begins about the fourth month and continues throughout life. A defines the paranoid position. C defines the Oedipal crisis. D defines fragmentation. E defines optimal frustration. Teaching point: depressive position = ambivalence and concern for the object, not clinical depression alone.
clinical_application: When a patient shifts from pure idealization/devaluation to guilt and fear of harming a valued other, consider movement toward the depressive position.
video_query: psychodynamic Klein depressive position
context: Appendix A glossary entry for depressive position (Klein).

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 151.

bienenfeld.quote: depressive position—an object relations configuration that accepts the good and bad aspects of objects, but still believes in the destructive power of aggressive impulses. In Melanie Klein's scheme, the child in this position is fearful of the effects of his or her hostile wishes on the object of libidinal attachment.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In Bienenfeld’s glossary, adaptation is the process of coping with the environment to optimize physical and emotional survival. Adaptation may be alloplastic or autoplastic. What do these terms mean?

options.text: Alloplastic: changing the environment; autoplastic: changing some part of the self
Alloplastic: changing the self; autoplastic: changing the environment
Both mean changing only the therapist
Both mean changing only childhood memories
Neither involves coping with the environment

answer_text: Alloplastic: changing the environment; autoplastic: changing some part of the self
answer_raw: A. Alloplastic: changing the environment; autoplastic: changing some part of the self
explanation_text: A is correct: Bienenfeld’s glossary defines alloplastic adaptation as changing the environment and autoplastic adaptation as changing some part of the self—both forms of coping with the environment for physical and emotional survival. B reverses the terms: allo- points to altering the other/environment, not the self; auto- points to altering the self, not the surroundings. C is incorrect: adaptation is the person’s (or ego’s) coping process, not a change confined to the therapist. D is incorrect: the glossary does not equate adaptation with rewriting childhood memories alone; it is broader environmental coping. E is incorrect: adaptation is explicitly defined as coping with the environment, so both alloplastic and autoplastic routes serve that aim. Teaching point: know Hartmann’s adaptive vocabulary—allo- vs autoplastic—as core ego-psychology language.
clinical_application: When a patient only self-blames, ask whether an alloplastic (environment-changing) adaptation is available too.
video_query: psychodynamic glossary adaptation alloplastic autoplastic Hartmann
context: Appendix A glossary opening terms (printed with Chapter 9 pack end).

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

bienenfeld.quote: Adaptation may be alloplastic (changing the environment) or autoplastic (changing some part of the self).

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Heinz Hartmann saw adaptation as which of the following?

options.text: The driving force behind ego development
Irrelevant to ego psychology
Only a behavioral concept without psychic meaning
Identical to the depressive position
A Jungian archetype

answer_text: The driving force behind ego development
answer_raw: A. The driving force behind ego development
explanation_text: A is correct: the glossary states that Heinz Hartmann saw adaptation as the driving force behind ego development. B is incorrect: adaptation is central to ego psychology, not irrelevant to it—Hartmann made it the developmental engine. C is incorrect: in this model adaptation is a psychic/ego concept (alloplastic and autoplastic coping), not a purely behavioral idea stripped of inner meaning. D is incorrect: the depressive position is a Kleinian object-relations configuration, not Hartmann’s term for adaptation. E is incorrect: archetype is a Jungian glossary entry (inborn form-tendency), not Hartmann’s adaptation concept. Teaching point: link adaptation to Hartmann’s ego psychology as the force that organizes ego growth.
clinical_application: In ego-psychological formulations, ask how symptoms once served adaptation.
video_query: psychodynamic Hartmann adaptation ego development
context: Glossary: Hartmann on adaptation.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

bienenfeld.quote: Heinz Hartmann saw adaptation as the driving force behind ego development.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: An archetype, in Carl Jung’s model as glossed by Bienenfeld, is an inborn tendency to sense things in a certain way, organized around stereotypes. Examples include which figures?

options.text: Mother and hero
Only the modern CEO and influencer
Only the patient’s actual parents by name
Only drive derivatives of the id
Only conditioned stimuli

answer_text: Mother and hero
answer_raw: A. Mother and hero
explanation_text: A is correct: Bienenfeld’s Jungian gloss says archetypes include such figures as mother and hero, and the collective unconscious is organized around these archetypes. B is incorrect: modern occupational labels (CEO, influencer) are not the glossary’s archetypal examples—archetypes are transcultural form-tendencies, not current-media roles. C is incorrect: archetypes are inborn stereotypes/templates, not merely the patient’s named actual parents as unique individuals. D is incorrect: drive derivatives of the id are Freudian structural concepts, not Jungian archetypes. E is incorrect: conditioned stimuli are learning-theory terms; archetypes are innate organizing tendencies, not classically conditioned cues. Teaching point: archetypes are universal form-tendencies (e.g., mother, hero), not personal memories or behavioral contingencies alone.
clinical_application: When a patient speaks in mythic/ideal types (hero, mother), consider Jungian archetype language as one possible frame.
video_query: psychodynamic Jung archetype mother hero
context: Glossary: archetype.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

bienenfeld.quote: In Carl Jung’s model, archetypes include such figures as mother and hero.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: The collective unconscious is defined as an inborn collection of potentials that all humans share. Central to Jung’s model, it is inherited across cultures and constitutes which element of the human psyche?

options.text: The transpersonal element
Only the personal repressed unconscious of Freud
Only the ego’s conflict-free sphere
Only learned cultural customs with no inborn basis
Only the superego’s moral rules

answer_text: The transpersonal element
answer_raw: A. The transpersonal element
explanation_text: A is correct: it constitutes the transpersonal element of the human psyche. B is Freudian personal unconscious. C is Hartmann. D denies inborn basis. E is structural theory. Teaching point: Jung’s collective unconscious is transpersonal and shared.
clinical_application: Distinguish personal repressed material from possibly universal archetypal themes when teaching Jung.

context: Glossary: collective unconscious.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Conflict, in the glossary, is struggle among, between, or within psychic structures or between structures and reality. In which psychologies does conflict propel both normal development and psychopathology?

options.text: Drive, ego, and object relations psychologies
Only self psychology
Only behavioral psychology
Only Jungian analytic psychology exclusively
Only interpersonal psychiatry of Sullivan exclusively

answer_text: Drive, ego, and object relations psychologies
answer_raw: A. Drive, ego, and object relations psychologies
explanation_text: A is correct: the glossary states that in drive, ego, and object relations psychologies, conflict propels both normal development and psychopathology. B is incorrect: “only self psychology” is not the glossary’s list—self psychology is the major model among those emphasized in this book that centers deficit/cohesion more than structural conflict as the engine. C is incorrect: behavioral psychology is not named in the glossary’s conflict definition; the triad is drive, ego, and object relations. D is incorrect: Jungian analytic psychology is not listed as the exclusive set for conflict propelling development and pathology. E is incorrect: Sullivan’s interpersonal psychiatry is not the glossary’s answer; the named schools are drive, ego, and object relations. Teaching point: conflict is the motor in drive/ego/object-relations models; self psychology is the main exception among the book’s four perspectives.
clinical_application: When a case is “all conflict,” ask whether a self-psychological deficit formulation might also fit.
video_query: psychodynamic glossary conflict drive ego object relations
context: Glossary: conflict.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

bienenfeld.quote: In drive, ego, and object relations psychologies, conflict propels both normal development and psychopathology.

options.text: Locomotion, perception, and memory

Only free association

answer_raw: A. Locomotion, perception, and memory
explanation_text: A is correct: locomotion, perception, and memory are listed conflict-free sphere functions. B is drive conflict. C is object relations. D is Jungian. E is technique. Teaching point: not all ego functions are born of conflict.
clinical_application: Assess conflict-free capacities (memory, perception, motor skill) when estimating ego strength.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: The depressive position, in Melanie Klein’s scheme as glossed here, is an object relations configuration that accepts good and bad aspects of objects but still believes in the destructive power of aggressive impulses. The child in this position is fearful of the effects of hostile wishes on the object of libidinal attachment. When does this position begin?

options.text: In about the fourth month, and continues throughout life
Only after adolescence ends
Only in the Oedipal stage at ages 4–6 exclusively
Only in adulthood under stress
Never; it is purely theoretical without developmental timing

answer_text: In about the fourth month, and continues throughout life
answer_raw: A. In about the fourth month, and continues throughout life
explanation_text: A is correct: Klein’s depressive position, as glossed, begins in about the fourth month and continues throughout life. B is incorrect: the position does not begin only after adolescence ends; the glossary places onset around the fourth month with lifelong continuation. C is incorrect: it is not confined exclusively to the Oedipal stage at ages 4–6; timing is earlier (≈4 months) and ongoing. D is incorrect: it is not limited to adulthood under stress; it begins in infancy and persists across life. E is incorrect: the glossary is not “purely theoretical without developmental timing”—it explicitly times onset at about the fourth month. Teaching point: the depressive position is lifelong—integrating good and bad objects while fearing aggressive wishes’ effects—not a brief or adult-only phase.
clinical_application: When a patient fears their anger will destroy a loved one, consider Kleinian depressive-position anxiety, not only DSM major depression.
video_query: psychodynamic Klein depressive position fourth month
context: Glossary: depressive position.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 150.

bienenfeld.quote: This position begins in about the fourth month and continues throughout life.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In Sigmund Freud’s model as summarized in Bienenfeld’s glossary, the two drives are:

options.text: Attachment and mastery
Life instinct and superiority striving
Aggression and libido
Empathy and mirroring
Primary process and secondary process

answer_text: Aggression and libido
answer_raw: C. Aggression and libido
explanation_text: C is correct: a drive is a motivational force impelling human behavior; in Freud’s model the two drives are aggression and libido. A uses non-Freudian motivational pair. B mixes life-instinct language with Adlerian striving. D names self-psychological functions, not drives. E names modes of mental function, not drives. Teaching point: classical dual-drive theory = libido + aggression.
clinical_application: When a case formulation invokes ‘drive,’ specify whether sexual/libidinal or aggressive aims are hypothesized to fuel the behavior.

context: Appendix A glossary entry for drive.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: drive—a motivational force that impels human behavior. In Sigmund Freud's model, the two drives are aggression and libido.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Which statement best captures Bienenfeld’s glossary definition of the ego?

options.text: Innate structure containing mental representations of the drives
Mental structure that contains ideals and prohibitions as a product of the Oedipal crisis
System of unconscious, preconscious, and conscious articulated in 1915
Psychic structure that manages demands of id, superego, and reality; mounts defenses; contains the object world; develops capacities such as locomotion, memory, and speech
Configuration of attitudes adopted to meet demands of objects who cannot respond to genuine potentials

answer_text: Psychic structure that manages demands of id, superego, and reality; mounts defenses; contains the object world; develops capacities such as locomotion, memory, and speech
answer_raw: D. Psychic structure that manages demands of id, superego, and reality; mounts defenses; contains the object world; develops capacities such as locomotion, memory, and speech
explanation_text: D is correct: the ego manages demands of id, superego, and reality, mounts defenses, contains the object world, and implements capacities including locomotion, memory, and speech. A defines the id. B defines the superego. C defines the topographic model. E defines the false self. Teaching point: assess ego as executive function among competing demands.
clinical_application: Assess ego functions separately (reality testing, defenses, memory, speech) rather than equating ‘ego strength’ with global wellness.
video_query: psychodynamic ego structure defenses
context: Appendix A glossary entry for ego.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: ego—the psychic structure that manages the demands of id, superego, and reality. The ego mounts the defense mechanisms and contains the object world. It also develops and implements capacities including locomotion, memory, and speech.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In self psychology, Bienenfeld’s glossary equates empathy with which phrase and clinical necessity?

options.text: Free association necessary only for recovering repressed wishes
Optimal frustration necessary to dismantle the false self
Holding environment necessary only in the first 3 months of life
Secondary process necessary for dream work
Vicarious introspection necessary for normal development and for effective psychotherapy

answer_text: Vicarious introspection necessary for normal development and for effective psychotherapy
answer_raw: E. Vicarious introspection necessary for normal development and for effective psychotherapy
explanation_text: E is correct: empathy is sharing another’s perspective and experience; in self psychology this “vicarious introspection” is necessary for normal development and effective psychotherapy. A names free association, not empathy. B misapplies optimal frustration. C misstates the holding environment. D confuses a mode of thought with empathy. Teaching point: Kohutian empathy is both a developmental need and a therapeutic instrument.
clinical_application: Use sustained empathic immersion first; explanation without felt understanding often fails as a mutative intervention in self psychology.
video_query: psychodynamic empathy vicarious introspection Kohut
context: Appendix A glossary entry for empathy (self psychology).

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: empathy—the capacity to share the perspective and experience of another person. In self psychology, this function of "vicarious introspection" is necessary for normal development and for effective psychotherapy.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: The epigenetic model, as defined in Bienenfeld’s glossary, refers to:

options.text: Erik Erikson’s scheme of successive tasks and crises faced by the ego across the lifespan
Freud’s 1923 tripartite model of id, ego, and superego
Melanie Klein’s sequence of paranoid then depressive positions
Margaret Mahler’s separation-individuation process from 5 months onward
Heinz Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere of autonomous ego functions

answer_text: Erik Erikson’s scheme of successive tasks and crises faced by the ego across the lifespan
answer_raw: A. Erik Erikson’s scheme of successive tasks and crises faced by the ego across the lifespan
explanation_text: A is correct: the epigenetic model is Erikson’s scheme of successive tasks and crises faced by the ego across the lifespan. B is Freud’s structural model. C is Klein’s positional sequence. D is Mahler’s separation-individuation. E is Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere. Teaching point: epigenetic = stage-upon-stage ego tasks (Erikson), not genetics.
clinical_application: Map adult presentation to unresolved stage-specific crises (trust, autonomy, identity, generativity) using Erikson’s epigenetic frame.
video_query: psychodynamic Erikson epigenetic model
context: Appendix A glossary entry for epigenetic model.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: epigenetic model—the scheme elaborated by Erik Erikson to describe the succession of tasks and crises faced by the ego in a lifelong process of development.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In D.W. Winnicott’s object relations model as glossed by Bienenfeld, what is the false self?

options.text: Loss of cohesion of the self under stress with breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion
A configuration of attitudes and behaviors adopted in reaction to objects who cannot appreciate and respond to one’s genuine innate potentials
The first product of the child’s creativity invested with magical soothing properties
The subjective experience of another person within a shared selfobject matrix
Confirmation by a selfobject of one’s goodness and wholeness

answer_text: A configuration of attitudes and behaviors adopted in reaction to objects who cannot appreciate and respond to one’s genuine innate potentials
answer_raw: B. A configuration of attitudes and behaviors adopted in reaction to objects who cannot appreciate and respond to one’s genuine innate potentials
explanation_text: B is correct: the false self is a configuration of attitudes and behaviors adopted when objects cannot appreciate genuine innate potentials; in Winnicott’s model the true–false self struggle is core psychopathology. A defines fragmentation. C defines the transitional object. D defines the selfobject. E defines mirroring. Teaching point: false self protects by compliance; pathology is the true–false struggle.
clinical_application: When a high-functioning patient seems perfectly adapted yet empty, explore whether a false self developed around caregivers’ needs rather than the patient’s own.
video_query: psychodynamic Winnicott false self true self
context: Appendix A glossary entry for false self.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: false self—a configuration of attitudes and behaviors adopted in reaction to the demands of objects who cannot appreciate and respond to one's genuine innate potentials. In D.W. Winnicott's model of object relations, the struggle between the true and false selves is at the core of psychopathology.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In self psychology, pathological symptoms are understood as manifestations of which process?

options.text: Parapraxis reflecting repressed motives
Paranoid position with projected hostility
Fragmentation—loss of cohesion of the self, the breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion
Oedipus complex as adult residue of childhood crisis
Inferiority complex at the base of neurotic emotion

answer_text: Fragmentation—loss of cohesion of the self, the breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion
answer_raw: C. Fragmentation—loss of cohesion of the self, the breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion
explanation_text: C is correct: fragmentation is loss of self-cohesion under stress; in self psychology symptoms are manifestations of fragmentation—breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion. A defines parapraxis. B defines the paranoid position. D defines the Oedipus complex. E defines Adler’s inferiority complex. Teaching point: in self psychology, symptoms may be disintegration products, not only compromise formations.
clinical_application: When a narcissistic patient becomes rageful or empty after a slight, formulate the symptom as self fragmentation under selfobject failure.
video_query: psychodynamic fragmentation self cohesion Kohut
context: Appendix A glossary entry for fragmentation.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: fragmentation—loss of cohesion of the self, usually under stress. In self psychology, pathological symptoms are manifestations of fragmentation, the breakdown products of deficient self-cohesion.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Bienenfeld’s glossary defines the holding environment as the state in which the caregiver anticipates and provides the child’s needs and protects the child from discomfort. Who saw this environment as the breeding ground for the healthy ego and a necessity for adaptive object relations?

options.text: Heinz Kohut
Melanie Klein
Otto Kernberg
D.W. Winnicott
Harry Stack Sullivan

answer_text: D.W. Winnicott
answer_raw: D. D.W. Winnicott
explanation_text: D is correct: Winnicott saw the holding environment—caregiver anticipates needs and protects from discomfort—as the breeding ground for the healthy ego and a necessity for adaptive object relations. A Kohut is associated with selfobjects/mirroring, not the holding environment term. B Klein is associated with positions, not holding. C Kernberg is not the source of the holding environment concept. E Sullivan is an interpersonalist, not the source of this term. Teaching point: holding = reliable anticipatory care enabling ego and object relations.
clinical_application: In therapy, ‘holding’ means reliable containment of affect and need—not permissiveness without limits—so the patient can use the relationship safely.
video_query: psychodynamic Winnicott holding environment
context: Appendix A glossary entry for holding environment.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: holding environment—the state in which the caregiver, usually the mother, anticipates and provides the child's needs and protects him or her from discomfort. D.W. Winnicott saw this environment as the breeding ground for the healthy ego and as a necessity for adaptive object relations.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: How do Freud, Hartmann, and Kernberg differ regarding the origin of the id, according to Bienenfeld’s glossary?

options.text: All three hold that id, ego, and superego are innate and coeval
Freud and Hartmann: id arises from the Oedipal crisis; Kernberg: id is innate
Hartmann: id contains ideals and prohibitions; Freud: id is a product of the false self
Kernberg: id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; Freud: id is a selfobject experience
Freud: id is innate and ego/superego arise from it; Hartmann: id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; Kernberg: id is the product of material repressed by ego

answer_text: Freud: id is innate and ego/superego arise from it; Hartmann: id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; Kernberg: id is the product of material repressed by ego
answer_raw: E. Freud: id is innate and ego/superego arise from it; Hartmann: id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; Kernberg: id is the product of material repressed by ego
explanation_text: E is correct: Freud: id is innate and ego/superego arise from it; Hartmann: id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; Kernberg: id is the product of material repressed by ego. A erases the model differences the glossary stresses. B reverses Freud’s account (id is innate, not Oedipal). C misassigns superego/false-self ideas to Hartmann and Freud. D misattributes Hartmann and confuses self psychology with structural theory. Teaching point: “id” is model-dependent—specify Freud, Hartmann, or Kernberg.
clinical_application: In case conference, specify whether you mean Freud’s innate drive reservoir or Kernberg’s later product of repressed object-relational material.
video_query: psychodynamic id Freud Hartmann Kernberg
context: Appendix A glossary entry for id (model contrasts).

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 152.

bienenfeld.quote: In Sigmund Freud's structural model, id is innate; ego and superego arise from it. In Heinz Hartmann's ego psychological model, id and ego arise from an undifferentiated matrix; in Otto Kernberg's object relations model, id is the product of material repressed by ego.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Latent content is converted to the story and images perceived by the dreamer by which process?

options.text: Dream work
Secondary revision
Free association alone
Signal anxiety
Psychic determinism

answer_text: Dream work
answer_raw: A. Dream work
explanation_text: A is correct: manifest content is the story and images perceived by the dreamer; latent content is converted to it by dream work. B is secondary revision (post-waking change), not dream work. C is a method of access, not the latent→manifest conversion process. D is signal anxiety. E is psychic determinism. Teaching point: dream work transforms latent → manifest.
clinical_application: When interpreting a dream, separate the patient’s reported story (manifest) from inferred wishes/conflicts (latent) and the operations that disguise one as the other (dream work).
video_query: psychodynamic dream work manifest latent content
context: Appendix A glossary entries for manifest content and dream work.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: manifest content—the story and images perceived by the dreamer. Latent content is converted to manifest content by the process of dream work.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In self psychology, mirroring selfobjects promote development of which pole of the self?

options.text: Idealized parent imago and idealizing needs
Pole of self-assertive ambitions
Twinship/alter-ego needs exclusively
Conflict-free sphere of autonomous functions
Superego ideals and prohibitions

answer_text: Pole of self-assertive ambitions
answer_raw: B. Pole of self-assertive ambitions
explanation_text: B is correct: mirroring is selfobject confirmation of one’s goodness and wholeness and promotes the pole of self-assertive ambitions. A describes the idealizing line, not what mirroring builds. C names twinship/alter-ego needs, not the mirroring pole. D is Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere. E is the structural superego. Teaching point: mirroring builds the ambitions/assertiveness pole.
clinical_application: When a patient lights up after accurate recognition of competence, note mirroring as a possible developmental repair opportunity.
video_query: psychodynamic mirroring selfobject ambitions Kohut
context: Appendix A glossary entry for mirroring.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: mirroring—the confirmation by a selfobject of one's goodness and wholeness. In self psychology, mirroring selfobjects promote the development of the pole of self-assertive ambitions.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Which feature does Bienenfeld’s glossary use to differentiate neuroses from psychoses in most nosologic schemes?

options.text: Presence of dream work and primary process only in neuroses
Neuroses lack intrapsychic conflict
Reality testing is intact in neuroses
Neuroses are identical to Freud’s ‘actual neuroses’
Neuroses always result from Oedipal failure alone

answer_text: Reality testing is intact in neuroses
answer_raw: C. Reality testing is intact in neuroses
explanation_text: C is correct: neurosis is symptoms from intrapsychic conflict (Freud’s psychoneuroses vs discarded “actual neuroses”); intact reality testing differentiates neuroses from psychoses in most nosologic schemes. A falsely limits dream work/primary process to neuroses. B contradicts the glossary (neuroses result from conflict). D reverses Freud’s psychoneuroses vs actual neuroses distinction. E overrestricts etiology to Oedipal failure alone. Teaching point: conflict + intact reality testing ≈ neurosis in this framework.
clinical_application: Do not equate ‘neurotic’ with mild severity only—use the structural criterion of preserved reality testing versus psychosis.
video_query: psychodynamic neurosis reality testing
context: Appendix A glossary entry for neurosis.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: neurosis—a complex of psychiatric symptoms resulting from intrapsychic conflict. ... In most nosologic schemes, reality testing is intact in neuroses, differentiating them from psychoses.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Regarding the Oedipal crisis and Oedipus complex, Bienenfeld’s glossary states that:

options.text: Both terms refer only to literal incestuous wishes between ages 0 and 3 months
Drive psychology treats Oedipal material purely metaphorically; object relations treat it literally
The Oedipus complex is identical to Klein’s paranoid position
The Oedipal crisis usually occurs around ages 3 through 6; the Oedipus complex is its adult residue
The Oedipal crisis produces the id in Freud’s topographic model

answer_text: The Oedipal crisis usually occurs around ages 3 through 6; the Oedipus complex is its adult residue
answer_raw: D. The Oedipal crisis usually occurs around ages 3 through 6; the Oedipus complex is its adult residue
explanation_text: D is correct: the Oedipal crisis (wish for opposite-sex parent, destruction of same-sex parent) usually occurs around ages 3–6; the Oedipus complex is its adult residue; drive psychology is more literal, ego psychology and object relations more metaphorical. A wrong ages and overstates literalism for all schools. B reverses how drive vs ego/object relations treat Oedipal material. C confuses Oedipal theory with Klein’s paranoid position. E confuses Oedipal development with topographic/structural genesis of the id. Teaching point: crisis = childhood phase; complex = adult residue.
clinical_application: In adult therapy, ‘Oedipal’ formulations often mean competitive/triangular residues—not necessarily literal incestuous fantasy.
video_query: psychodynamic Oedipus complex crisis ages
context: Appendix A glossary entry for Oedipal crisis / Oedipus complex.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: The Oedipal crisis usually occurs around ages 3 through 6; the Oedipus complex is its adult residue.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Optimal frustration, in self psychology as defined by Bienenfeld, is:

options.text: Traumatic deprivation that shatters the self and produces permanent fragmentation
The caregiver’s perfect anticipation of every need without any delay
Hostile projection onto objects in the first 3 months of life
The process of changing dream content after waking
A nontraumatic failure to gratify a person’s needs that fosters new learning and personal growth in development and psychotherapy

answer_text: A nontraumatic failure to gratify a person’s needs that fosters new learning and personal growth in development and psychotherapy
answer_raw: E. A nontraumatic failure to gratify a person’s needs that fosters new learning and personal growth in development and psychotherapy
explanation_text: E is correct: optimal frustration is a nontraumatic failure to gratify needs that fosters new learning and growth in development and psychotherapy. A describes trauma, not nontraumatic optimal frustration. B is the opposite (no frustration). C defines the paranoid position. D defines secondary revision. Teaching point: dose-limited frustration is growth-promoting, not neglect.
clinical_application: In therapy, small, survivable empathic misses followed by repair can be optimally frustrating and growth-promoting—if not traumatic in scale.
video_query: psychodynamic optimal frustration self psychology
context: Appendix A glossary entry for optimal frustration.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: optimal frustration—a nontraumatic failure to gratify a person's needs. In self psychology, it is a necessary element that fosters new learning and personal growth, both in normal development and in psychotherapy.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Melanie Klein’s paranoid position, per Bienenfeld’s glossary, is characterized by:

options.text: Projection of hostile impulses onto objects, characterizing the first 3 months of life, with fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects
Acceptance of good and bad aspects of objects with concern for harming the loved object
Wish for union with the opposite-sex parent around ages 3 through 6
Intact reality testing with intrapsychic conflict producing neurotic symptoms
Development of self-assertive ambitions through mirroring

answer_text: Projection of hostile impulses onto objects, characterizing the first 3 months of life, with fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects
answer_raw: A. Projection of hostile impulses onto objects, characterizing the first 3 months of life, with fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects
explanation_text: A is correct: Klein’s paranoid position projects hostile impulses onto objects in the first 3 months, with fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects. B defines the Oedipal crisis. C defines the Oedipal crisis. D defines neurosis. E describes mirroring’s developmental effect. Teaching point: paranoid position = early projective, persecutory object relations.
clinical_application: Extreme, one-dimensional ‘all bad’ others and persecutory fear may signal residual paranoid-position dynamics in adult borderline presentations.
video_query: psychodynamic Klein paranoid position
context: Appendix A glossary entry for paranoid position.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: paranoid position—a primitive object relations configuration in which hostile impulses are projected onto objects. In Melanie Klein's scheme, this position characterizes the first 3 months of life and is accompanied by the fear of abandonment or destruction by bad objects.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: A resident says, ‘I meant to email my attending but sent the message to my patient instead—Freud would call that…’ Which glossary term fits?

options.text: Primary process
Parapraxis—an error of everyday life that reflects repressed unconscious motives (a ‘Freudian slip’)
Secondary process
Preconscious retrieval failure without motive
Manifest content of a dream

answer_text: Parapraxis—an error of everyday life that reflects repressed unconscious motives (a ‘Freudian slip’)
answer_raw: B. Parapraxis—an error of everyday life that reflects repressed unconscious motives (a ‘Freudian slip’)
explanation_text: B is correct: parapraxis is an everyday error reflecting repressed unconscious motives—a “Freudian slip”. A names a mode of mental function, not an everyday error. C names mature conscious function, not a slip. D denies the motivational claim central to parapraxis. E is dream report content, not a waking slip. Teaching point: slips are meaningful under psychic determinism.
clinical_application: Treat slips, misnamings, and ‘accidental’ acts as data—ask what motive might be peeking through.
video_query: psychodynamic parapraxis Freudian slip
context: Appendix A glossary entry for parapraxis.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: parapraxis—an error of everyday life that reflects repressed unconscious motives. Such an error is commonly called a "Freudian slip."

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Which contrast between primary process and secondary process is accurate per Bienenfeld’s glossary?

options.text: Primary process is mature verbal thought; secondary process seeks immediate drive discharge
Both processes are limited to conscious mental activity

Primary process is the earliest form of mental function, drive-connected, immediate discharge, free symbols/substitutions, no chronology, shapes dream manifest content; secondary process is mature, verbal, chronological, avoids contradictions
Secondary process has no regard for chronology; primary process avoids inconsistencies
Primary process is identical to the preconscious system

answer_text: Primary process is the earliest form of mental function, drive-connected, immediate discharge, free symbols/substitutions, no chronology, shapes dream manifest content; secondary process is mature, verbal, chronological, avoids contradictions
answer_raw: C. Primary process is the earliest form of mental function, drive-connected, immediate discharge, free symbols/substitutions, no chronology, shapes dream manifest content; secondary process is mature, verbal, chronological, avoids contradictions
explanation_text: C is correct: primary process is primitive, drive-linked, immediate, free with symbols, without chronology, shaping dream manifest content; secondary process is mature, verbal, chronological, and avoids contradictions. A reverses primary and secondary process. B wrongly limits primary process to consciousness. D reverses the chronology claims. E confuses a mode of function with the preconscious system. Teaching point: primary ≠ secondary is a core process distinction.
clinical_application: Dreams, jokes, and acute psychosis often show primary-process features; reality-based planning shows secondary process.
video_query: psychodynamic primary secondary process
context: Appendix A glossary entries for primary and secondary process.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 153.

bienenfeld.quote: primary process—the earliest, most primitive form of mental function. It is directly connected to drive impulses and seeks immediate discharge. ... secondary process—the mature form of mental function. Characteristic of conscious mental activity, it uses verbal representation and readily understood symbols.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Secondary revision of dreams, according to Bienenfeld, is best described as:

options.text: Conversion of latent content into manifest content by dream work during sleep
Immediate drive discharge without regard for chronology
Confirmation by a selfobject of one’s goodness and wholeness
The process of changing dream content after waking, both conscious and unconscious, presumed to influence all dreams reported in therapy
Separation of good and bad object representations

answer_text: The process of changing dream content after waking, both conscious and unconscious, presumed to influence all dreams reported in therapy
answer_raw: D. The process of changing dream content after waking, both conscious and unconscious, presumed to influence all dreams reported in therapy
explanation_text: D is correct: secondary revision changes dream content after waking (conscious and unconscious) and is presumed to influence all dreams reported in therapy. A describes dream work (latent→manifest), not post-waking revision. B describes primary process. C defines mirroring. E describes splitting. Teaching point: dreams as told are already revised after waking.
clinical_application: Treat dream reports as twice-processed material: night dream work plus waking secondary revision.
video_query: psychodynamic secondary revision dreams therapy
context: Appendix A glossary entry for secondary revision.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: secondary revision—the process of changing dream content after waking. Secondary revision can be both conscious and unconscious and can be presumed to influence all dreams reported in therapy.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In self psychology, which definition of selfobject does Bienenfeld emphasize?

options.text: An inanimate object with magical soothing properties that is the first product of the child’s creativity
The psychic structure managing id, superego, and reality
Hostile impulses projected onto objects in the first 3 months
Ideals and prohibitions arising from the Oedipal crisis
The subjective experience of another person or entity—more properly the selfobject experience within a shared selfobject matrix

answer_text: The subjective experience of another person or entity—more properly the selfobject experience within a shared selfobject matrix
answer_raw: E. The subjective experience of another person or entity—more properly the selfobject experience within a shared selfobject matrix
explanation_text: E is correct: selfobject is the subjective experience of another person or entity—more properly the selfobject experience within a shared selfobject matrix. A defines the transitional object. B defines the transitional object. C defines the paranoid position. D defines the superego. Teaching point: selfobject is experiential/functional, not merely an external person.
clinical_application: Ask what function the other is serving for the self (mirroring, idealizing, twinship), not only who the other is biographically.
video_query: psychodynamic selfobject Kohut matrix
context: Appendix A glossary entry for selfobject.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: selfobject—the subjective experience of another person or entity. In self psychology, it is more properly termed the selfobject experience and occurs within a shared selfobject matrix.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In Margaret Mahler’s formulation as glossed by Bienenfeld, separation-individuation refers to:

options.text: The major process of development of autonomy and identity: separation = differentiation of self from other; individuation = defining the self; begins ~ age 5 months and continues throughout life
Oedipal crisis and its adult residue only
Alloplastic versus autoplastic adaptation in Hartmann’s scheme
Conversion of latent to manifest dream content
Innate collection of potentials shared by all humans

answer_text: The major process of development of autonomy and identity: separation = differentiation of self from other; individuation = defining the self; begins ~ age 5 months and continues throughout life
answer_raw: A. The major process of development of autonomy and identity: separation = differentiation of self from other; individuation = defining the self; begins ~ age 5 months and continues throughout life
explanation_text: A is correct: Mahler’s separation-individuation is the major process of autonomy and identity: separation differentiates self from other; individuation defines the self; it begins about age 5 months and continues lifelong. B is Freudian Oedipal theory, not Mahler. C is Hartmann’s adaptation typology. D is dream work. E is Freudian Oedipal theory, not Mahler. Teaching point: separation and individuation are linked but distinct strands.
clinical_application: In adult work, clinging vs premature distancing may re-enact incomplete separation-individuation tasks, not only attachment style labels.
video_query: psychodynamic Mahler separation individuation
context: Appendix A glossary entry for separation-individuation.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: separation-individuation—in Margaret Mahler's formulation, the major process of development of autonomy and identity. Separation is the differentiation of self from other, and individuation is the process of defining the self. This process begins at about age 5 months, and continues throughout life.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Signal anxiety in Freud’s formulation, per Bienenfeld’s glossary:

options.text: Is identical to free-floating panic without anticipatory function
Is tension arising in anticipation of a dangerous development; it triggers defense mechanisms that prevent overwhelming affect but may also lead to neurotic distress
Is the same as fragmentation of the self under stress
Occurs only during the first 3 months as fear of bad objects
Is the mature form of mental function using verbal representation

answer_text: Is tension arising in anticipation of a dangerous development; it triggers defense mechanisms that prevent overwhelming affect but may also lead to neurotic distress
answer_raw: B. Is tension arising in anticipation of a dangerous development; it triggers defense mechanisms that prevent overwhelming affect but may also lead to neurotic distress
explanation_text: B is correct: signal anxiety is anticipatory tension before danger; it triggers defenses that prevent overwhelming affect but may also produce neurotic distress. A denies the anticipatory/signal function. C is self-psychological fragmentation. D describes paranoid-position fear. E describes secondary process. Teaching point: signal anxiety recruits defense and can overshoot into neurosis.
clinical_application: When a patient tenses before a known trigger and then deploys a familiar defense, label that sequence as signal anxiety → defense.
video_query: psychodynamic signal anxiety Freud defense
context: Appendix A glossary entry for signal anxiety.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: signal anxiety—tension that arises in the anticipation of a dangerous development or traumatic occurrence. In Sigmund Freud's formulation, signal anxiety triggers defense mechanisms that prevent the emergence of overwhelming affect, but may also lead to neurotic levels of distress.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Which statement about splitting matches Bienenfeld’s glossary?

options.text: Splitting is a mature defense that consolidates ambivalence in healthy adult relationships
Splitting is identical to secondary process verbal thought

Splitting separates psychological content by extremes or opposites; object relations theorists define it between good/bad objects, affect/cognition, and self/object; it usually yields pathological results in adult life
Splitting is the confirmation of goodness by a mirroring selfobject
Splitting is limited to dream work converting latent to manifest content

answer_text: Splitting separates psychological content by extremes or opposites; object relations theorists define it between good/bad objects, affect/cognition, and self/object; it usually yields pathological results in adult life
answer_raw: C. Splitting separates psychological content by extremes or opposites; object relations theorists define it between good/bad objects, affect/cognition, and self/object; it usually yields pathological results in adult life
explanation_text: C is correct: splitting separates psychological content by extremes/opposites (good/bad objects, affect/cognition, self/object) and usually yields pathological results in adult life. A wrongly calls splitting mature/healthy. B confuses splitting with secondary process. D defines mirroring. E describes dream work. Teaching point: splitting keeps polarities unintegrated.
clinical_application: Track session-to-session idealization/devaluation of you or others as possible splitting rather than as purely realistic appraisal.
video_query: psychodynamic splitting object relations
context: Appendix A glossary entry for splitting.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: splitting—the process of separating psychological content by extremes or opposites. In the object relations school, splitting is defined by various theorists between good and bad objects, between affect and cognition, and between self and object. Splitting is a primitive mental process that usually yields pathological results in adult life.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: Freud’s structural model (also called the tripartite model), as dated in Bienenfeld’s glossary, consists of which system and was defined in which year?

options.text: Unconscious, preconscious, and conscious; 1915
Paranoid and depressive positions; 1946
True self and false self; 1960
Id, ego, and superego; 1923
Self and selfobject matrix; 1971

answer_text: Id, ego, and superego; 1923
answer_raw: D. Id, ego, and superego; 1923
explanation_text: D is correct: the structural (tripartite) model is id, ego, and superego, defined by Freud in 1923. A is the topographic model (1915). B is Kleinian positions. C is Winnicott’s true/false self. E is the topographic model (1915). Teaching point: structural (1923) ≠ topographic (1915).
clinical_application: When a learner says ‘unconscious ego,’ clarify you are mixing topographic and structural vocabularies that Freud developed at different times.
video_query: psychodynamic structural model tripartite 1923
context: Appendix A glossary entry for structural model.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: structural model—the system of id, ego, and superego. Sigmund Freud defined the structural model (also called the "tripartite model") in 1923.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: In Sigmund Freud’s model as glossed by Bienenfeld, the superego:

options.text: Is innate and gives rise to ego and id
Is identical to the preconscious system of retrievable memory
Is the first product of the child’s creativity invested with magical properties
Is the process of putting into words the therapist’s understanding of mental life
Contains ideals and prohibitions and is a product of the Oedipal crisis

answer_text: Contains ideals and prohibitions and is a product of the Oedipal crisis
answer_raw: E. Contains ideals and prohibitions and is a product of the Oedipal crisis
explanation_text: E is correct: the superego contains ideals and prohibitions and, in Freud’s model, is a product of the Oedipal crisis. A reverses structural genesis (describes id, not superego). B defines the preconscious. C defines the transitional object. D defines interpretation. Teaching point: superego = moral/ideal agency from Oedipal resolution.
clinical_application: Harsh self-attack after competitive triumph may signal superego activity residual from Oedipal-level conflict.
video_query: psychodynamic superego Oedipal ideals prohibitions
context: Appendix A glossary entry for superego.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: superego—the mental structure that contains ideals and prohibitions. In Sigmund Freud's model, it is a product of the Oedipal crisis.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — A  Glossary of Psychodynamic Terminology
stem: A supervision question contrasts Freud’s first model of mental operations with his later tripartite model. Which description matches the topographic model in Bienenfeld’s glossary?

options.text: System of unconscious, preconscious, and conscious; Freud’s first model of mental operations, articulated in 1915
System of id, ego, and superego defined in 1923
System of true self, false self, and transitional object
System of paranoid position, depressive position, and Oedipal crisis
System of mirroring, idealizing, and twinship selfobjects

answer_text: System of unconscious, preconscious, and conscious; Freud’s first model of mental operations, articulated in 1915
answer_raw: A. System of unconscious, preconscious, and conscious; Freud’s first model of mental operations, articulated in 1915
explanation_text: A is correct: the topographic model is unconscious, preconscious, and conscious—Freud’s first model of mental operations, articulated in 1915. B is the structural model (1923). C is Winnicottian language. D mixes Klein and Freud. E is self psychology’s selfobject needs. Teaching point: topography maps access to awareness; structure maps agencies.
clinical_application: Use topographic language for ‘what is available to awareness’ and structural language for ‘which agency is acting.’
video_query: psychodynamic topographic model 1915 unconscious
context: Appendix A glossary entry for topographic model.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 154.

bienenfeld.quote: topographic model—the system of unconscious, preconscious, and conscious. It was Sigmund Freud's first model of mental operations, articulated in 1915.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — B  Chronology of Major Contributors to Psychodynamic Theory
year: B  Chronology of Major Contributors to Psychodynamic Theory
stem: In Bienenfeld’s Appendix B chronology (Drive row), which figure is listed as Freud’s first collaborator?

options.text: Karl Abraham
Josef Breuer
Ernest Jones
Otto Rank
Alfred Adler

answer_text: Josef Breuer

stem: According to Andrew B. Klafter’s Appendix C introduction, a psychodynamic formulation is best defined as which of the following?

An explanation of how a patient’s psychological development and personal history have led to symptoms, relationship patterns, cognitive style, affective responses, and impulse regulation
A list of unconscious defenses to be confronted in the first session
A structural summary limited to id, ego, and superego strength ratings

answer_text: An explanation of how a patient’s psychological development and personal history have led to symptoms, relationship patterns, cognitive style, affective responses, and impulse regulation
answer_raw: B. An explanation of how a patient’s psychological development and personal history have led to symptoms, relationship patterns, cognitive style, affective responses, and impulse regulation
explanation_text: Klafter defines a psychodynamic formulation as an explanation linking psychological development and personal history to the patient’s symptoms and problems, interpersonal patterns, cognitive style, affective responses, and impulse regulation. (A) is diagnostic ranking, not a psychodynamic formulation. (C) reduces formulation to a technique checklist. (D) is only a structural sketch from classical metapsychology, narrower than Klafter’s definition. (E) is family history alone. Teaching point: formulation explains how history became the present pattern of mind and relationships.

answer_raw: B. Are free to use those terms if familiar, but a simple ordinary-language description of how important people influenced the patient’s view of self is probably more useful

options.text: Drive/ego (wishes and defenses)
Object relations (recurring interpersonal drama with the therapist as father)

answer_raw: A. Drive/ego (wishes and defenses)

stem: What is one purpose of the multi-perspective worksheet exercise for novice therapists, according to Klafter?

options.text: To force trainees to pick one school on day one and never reconsider

To give trainees an opportunity to formulate each patient from all the major psychoanalytic perspectives and see how successful each model is in suggesting how treatment might be helpful—considering all before settling on one
To prove that only one model can ever fit any patient
To eliminate the influence of supervisors entirely
To replace empathy with theory

answer_text: To give trainees an opportunity to formulate each patient from all the major psychoanalytic perspectives and see how successful each model is in suggesting how treatment might be helpful—considering all before settling on one
answer_raw: B. To give trainees an opportunity to formulate each patient from all the major psychoanalytic perspectives and see how successful each model is in suggesting how treatment might be helpful—considering all before settling on one
explanation_text: Novices lack a stable bias; they are influenced by supervisors and by which theory feels compelling. The exercise is to try all major perspectives, compare clinical usefulness, and—while one model may be easier for a given case—consider all before settling on one. (A), (C) reverse the message. (D)–(E) are not stated. Teaching point: multi-model tryouts precede model preference.
clinical_application: On a tough case, write three mini-formulations (drive/ego, OR, self); choose the intervention path that yields the clearest next session focus, and note why the others fit less well.

bienenfeld.chapter_title: C  An Outline for Comprehensive Psychodynamic Formulation
bienenfeld.quote: One of the purposes of this worksheet exercise is to give psychotherapy trainees an opportunity to attempt to formulate each patient from all the major psychoanalytic perspectives, and to then see for themselves how successful each model is in suggesting how psychotherapy treatment might be helpful. Therefore, it is expected that for a given case, one or the other model will be easier to apply. However, it is important to consider all of them before settling on one.

She also imagines he is happily married to a beautiful woman about to give birth. How does she initially experience his interest in her dreams and associations?

options.text: As immediately natural and identical to her father’s style
As puzzling and “very touchy feely”; she says her father would think the work is “absolutely crazy” and wouldn’t see how it helps
As identical to prior Socratic CBT arguing
As proof he does not believe in CFS
As irrelevant because she has no dreams

answer_text: As puzzling and “very touchy feely”; she says her father would think the work is “absolutely crazy” and wouldn’t see how it helps
answer_raw: B. As puzzling and “very touchy feely”; she says her father would think the work is “absolutely crazy” and wouldn’t see how it helps
explanation_text: B is correct: Miss R. experiences the therapist’s stance as puzzling and “very touchy feely,” and says her father would think the work is “absolutely crazy” and wouldn’t see how it helps. A is incorrect: she does not find the work immediately natural or identical to her father’s style—she contrasts it with his anti-emotion stance. C is incorrect: she does not equate the work with prior Socratic CBT arguing; her complaint is that it feels touchy-feely and father-alien. D is incorrect: this moment is not framed as proof the therapist disbelieves CFS; the quote is about the style of exploratory work. E is incorrect: relevance is not denied for lack of dreams; she has dream material elsewhere and is reacting to the emotional method. Teaching point: the treatment relationship itself contrasts with the father’s anti-emotion stance and may feel alien or crazy-making at first.
clinical_application: Expect patients raised by anti-emotion parents to pathologize exploratory therapy until a new object experience consolidates.

answer_text: The same struggle over being taken seriously and nurtured physically, present with father, mentor, fiancé, and in the transference

stem: How successful/adaptive is repression of these oedipal wishes, according to the worksheet's evaluation column?

options.text: Fully adaptive with no costs

It helps her avoid acknowledging distressing unconscious wishes and father's rejection, but is maladaptive because inability to understand how severely she longs for father leads to poorly informed decisions and unnecessary distancing from mother
It causes psychosis and hospitalization
It is the recommended long-term solution without further work
It has already been completely abandoned with full conscious incestuous awareness

answer_text: It helps her avoid acknowledging distressing unconscious wishes and father's rejection, but is maladaptive because inability to understand how severely she longs for father leads to poorly informed decisions and unnecessary distancing from mother
answer_raw: B. It helps her avoid acknowledging distressing unconscious wishes and father's rejection, but is maladaptive because inability to understand how severely she longs for father leads to poorly informed decisions and unnecessary distancing from mother
explanation_text: B is correct: repression helps her avoid acknowledging distressing unconscious wishes and father’s rejection, but is maladaptive (poor decisions from not knowing the longing’s severity; unnecessary distance from mother). A is incorrect: repression is not fully adaptive with no costs—the worksheet scores both help and harm. C is incorrect: the worksheet does not claim repression causes psychosis and hospitalization. D is incorrect: repression is not recommended as a long-term solution without further work; maladaptive costs motivate therapeutic attention. E is incorrect: repression has not already been completely abandoned with full conscious incestuous awareness at this worksheet stage. Teaching point: defenses work partially; always score both help and harm.
clinical_application: When teaching defenses, require a two-part verdict: what pain is avoided, and what life cost is paid.

answer_raw: B. The office of the neurologist
explanation_text:
B is correct: Bienenfeld opens the historical origins section by stating that the roots of psychodynamic thought and practice "arguably were established in the office of the neurologist," where late-19th-century physicians confronted young women with unexplained "hysterical" symptoms (fainting, paralysis, sensory disturbances).
(A) The asylum ward of the alienist was the classic setting for custodial care of the insane; Bienenfeld’s origin story starts with ambulatory hysterics consulting neurologists, not institutional alienism.
(C) The experimental psychology laboratory (Wundt-style psychophysics) was a contemporary scientific setting, but Bienenfeld's account anchors psychodynamics in clinical neurology, not laboratory measurement.
(D) The child guidance clinic is a later 20th-century site for applied psychodynamics and developmental work; it is not where Bienenfeld places the roots of the field.
(E) The military medical infirmary figures in later trauma and shell-shock history, not in Bienenfeld's discussion of drive psychology’s account of psychoanalysis’s beginnings.
Teaching point: When a patient has dramatic neurologic-looking complaints without a lesion, you are in the clinical space that first forced drive psychology into being—listen for meaning, not only for localization.

stem: At the University of Vienna, Freud worked in the laboratory of physiologist Ernst Brücke. Which scientific stance of Brücke most appealed to Freud?

options.text: Vitalism: living organisms are governed by irreducible life force
Reductionism: all forces in an organism reduce to known physical and chemical ones
Phenomenology: only first-person description has scientific status
Dualism: mind and body are fully independent substances
Teleology: all behavior is explained by conscious purpose alone

answer_text: Reductionism: all forces in an organism reduce to known physical and chemical ones
answer_raw: B. Reductionism: all forces in an organism reduce to known physical and chemical ones
explanation_text:
B is correct: At Vienna, Freud worked under physiologist Ernst Brücke, who—amid medicine still "tainted with remnants of folk wisdom and mystical philosophies"—maintained that all forces in an organism reduce to known physical and chemical ones; that reductionism appealed to Freud and shaped his early aim to reduce psychological phenomena to neurological bases.
(A) Vitalism posits an irreducible life force; Brücke’s stance rejected such mystical leftovers, so vitalism is the opposite of what appealed to Freud here.
(C) Phenomenology privileges first-person description as science; Brücke’s appeal was mechanistic reduction to physics and chemistry, not pure lived experience as method.
(D) Dualism treats mind and body as fully independent substances; reductionism collapses organismic forces into physical-chemical ones rather than insulating mind as a separate substance.
(E) Teleology explains behavior only by conscious purpose; Freud’s later dynamic unconscious and Brücke’s physicalism both reject purpose-only accounts of mental life.
Teaching point: Freud’s early neurology roots explain why he kept hunting for lawful forces behind symptoms—even after he abandoned the Project’s pure neural reduction.
clinical_application: When a resident insists psychodynamics is 'anti-science,' note Freud's early reductionist training and later pragmatic turn away from strict neurology.
