C is wrong: Hartmannian physical adaptation without the relational shift Fairbairn makes. D is wrong: Ego-psychology emphasis. E is wrong: Mature dependence remains dependence; it is not abandoned. Teaching point: Fairbairn is a relational-mode developmental theory, not primarily a structural one.

Formation of the anti-libidinal ego alone
Conscious reparation only

answer_raw: B. Mother's presence and attunement
explanation_text: B is correct: Survival depends on mother's presence and attunement; merger means world and self are a single object. A is wrong: Mahler practicing marker. C is wrong: Classical developmental milestone, not this definition. D is wrong: Later Fairbairn ego-split structure. E is wrong: Kleinian reparation theme. deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: During Fairbairn's transitional stage, relationships emerge based on differentiation and exchange; relinquishing the merger of infantile dependence, the child fears:

options.text: Only physical injury without object loss
Mature altruistic generosity
The loss of objects
The end of all barter
Psychological birth via upright locomotion exclusively

answer_text: The loss of objects
answer_raw: C. The loss of objects
explanation_text: C is correct: The transitional stage is a long process of separation; relinquishing merger, the child fears the loss of objects. A is wrong: Object loss, not only physical injury, is the stated fear. B is wrong: That is a feature of mature dependence. D is wrong: Barter characterizes the transitional phase rather than ending it. E is wrong: Mahlerian practicing language. Teaching point: Transitional-stage anxiety centers on losing objects while differentiating.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: For Fairbairn, the natural or primary objects of the ego are other people, but reality interferes with the mother–infant bond and requires creation of internal objects. To contain bad or frustrating objects, the ego splits. The exciting, provocative, intensely attractive image of mother is contained in the libidinal ego as an exciting object, while the unavailable mother gives rise to a frustrating object representation contained in the:

options.text: Central ego
Conflict-free autonomous ego
Superego alone without splitting
Anti-libidinal ego
Paranoid-schizoid position only

answer_text: Anti-libidinal ego
answer_raw: D. Anti-libidinal ego
explanation_text: D is correct: The unavailable mother gives rise to a frustrating object representation contained in the anti-libidinal ego; the exciting object is in the libidinal ego; the central ego holds positive objects/experiences and conscious relational function. If relations remain unsatisfactory, splits persist; otherwise they merge into a healthy ego and object world. A is wrong: Central ego holds positive objects and conscious relational function. B is wrong: Hartmannian language. C is wrong: Not Fairbairn's described split for frustrating objects. E is wrong: Kleinian position language. Teaching point: Fairbairn's tripartite ego split maps exciting versus rejecting internal objects.
clinical_application: Map a patient's push-pull toward an unavailable-yet-exciting other onto libidinal versus anti-libidinal ego splits.

Failure of upright locomotion

answer_raw: E. The irreconcilable features of others in external reality
explanation_text: E is correct: Psychopathology reflected the basic struggle between intense longings for contact and the irreconcilable features of others in external reality. A is wrong: Aggression is secondary to frustration, not simply absent. B is wrong: Kleinian death-instinct framing, not Fairbairn's claim here. C is wrong: Mahlerian marker, not Fairbairn psychopathology. D is wrong: Opposite of pathogenic environmental failure. Teaching point: Fairbairnian pathology is relational—desire for contact colliding with real others' frustrating, irreconcilable qualities.
clinical_application: Formulate much character pathology as contact-longing versus unbearable otherness, not only as drive excess.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: According to Fairbairn’s therapeutic model as summarized by Bienenfeld, the central aim of treatment is to:

options.text: Interpret oedipal wishes and strengthen repression of the id
Unify the split elements of the ego so bad objects can be surrendered from repression and reattached into an integrated adult self
Provide only supportive holding without addressing repressed bad objects
Eliminate all transference so the patient experiences the therapist solely as a real person
Replace object seeking with drive discharge through free association

answer_text: Unify the split elements of the ego so bad objects can be surrendered from repression and reattached into an integrated adult self
answer_raw: B. Unify the split elements of the ego so bad objects can be surrendered from repression and reattached into an integrated adult self
explanation_text: B is correct: Fairbairn-oriented therapy aims at unifying split ego elements; with a strong real and transferential relationship, the patient experiences the therapist as a good object, surrenders bad objects from repression, loosens libidinal ties to them, and reattaches them into an integrated genuine adult self. A is drive/ego-psychology Oedipal work, not Fairbairn’s focus here. C omits the active work with repressed bad objects. D is wrong because the text requires a strong transferential as well as real relationship. E inverts Fairbairn’s object-seeking stance. Teaching point: Fairbairn therapy heals by reunifying split ego around a good object experience with the therapist.
clinical_application: When a patient clings to internalized bad objects, aim for a reliable good-object experience in the alliance that can eventually permit those repressed ties to loosen and be reintegrated.

stem: Winnicott’s view of human nature, as contrasted with Freud’s in Bienenfeld's account, is best summarized as:

options.text: Humankind is inherently depraved and driven by death instinct
Human nature is basically good, shaped for better or worse by the specific interpersonal environment
Infants are blank slates with no innate tendencies until Oedipal conflict
Aggression is primary and more powerful than libido from birth

answer_text: Human nature is basically good, shaped for better or worse by the specific interpersonal environment
answer_raw: B. Human nature is basically good, shaped for better or worse by the specific interpersonal environment
explanation_text: B is correct: Winnicott rejected Freud’s view of the depravity of mankind and saw human nature as basically good, emphasizing the specific interpersonal environment. A is the Freudian view he rejected. C is not Winnicott’s claim. D is closer to Klein. E denies the environmental emphasis central to Bienenfeld. Teaching point: Winnicott relocates pathology from innate depravity to failures of the caregiving environment.
clinical_application: Frame early developmental pathology as environmental failure of attunement rather than as proof of an essentially bad infant.

stem: Winnicott’s famous declaration “There is no such thing as a baby without a mother” implies that early development is best understood as:

options.text: A solitary organism maturing by innate drive stages alone
A nursing couple bonded more by emotion than by the physical tie of Mahler’s stage of symbiosis
A one-person psychology of conflict between id and superego
A purely physical attachment without affective bonding
An Oedipal triangle already present at birth

answer_text: A nursing couple bonded more by emotion than by the physical tie of Mahler’s stage of symbiosis
answer_raw: B. A nursing couple bonded more by emotion than by the physical tie of Mahler’s stage of symbiosis
explanation_text: B is correct: Winnicott held that there is a nursing couple bonded more by emotion than by the physical tie of Mahler’s symbiosis. A and C are one-organism/drive models he moved beyond. D reverses his emotional emphasis. E is not Bienenfeld's claim. Teaching point: For Winnicott, the unit of early life is the mother–infant couple, not the isolated baby.

stem: In Winnicott’s model, “good enough mothering” begins with primary maternal preoccupation lasting approximately:

options.text: The entire first year of life without interruption
2 to 3 weeks at the outset of mothering
Only the first 48 hours after birth
From weaning until the child’s third birthday
Throughout adolescence as a renewed phase

answer_text: 2 to 3 weeks at the outset of mothering
answer_raw: B. 2 to 3 weeks at the outset of mothering
explanation_text: B is correct: good enough mothering entails a beginning stage of primary maternal preoccupation lasting 2 to 3 weeks; intense attunement then continues for the first few months. A overextends the named preoccupation stage. C is too short. D and E misplace the timing. Teaching point: Primary maternal preoccupation is a brief, intense early phase that launches the holding environment.
clinical_application: When assessing postpartum dyads, ask about the mother’s capacity for early intense preoccupation and subsequent “good enough” (not perfect ongoing) attunement.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: Which set of maternal functions does Winnicott include in the early holding environment?

options.text: Strict frustration of all wishes to promote early reality testing
Protecting the child from discomfort, anticipating needs on the verge of fantasy, mirroring the baby’s existence, and offering a nondemanding presence during rest
Enforcing toilet training and Oedipal prohibitions
Remaining emotionally unavailable so the infant discovers autonomy
Interpreting unconscious conflict from the first weeks of life

answer_text: Protecting the child from discomfort, anticipating needs on the verge of fantasy, mirroring the baby’s existence, and offering a nondemanding presence during rest
answer_raw: B. Protecting the child from discomfort, anticipating needs on the verge of fantasy, mirroring the baby’s existence, and offering a nondemanding presence during rest
explanation_text: B is correct: the mother provides a holding environment protecting from discomfort, anticipates needs as the infant is about to summon them in fantasy, mirrors the baby’s existence, and is a nondemanding presence during rest so spontaneous gestures can emerge. A contradicts early attunement. C is later structural/drive themes. D is the opposite of holding. E is not Winnicott’s early maternal task. Teaching point: Holding, mirroring, and nonintrusive presence create the conditions for omnipotence and true self emergence.
clinical_application: In therapy, aim for a holding stance: contain distress, anticipate needs without intrusion, mirror affect, and allow quiet space for spontaneous material.

explanation_text: B is correct: once the illusion of omnipotence is fostered by near-perfect early attunement, inevitable maternal failures allow the infant to learn about reality. A overpathologizes ordinary failures. C contradicts “good enough” (not perfect forever). D is not the claim in Bienenfeld's account. E is not discussed here. Teaching point: Optimal development needs early near-perfect attunement followed by tolerable disillusionment.
clinical_application: Help parents and supervisees distinguish ordinary, growth-promoting maternal failures from chronic misattunement that buries the true self.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: According to Winnicott in Bienenfeld's account, a false self develops when the mother:

options.text: Protects the omnipotent illusion and remains nondemanding during quiet periods
Does not protect the omnipotent illusion, or intrudes on formless quiet periods with needs of her own
Provides only physical caretaking without any emotional bond
Weans the infant after the first year
Encourages language and motor development

answer_text: Does not protect the omnipotent illusion, or intrudes on formless quiet periods with needs of her own
answer_raw: B. Does not protect the omnipotent illusion, or intrudes on formless quiet periods with needs of her own
explanation_text: B is correct: failure to protect the omnipotent illusion or intrusion with maternal needs yields a false self compliant to parental expectations; the true self is buried because survival still depends on mother. A describes good enough mothering. C is not the mechanism named here. D and E are not the false-self pathway in Bienenfeld's account. Teaching point: Intrusive or nonprotective mothering forces compliance (false self) and burial of the true self.
clinical_application: When a patient is overly compliant and self-defeating, consider early maternal intrusion or failure to protect omnipotence as a false-self adaptation.

options.text: Healthy identification consolidating a true self

answer_raw: B. Pursuit of a false self after lack of good enough mothering
explanation_text: B is correct: Mr. Brown lacked good enough mothering; imitating his father is repair via a false self, with conflict showing as social timidity and professional self-defeat. A is the opposite of the vignette’s reading. C, D, and E are not how the vignette frames the imitation. Teaching point: Compliant imitation of a parent can be false-self repair rather than true-self consolidation.
clinical_application: Ask whether a patient’s professional persona feels like authentic self or compliant imitation adopted to survive early misattunement.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: As object relations become structuralized into the self, Winnicott emphasizes that what becomes more important than the content of maternal gratifications is:

options.text: The quantity of calories and sleep the infant receives
The maternal position, her attitudes, and emotions
The father’s Oedipal prohibitions
The infant’s innate death instinct
Sibling rivalry

answer_text: The maternal position, her attitudes, and emotions
answer_raw: B. The maternal position, her attitudes, and emotions
explanation_text: B is correct: as object needs separate from early drive needs, “The maternal position, her attitudes, and emotions, become more important than the content of her gratifications. Such object relations become structuralized into the self.” A (quantity of calories and sleep) stays at physical provision—the “content of gratifications”—which Winnicott subordinates to maternal attitude and emotion. C (father’s Oedipal prohibitions) is classical triangular structure, not Winnicott’s emphasis on maternal position structuring the self here. D (infant’s innate death instinct) is Kleinian innate aggression/death-instinct language, not Bienenfeld's account’s maternal-attitude claim. E (sibling rivalry) is a peer/family-competition theme not used to explain structuralization of object relations into the self here. Teaching point: quality of maternal relatedness (position, attitudes, emotions), not mere drive gratification content, becomes structuralized into the self.
clinical_application: In history taking, explore how the caregiver felt and positioned herself with the child, not only whether basic needs were met.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: A toddler’s beloved blanket that neither parent nor child questions, occupying a space between illusion and reality, is best classified as:

options.text: A fetish in the Freudian sense
A transitional object
An introject of the bad breast
A false self structure
A superego precursor

answer_text: A transitional object
answer_raw: B. A transitional object
explanation_text: B is correct: growing from omnipotence toward external reality, the child relies on “a transitional object… (often something like a blanket or teddy bear) [that] occupies a vague space between illusion and reality.” Neither child nor parent questions its source or nature; it can mark the beginning of human creativity. A (fetish in the Freudian sense) is a sexualized perverse substitute, not Winnicott’s developmental bridge object. C (introject of the bad breast) is Kleinian part-object language, not the blanket/teddy transitional space described. D (false self structure) is Winnicott’s compliant adaptation when mothering fails to protect omnipotence—not the beloved transitional object. E (superego precursor) is structural-agency language; the transitional object is a creativity/illusion–reality bridge, not a moral agency precursor here. Teaching point: transitional objects sit between omnipotent wish and cold external reality and may inaugurate creativity.
clinical_application: Normalize and protect a child’s transitional object; avoid ridiculing the attachment as mere irrationality.

explanation_text: A is correct: as the first creation of the child’s mind, the transitional object may be the beginning of human creativity. B is too advanced developmentally. C pathologizes a normal phenomenon. D contradicts its intermediate status. E is false; language and motor functions are used alongside it. Teaching point: Creativity begins in the transitional space between wish and reality.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: Although Winnicott professed allegiance to Freud’s model, Bienenfeld notes that he:

options.text: Placed drives at the center of motivation and retained a full id–ego–superego system
Relegated the drives to a marginal position compared with the need for connection and had little use for the structures of id and ego
Denied any role for frustration in development
Argued that aggression is an innate primary drive more powerful than libido

answer_text: Relegated the drives to a marginal position compared with the need for connection and had little use for the structures of id and ego
answer_raw: B. Relegated the drives to a marginal position compared with the need for connection and had little use for the structures of id and ego
explanation_text: B is correct: connection outweighs drives, and id/ego structures are of little use in his model. A restates classical drive theory he marginalizes. C is false; frustration of libido produces aggression. D is Kleinian, not Winnicott. E contradicts his practice with psychotic adults (p. 81). Teaching point: Winnicott is nominally Freudian but functionally a connection-first, structure-light theorist.
clinical_application: When using Winnicottian language in case formulation, prioritize connection and true/false self over classical drive conflicts.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory

A direct result of frustration of libidinal wishes, not a primary drive

Absent in normal development

D and E are unsupported. Teaching point: For Winnicott, libido is primary; aggression is secondary to frustrated connection/libido.

stem: For Winnicott, most psychopathology represents:

answer_text: Developmental arrest where proper parenting would have facilitated true-self emergence, or where parental needs forced elements of the false self
answer_raw: B. Developmental arrest where proper parenting would have facilitated true-self emergence, or where parental needs forced elements of the false self

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: According to Kernberg as summarized here, the ego is born as a product of:

options.text: Innate mature structure present from birth
Introjection of object experiences
Repression of the Oedipus complex alone
Identification with the father’s superego only
Language acquisition in latency

answer_text: Introjection of object experiences
answer_raw: B. Introjection of object experiences
explanation_text: B is correct: “In infancy, there are originally no psychic structures. Perception is a function of a forerunner of the ego. Ego is born as a product of introjection of object experiences.” A (innate mature structure from birth) is closer to Klein’s nearly mature id/ego from birth, not Kernberg’s original absence of structures. C (repression of the Oedipus complex alone) times structure to Oedipal repression; Kernberg roots ego in early introjected object experience. D (identification with the father’s superego only) is classical superego formation via paternal identification, not ego’s birth from object introjection. E (language acquisition in latency) is far later than infancy and not the origin of ego in this model. Teaching point: for Kernberg, ego structure is built from introjected object experience; structures are not present ready-made at birth.
clinical_application: Think of early ego as accumulated introjects of caregivers’ good and bad experiences, not as a preformed Freudian apparatus.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: Developmentally, when splitting becomes untenable, the ego progresses to:

options.text: Ambivalence—holding simultaneous good and bad properties of an object in a single representation
Total foreclosure of all object representations
Exclusive use of projective identification without integration
Return to primary maternal preoccupation
Elimination of all aggressive drive energy

answer_text: Ambivalence—holding simultaneous good and bad properties of an object in a single representation
answer_raw: A. Ambivalence—holding simultaneous good and bad properties of an object in a single representation
explanation_text: A is correct: “Eventually, splitting becomes an untenable process and the ego progresses to ambivalence, holding simultaneous good and bad properties of an object in a single representation” (Figure 5-1). B (total foreclosure of all object representations) is not the stated developmental step after splitting. C (exclusive projective identification without integration) keeps primitive unintegration; Bienenfeld’s progress is toward integrated ambivalence. D (return to primary maternal preoccupation) is Winnicottian maternal state language, not Kernberg’s post-splitting ego achievement. E (elimination of all aggressive drive energy) is not required; ambivalence holds good and bad together, including aggression’s residue. Teaching point: ambivalence—one representation holding good and bad—is the developmental achievement that replaces primitive splitting.
clinical_application: Therapeutic progress in severe personality pathology often shows capacity to hold mixed feelings about the same person rather than all-good/all-bad shifts.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: Bienenfeld states that although Kernberg uses Freudian terms, his model “turns drive theory upside down” because:

options.text: Drives create objects, and the id creates the ego out of free libido
Object relations are primary and exist before structures; experiences create the drives; since affect and splitting are ego functions, the ego creates the id out of repressed drive derivatives
There are no affects in development
Superego is present at birth and generates all object images
Aggression is denied any developmental role

answer_text: Object relations are primary and exist before structures; experiences create the drives; since affect and splitting are ego functions, the ego creates the id out of repressed drive derivatives
answer_raw: B. Object relations are primary and exist before structures; experiences create the drives; since affect and splitting are ego functions, the ego creates the id out of repressed drive derivatives
explanation_text: B is correct: Kernberg “turns drive theory upside down”: “object relations are primary; they exist before any of the structures. Affects flow directly from the nature of the object experiences and are managed primarily by splitting. These experiences actually create the drives. Since affect and splitting are ego functions, the ego creates the id out of repressed drive derivatives.” A restates classical direction (drives create objects; id creates ego from free libido)—the reverse of Kernberg’s inversion. C (no affects in development) contradicts Bienenfeld: affects flow from object experiences and organize the model. D (superego present at birth generating all object images) contradicts original absence of structures and later superego differentiation. E (aggression denied any developmental role) is false; hate/aggression is central (e.g., Ms. Gray’s reservoir of aggressive drive energy). Teaching point: Kernberg inverts Freud—relations and ego processes (affect, splitting) generate drives and id, not vice versa.
clinical_application: Formulate severe pathology from relational-affective history first, then derive drive language—not the reverse.

A (id, ego, and superego only) appears as derived structural outcomes lower in the model, not the basic relational unit itself. C (oral, anal, and phallic stages) is classical Freudian psychosexual staging, not Kernberg’s self–object–affect unit. D (true self, false self, and holding environment) is Winnicott’s vocabulary, not the figure’s basic relational unit. E (separation, individuation, and rapprochement) is Mahler’s separation–individuation sequence, not Kernberg’s unit diagram. deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: In the section “Refinement of the Theories,” object relations theorists are said to range from modest modifications of the drive-structure model by Klein and Mahler to near-complete rejection of that model by:

options.text: Freud and Hartmann

answer_raw: B. Winnicott and Kernberg

C (Sullivan and Fromm only) are interpersonalists of Chapter 4, outside this object-relations continuum comparison. D (Anna Freud and Spitz) are ego-psychology figures (defenses; infant organizers), not the rejection pair. E (Jung and Adler) are early non-object-relations breakaways from Freud, not named in this continuum. Teaching point: place OR theorists on a continuum—Klein/Mahler modify drive-structure modestly; Winnicott/Kernberg nearly reject it.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 5  Object Relations Theory
stem: According to Bienenfeld, increasing complexity and idiosyncrasies of object relations theories contributed to the alternative or parallel development of:

options.text: Classical hypnotism
The school of self psychology
Behaviorism as the only remaining model
Phrenology
Exclusive reliance on drive psychology without interpersonal theory

answer_text: The school of self psychology
answer_raw: B. The school of self psychology
explanation_text: B is correct: complexity and idiosyncrasies that made object-relations theories “inaccessible to many practitioners and epistemologically undesirable to many theorists… contributed to the alternative, or parallel, development of the school of self psychology.” A (classical hypnotism) is pre-analytic technique, not the parallel school named. C (behaviorism as the only remaining model) overstates and misnames the alternative; Bienenfeld names self psychology. D (phrenology) is historical pseudoscience, not a parallel psychodynamic school. E (exclusive reliance on drive psychology without interpersonal theory) is the opposite of the relational turn; the parallel school is self psychology. Teaching point: self psychology is framed as a parallel response to problems left by ego psychology and the complexity of object-relations theories.

stem: Bienenfeld identifies two problems left by ego psychology. The first is that ego psychology was:

options.text: A multi-person field theory with no individual focus
A one-person psychology treating the mind of the individual as a self-contained entity
A purely biological model without psychic structure
Focused only on group therapy technique
Unable to describe any Oedipal conflict

answer_text: A one-person psychology treating the mind of the individual as a self-contained entity
answer_raw: B. A one-person psychology treating the mind of the individual as a self-contained entity
explanation_text: B is correct: Bienenfeld’s first leftover problem of ego psychology is stated in so many words: “it was a one-person psychology, treating the mind of the individual as a self-contained entity.” (A) A multi-person field theory with no individual focus names the interpersonal/Sullivanian field tradition (and later two-person models), which is the opposite of the one-person, self-contained-mind critique this sentence levels at ego psychology. (C) A purely biological model without psychic structure names somatic/reductionist psychiatry; ego psychology is a structural psychology of ego functions, not a biology-only account, so that is not the first problem named here. (D) Focus on group therapy technique names a group-dynamics method (e.g., Bion/group work), not the metapsychological limit Bienenfeld assigns to ego psychology. (E) Inability to describe any Oedipal conflict is false to this paragraph: drive and ego theories are said to address Oedipal-level conflicts; the second problem is patients whose troubles were deeper than those conflicts, not that ego psychology could describe none. Teaching point: When a formulation treats the patient as a closed psychic system, you are still in one-person ego psychology—ask what the other person is doing for the self.
clinical_application: When a formulation ignores how others co-constitute the patient’s mind, notice the residual one-person bias of classical ego psychology.

answer_text: More deep-rooted than the Oedipal-level conflicts addressed by drive and ego theories
answer_raw: B. More deep-rooted than the Oedipal-level conflicts addressed by drive and ego theories
explanation_text: B is correct: The second leftover problem is that, “as its successes accumulated, people availed themselves of analysis whose problems were more deep-rooted than the Oedipal-level conflicts addressed by drive and ego theories.” (A) Simple phobias cured by interpretation alone names a narrow, classical-neurotic picture; the historical shift here is toward deeper, not simpler, pathology. (C) Exclusively medical, non-psychological problems name internist/neurologic caseloads, not the analytic patients Bienenfeld says now presented with pre-Oedipal-depth character trouble. (D) Conflicts confined to childhood with no adult manifestations contradict the scene: adults were seeking analysis for problems that outran Oedipal-level theory. (E) Problems already fully explained by classical drive theory is the opposite of the gap: drive/ego maps were not enough for these deeper-rooted presentations. Teaching point: A high-functioning adult with empty, brittle, or pre-Oedipal character pain is the caseload that pushed theory past ego psychology—do not force an Oedipal-only story.

stem: Object relations theories addressed the two problems left by ego psychology by describing interpersonal dimensions of the psyche and concurrently addressing:

options.text: Only adult Oedipal triangulation without early development
Pre-Oedipal development and serious personality pathology
Pharmacologic algorithms exclusively
Group dynamics without individual mind

answer_text: Pre-Oedipal development and serious personality pathology
answer_raw: B. Pre-Oedipal development and serious personality pathology
explanation_text: B is correct: Object relations “addressed both of these issues, finding principles to describe the interpersonal dimensions of the psyche and concurrently addressing pre-Oedipal development and serious personality pathology.” (A) Only adult Oedipal triangulation without early development restates the drive/ego focus this paragraph says OR theories went beyond, not what they added. (C) Pharmacologic algorithms exclusively name biological-treatment decision trees, which are not how OR answered one-person limits or deeper pathology in Bienenfeld's account. (D) Group dynamics without individual mind names group-process theory, not OR’s account of interpersonal dimensions of the individual psyche. (E) Denial of any caregiver role is the reverse of object-relations thinking, which is built around early others; Bienenfeld's account credits OR with interpersonal and pre-Oedipal reach, not caregiver erasure. Teaching point: Object relations is one answer to ego psychology’s two holes—other people in the mind, and pre-Oedipal/personality-level illness.

(B) The 1930s are when, elsewhere in Bienenfeld, ego psychology is still developing and interpersonal/object-relations schools branch off—not the decade this sentence assigns to the American “very different approach.” (D) The 1990s postdate Kohut’s life and this origin claim; they are too late for the rise Bienenfeld names. Teaching point: Date self psychology as the American 1960s path to the same two problems object relations also tried to solve.

explanation_text: C is correct: Bienenfeld places the self-psychology approach as “a very different approach to the same problems” that “arose in the United States in the 1960s,” not as a European offshoot of Freud, Klein, Lacan, or Jung. (A) Vienna in the 1920s as a direct extension of Freud’s structural model names the birthplace and era of the id–ego–superego map and early ego psychology—the tradition Kohut later left, not Bienenfeld's account’s location of self psychology. (B) London in the 1940s as a Kleinian school names British object relations (Melanie Klein’s wartime/postwar London group), which this paragraph treats as a different solution path from the U.S. 1960s approach. (D) Paris in the 1970s as Lacanian structuralism names Jacques Lacan’s linguistic/structural reading of Freud, a French school this sentence does not invoke. (E) Zurich in the 1910s as Jungian analytical psychology names Carl Jung’s early break and Swiss analytic psychology, historically earlier and theoretically other than the U.S. 1960s turn described here. Teaching point: On a map question, self psychology is Kohut’s American 1960s answer to ego psychology’s limits—not Klein, Lacan, Jung, or a 1920s Viennese extension of structure.

explanation_text: B is correct: Kohut “did not find object relations theory to be a satisfying answer because it was so abstract, seemingly too distant from human experience to be of scientific verifiability or clinical utility.” (A) Ignoring the Oedipus complex entirely is not the stated reason; Bienenfeld's account’s critique is abstraction and distance from experience, not a claim that OR erased Oedipus. stem: Self psychology, as Bienenfeld presents Kohut, rejects drive and structure as artificial constructs. The only structure for which Kohut saw a purpose was which of the following?

options.text: The id
The ego
The superego
The self
The system unconscious

answer_text: The self
answer_raw: D. The self
explanation_text: D is correct: Self psychology “rejects the notions of drive and structure as artificial constructs divorced from experience”; Kohut “saw them as simply unnecessary for a description of the mind. The only structure for which he saw a purpose was the self.” (A) The id is a Freudian structural agency of drive; it is among the structures Kohut set aside as unnecessary here. (B) The ego is Freud’s (and Hartmann’s) executive structure; Bienenfeld's account says self psychology eliminates the ego as the needed structure and keeps the self. (C) The superego is the structural agency of conscience and ideals; it is not the one structure Kohut retained. (E) The system unconscious is a topographic (Ucs/Pcs/Cs) construct, not the single structure this paragraph preserves. Teaching point: Kohut’s model is one-structure: formulate around the self’s cohesion and esteem, not id–ego–superego agencies.

options.text: Selfobjects are id derivatives only

answer_raw: B. The selfobject is not an external person (or an internal representation as in object relations); it is an experience of interaction necessary for nurture and/or maintenance of the self
explanation_text: B is correct: Selfobject experiences are “interactions shared between self and other,” “usually known less clumsily as selfobjects”; “the selfobject of self psychology is not an external person” (and, completing the definition later in Bienenfeld, not an internal representation as in object relations) but “an experience necessary for the nurture and/or maintenance of the self.” Calling mother or husband “the selfobjects” confuses the person with the function. (A) Id derivatives are drive-psychology products of instinct; they are not what Bienenfeld means by selfobject. (C) Existence only in childhood is false to the theory as Bienenfeld's self psychology discussion states it: the need for selfobjects is lifelong (explicit later in Bienenfeld). (D) Equating selfobjects with the classical superego imports Freud’s structural conscience; a selfobject is an experience that maintains the self, not an internalized moral agency. (E) Purely cognitive schemas without affect name CBT-style knowledge structures; selfobjects are felt interactional experiences that nurture or maintain the self, not affectless templates. answer_raw: B. An experience necessary for the nurture and/or maintenance of the self
explanation_text: B is correct: Completing the prior discussion, the selfobject is not “a structure of its own, or even an internal representation of another (as in object relations theory). Rather it is an experience necessary for the nurture and/or maintenance of the self.” (A) A repressed instinctual wish is a Freudian drive-unconscious unit, not Kohut’s selfobject experience. (C) A fixed character trait independent of relationships treats personality as a sealed attribute; selfobject is defined as a relational experience the self needs, not a trait that floats free of others. (D) Hartmann’s autonomous ego function is an ego-psychology idea (conflict-free capacities such as perception); it is not the selfobject definition given here. (E) A defense against oedipal anxiety only is classical structural/defense language aimed at triangular conflict; this sentence defines a lifelong maintenance experience for the self, not an Oedipal defense. stem: Which statement about the need for selfobjects is most accurate in Kohutian self psychology?

options.text: The need ends at the resolution of the Oedipus complex
The need is lifelong; there is no self without selfobjects, and this dynamic network is the selfobject matrix

answer_text: The need is lifelong; there is no self without selfobjects, and this dynamic network is the selfobject matrix
answer_raw: B. The need is lifelong; there is no self without selfobjects, and this dynamic network is the selfobject matrix
explanation_text: B is correct: “The need for selfobjects is a lifelong one. There is no self without selfobjects, and this dynamic network of experience is called the selfobject matrix.” (A) Ending the need at Oedipal resolution is a classical endpoint for childhood sexual conflict, not Kohut’s claim: selfobject need does not expire with the Oedipus complex. (C) Requirement only during acute psychiatric hospitalization shrinks a developmental/clinical necessity to a ward setting Bienenfeld's account never uses. (D) Healthy adults having no selfobject needs contradicts “lifelong” and “no self without selfobjects”; maturity changes sources, not the fact of the need. (E) Pathological-by-definition status reverses self psychology: selfobject need is normal infrastructure of the self, not a diagnosis. Teaching point: Do not pathologize a stable adult’s need for friends, mentors, or partners to feel real—ask whether the sources have matured, not whether the need should have vanished.
clinical_application: Normalize ongoing selfobject needs in adult patients (partners, mentors, vocation, spirituality) while assessing quality and destructiveness.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: Bienenfeld compares Kohut’s move to whose earlier rejection of the need for the structure ego in describing the energy of the self in a world of objects?

options.text: Freud
Hartmann
Winnicott
Adler
Jung

answer_text: Winnicott
answer_raw: C. Winnicott
explanation_text: C is correct: “Much as Winnicott had rejected the need for the structure ego and proceeded to describe the evolution of energy of the self in a world of objects, Kohut elucidated the evolution of the self within the selfobject matrix.” (A) Freud did not reject the structure ego in this comparison; he (and later structural theory) made ego central, and Bienenfeld's account contrasts Kohut with that structural inheritance via a Winnicott parallel. (B) Hartmann defined the self as a representation inside the structure ego (earlier in Bienenfeld); he is the ego psychologist Kohut was expected to succeed, not the one who discarded ego to describe self-in-a-world-of-objects. (D) Alfred Adler’s individual psychology (compensation, social interest, lifestyle) is a different dissent from Freud; he is not the comparison named here. (E) Carl Jung’s analytical psychology (collective unconscious, archetypes) is likewise another school; Bienenfeld’s analogy on this sentence is Winnicott, not Jung. Teaching point: Hear Kohut’s self-in-matrix as cousin to Winnicott’s self-in-facilitating-environment—both drop a standalone ego-structure as the main story.
clinical_application: Link ‘facilitating environment’ language with ‘selfobject matrix’ when teaching across OR and self psychology.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: If the self is the center of mental life, how does self psychology reconceptualize narcissism?

options.text: As only a transitional phase or pathological residue in adult life
As a lifelong focus; theory defines developmental needs that foster healthy narcissism and balances that avoid pathological manifestations
As synonymous with psychosis
As irrelevant once the superego forms
As caused solely by excess libido without developmental context

answer_text: As a lifelong focus; theory defines developmental needs that foster healthy narcissism and balances that avoid pathological manifestations
answer_raw: B. As a lifelong focus; theory defines developmental needs that foster healthy narcissism and balances that avoid pathological manifestations
explanation_text: B is correct: If the self is the center (or entirety) of mental life, “narcissism can no longer be seen as a transitional phase or as a pathological residue in adult life.” Self psychology instead “defines the needs of the developing self that foster healthy narcissism and the balances that must be struck to avoid pathological manifestations.” (A) Transitional phase or pathological residue in adult life is exactly the view this paragraph says self psychology discards. (C) Synonymy with psychosis confuses a severe clinical state with narcissism as a lifelong developmental line; Bienenfeld is reconceptualizing ordinary/healthy narcissistic development, not equating it with psychosis. (D) Irrelevance once the superego forms is structural-theory timing; here narcissism remains a lifelong focus after (and beyond) structural consolidation. (E) Excess libido without developmental context is a classical quantitative-drive explanation; Bienenfeld's account frames narcissism through developmental selfobject needs and balances, not libido surplus alone. Teaching point: Ask whether the patient’s narcissism is a needed line of self-esteem (healthy) or a brittle, unbalanced manifestation—not whether “narcissism” itself is a dirty word.
clinical_application: Do not equate all self-focused material with NPD; assess whether ambition/esteem needs were developmentally supported.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: A child lights up when a parent delights in her achievements, reflecting positively her qualities, capacities, and accomplishments. In Kohut’s terms, this parent is functioning primarily as which of the following?

options.text: An idealizable selfobject fostering the idealized parental imago
A mirroring selfobject fostering emergence of the grandiose self
A classical superego introject
A persecutory object in the paranoid-schizoid position
A transitional object in Winnicott’s strict sense only

answer_text: A mirroring selfobject fostering emergence of the grandiose self
answer_raw: B. A mirroring selfobject fostering emergence of the grandiose self
explanation_text: B is correct: “The presence of a mirroring selfobject (a parent or other vital figure who reflects positively the qualities, capacities, and accomplishments of the self) fosters the emergence of the grandiose self.” Delight that reflects the child’s achievements is mirroring, not idealizing. (A) An idealizable selfobject fostering the idealized parental imago is the other pole: a figure who supplies goals and aims so the child can internalize ideals (“I can be great”), not the gleam that says the child’s qualities are seen. (C) A classical superego introject is Freud’s internalized parental conscience; positive reflection of accomplishments is a selfobject function, not installation of a moral agency. (D) A persecutory object in the paranoid-schizoid position is Melanie Klein’s early split, threatening object; a delighted, reflecting parent is the opposite affective field. (E) A transitional object in Winnicott’s strict sense is the child’s first “not-me” possession (blanket/teddy) that bridges inner and outer; it is not Kohut’s mirroring function described here. Teaching point: When a parent’s face lights up at a child’s feat, label it mirroring—the food of the grandiose self (“I am good”).
clinical_application: When a patient hungers for recognition of achievements, consider a mirroring selfobject need rather than only secondary gain.

stem: Ms. Gray was raised deficient in both mirroring and idealizable selfobjects; she lacks capacities for regulating affect or self-esteem and keeps seeking missing infantile selfobject experiences. The pole that provides goals and aims and yields the idealized parental imago sings which line of Kohut’s duet?

options.text: “I am good”
“I can be great”
“I hate the bad object”
“I must repress the drive”
“I am my ego ideal alone”

answer_text: “I can be great”
answer_raw: B. “I can be great”
explanation_text: B is correct: An idealizable selfobject “provides goals and aims for the developing self” and “fosters the emergence of an internalized figure of ideals and aspirations, the idealized parental imago.” “The two poles sing a duet: ‘I am good’ and ‘I can be great.’” The idealizing pole’s line is “I can be great.” (Ms. Gray lacks both poles and so keeps hunting missing infantile selfobject experiences.) (A) “I am good” is the mirroring/grandiose-self line of the same duet, not the idealizing pole the stem asks for. (C) “I hate the bad object” is Kleinian split-object language, not either line of Kohut’s duet. (D) “I must repress the drive” is classical defense-against-instinct wording, not a bipolar-self lyric in Bienenfeld's account. (E) “I am my ego ideal alone” borrows structural “ego ideal” talk and drops the two-pole duet; Bienenfeld’s pairing is good/great via mirroring plus idealization, not a solo ego-ideal slogan. Teaching point: Idealizing hunger sounds like “I can be great if I can belong to someone admirable”—listen for mentors and heroes, not only for praise.

(B) Elimination of all ideals would collapse the idealizing pole and the arc, the opposite of the creative tension described. (C) Permanent pathological grandiosity is the unbalanced, not the “desirable circumstances,” product of the arc. (D) Abandonment of self-assertive ambitions would drop the mirroring pole’s ambitions box, not refine talents between poles. (E) Fusion of id and superego is structural-model language; the arc is between grandiose and idealizing poles of the self, not id–superego merger. deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: At the most abstract level, what role does empathy play in Kohut’s epistemology of psychoanalysis, according to Bienenfeld?

options.text: It is merely a friendly attitude without scientific status
It defines the field of psychoanalysis—the method by which data about the inner mind are obtained
It replaces all need for interpretation
It is identical to pharmacological response prediction
It is used only in supportive, not exploratory, therapy

answer_text: It defines the field of psychoanalysis—the method by which data about the inner mind are obtained
answer_raw: B. It defines the field of psychoanalysis—the method by which data about the inner mind are obtained
explanation_text: B is correct: “At the most abstract level, empathy defines the field of psychoanalysis.” As epistemologist, Kohut held that “any science is defined by the object of its study and the method by which data is obtained”; for the inner mind, that method is empathic investigation. (A) A merely friendly attitude without scientific status understates the claim: empathy is the defining method of the science, not bedside manner. (C) Replacing all need for interpretation overreaches; this paragraph makes empathy the data-gathering method that defines the field, not a ban on interpretation. (D) Identity with pharmacological response prediction names a psychopharmacology outcome measure, not Kohut’s method for studying the inner mind. (E) Restriction to supportive, not exploratory, therapy is a false split: empathy here is how exploratory analysis obtains its data, not a supportive-only tool. Teaching point: Empathy is how you get psychoanalytic data—temporary entry into the patient’s world—not a substitute for thinking, and not “just being nice.”
clinical_application: Defend empathic immersion as data-gathering, not as soft technique lacking rigor.

stem: Why, in Kohut’s view summarized by Bienenfeld, are the methods of the physical sciences inadequate for psychoanalysis?

options.text: Because psychoanalysis studies only laboratory animals
Because the field of study is the inner workings of the mind, not accessible with instruments or methods suited to external, concrete objects
Because empathy is forbidden in science
Because dreams cannot be remembered
Because patients never free-associate

answer_text: Because the field of study is the inner workings of the mind, not accessible with instruments or methods suited to external, concrete objects
answer_raw: B. Because the field of study is the inner workings of the mind, not accessible with instruments or methods suited to external, concrete objects
explanation_text: B is correct: Physical sciences study “external and concrete” objects with observational methods; “in psychoanalysis, the field of study is the inner workings of the mind, which are not accessible with the instruments or methods of the physical sciences.” (A) Studying only laboratory animals is not Kohut’s reason; the inadequacy is about access to inner mental life, not a claim that analysis is animal research. (C) Empathy being forbidden in science contradicts Bienenfeld: empathy is the scientific method proper to this object of study. (D) Dreams that cannot be remembered are a clinical inconvenience, not the epistemological argument given. (E) Patients who never free-associate misstate technique and are not why physical-science methods fail here. Teaching point: You cannot weigh a feeling on a scale; to study the inside of a mind you have to dwell in it briefly, then step back.
clinical_application: When supervisors demand only behavioral data, note that self psychology prioritizes experience-near subjective data as scientific for its object of study.

options.text: Permanently merging identities with the patient
Transiently placing himself or herself inside the subject’s experience
Administering structured psychometric batteries only
Observing only facial microexpressions without subjective inquiry

answer_text: Transiently placing himself or herself inside the subject’s experience
answer_raw: B. Transiently placing himself or herself inside the subject’s experience
explanation_text: B is correct: “The field of observation is defined by the analyst’s investigation of the subjective experience of the analysand through transiently placing himself or herself inside the subject’s experience.” (A) Permanently merging identities is pathological fusion, not the transient placement named; later in Bienenfeld stresses entering the patient’s world without losing one’s own identity. (C) Administering structured psychometric batteries only is a testing/assessment method, not Kohut’s empathic definition of the analytic field. (D) Observing only facial microexpressions without subjective inquiry is external, concrete observation of the physical-science type this paragraph says cannot reach inner experience. (E) Interpreting solely from countertransference dreams makes the analyst’s night life the data source; the method here is transient indwelling in the analysand’s experience. Teaching point: Empathic immersion is a visit, not a merger—go in, grasp the feel, come back as yourself.

answer_raw: B. Without losing his or her own identity and objectivity
explanation_text: B is correct: Empathy is “the tool for acquiring data,” “the means by which the psychotherapist enters into the world of the patient without losing his or her own identity and objectivity.” (A) Permanently adopting the patient’s identity is loss of the very identity and objectivity the sentence requires. (C) Avoiding any emotional resonance denies the entering-the-world half of the method; empathy is not sterile detachment. (D) Relying only on projective identification names a Kleinian/Bionian mechanism of putting parts into the other; it is not Bienenfeld’s definition of empathic data-gathering. (E) Disclosing all personal history is a technical choice about therapist transparency, not how empathy is defined as a data tool here. Teaching point: Stay porous enough to feel the patient’s world and boundaried enough to keep your own—that pair is the working definition of clinical empathy.

(B) All self-report questionnaires name paper-and-pencil assessment, not the comparison drawn on this sentence. (C) Only dream reports are a classical royal-road data type, not what empathy is said to outrank here. (D) Genetic history alone is a pedigree/biological data source, outside this contrast. (E) Neurologic examination findings are physical-exam data; Bienenfeld’s contrast is facial expression, spoken content, and the “anyone would feel” inference. explanation_text: A is correct: “At the most functional level, empathy serves a sustaining function. In the therapeutic setting, it provides implicit affirmation and mirroring. answer_raw: B. Because to provide selfobject needs, the other person must have some empathic sense of what those needs are
explanation_text: B is correct: Although defined mainly in therapy, empathy “serves an irreplaceable function in normal development. In order to provide selfobject needs, the other person must have some empathic sense of what those needs are.” (A) Inability to measure drives is a drive-theory measurement problem, not why empathy is irreplaceable for development in Bienenfeld's account. (C) Children forming no attachments otherwise names a Bowlby-style attachment-failure claim; this sentence is about sensing which selfobject needs to provide, not denying attachment as such. (D) Only fathers can mirror is a false sex restriction; Bienenfeld’s developmental example is the empathic mother sensing distress, not a father-only mirroring rule. (E) Empathy replacing nutrition confuses a psychological function with feeding; empathic sustenance is attuned response, not calories. deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: A mother waits for her infant to cry, then experiments with feeding, diapering, and cuddling because she cannot guess the source of distress. From a self-psychology view in Bienenfeld's account, she fails primarily to provide which of the following?

options.text: Classical drive interpretation
Empathic sustenance of the kind an ideally attuned mother provides by sensing distress early and specifically
Oedipal prohibition
Behavioral extinction of crying
Pharmacologic sedation

answer_text: Empathic sustenance of the kind an ideally attuned mother provides by sensing distress early and specifically
answer_raw: B. Empathic sustenance of the kind an ideally attuned mother provides by sensing distress early and specifically
explanation_text: B is correct: The ideal empathic mother “is in tune with her child closely enough that she can sense the source of the infant’s distress early and specifically and will respond to it without delay.” A mother who waits for crying and then trial-and-errors feeding, diapers, and cuddling “fails to provide such empathic sustenance.” (A) Classical drive interpretation is an adult verbal technique, not the infant-care failure this vignette names. (C) Oedipal prohibition is a later triangular limit, not what the delayed, guessing caregiver fails to give. (D) Behavioral extinction of crying is a learning-theory tactic (ignore to extinguish); the critique here is missed specific attunement, not failed extinction. (E) Pharmacologic sedation is a medication response, not the developmental function at issue. Teaching point: Trial-and-error soothing after a wail is not the same as sensing the need early—specificity and timing are the empathic part.
clinical_application: In adult patients, chronic ‘no one gets what I need until I explode’ often echoes early failures of specific empathic attunement.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: Although purists of both schools may reject the comparison, Bienenfeld finds a striking similarity between Kohut’s ideally empathic selfobject and which of Winnicott’s concepts?

options.text: The true self exclusively as pathology
The “good enough mother”
The antisocial tendency as cure
Hate in the countertransference as the only tool
The capacity to be alone as irrelevant

answer_text: The “good enough mother”
answer_raw: B. The “good enough mother”
explanation_text: B is correct: “While purists of both the object relations and self psychology schools reject the comparison, the similarity of Kohut’s ideally empathic selfobject and Winnicott’s ‘good enough mother’ are striking.” (A) The true self exclusively as pathology misuses Winnicott: the true self is the healthy, spontaneous core, not a disease label, and it is not the comparison drawn here. (C) The antisocial tendency as cure misreads Winnicott’s idea of the antisocial tendency as a signal of hope/need, not as a therapeutic method, and it is not the parallel Bienenfeld names. (D) Hate in the countertransference as the only tool names another Winnicott essay; useful clinically, but not the concept paired with Kohut’s empathic selfobject in Bienenfeld's account. (E) The capacity to be alone as irrelevant again names a real Winnicott achievement and then denies it; it is not the comparison made here. Teaching point: Good-enough, reliably attuned caregiving—not perfection—is the shared clinical ideal across Winnicott and Kohut.
clinical_application: Bridge OR and self-psychology language in case conference: good-enough mothering ≈ empathic selfobject provision.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: In an environment marked by a preponderance of empathic attunement, occasional inevitable failures of empathy constitute optimal frustration and force the developing self to absorb selfobject functions via which process?

options.text: Projective identification
Transmuting internalization
Repression proper
Classical castration
Stimulus barrier rupture only

answer_text: Transmuting internalization
answer_raw: B. Transmuting internalization
explanation_text: B is correct: No selfobject is always perfectly in tune; in a mostly attuned environment, occasional empathic failures “constitute optimal frustration and force the developing self to absorb selfobject functions into the self, a process called transmuting internalization.” (A) Projective identification is Klein/Bion’s unconscious putting of parts into another; it is not the internalization process named after optimal frustration. (C) Repression proper is Freud’s defense of pushing conflictual content out of awareness, not absorption of selfobject functions into the self. (D) Classical castration is an Oedipal threat/fantasy, not the mechanism that internalizes soothing and mirroring after small misses. (E) Stimulus-barrier rupture only evokes Freud’s Reizschutz (protective shield) being breached; it is not Kohut’s transmuting internalization. Teaching point: Small, survivable misses in an otherwise attuned therapy can become structure—do not rush to perfect attunement or to catastrophic blame for every empathic lapse.
clinical_application: Brief, nontraumatic empathic failures in therapy can be worked through as optimal frustrations that build structure—if the background attunement is good.

stem: In the age of the Freudian Oedipal period, self psychology describes the child’s selfobject needs as including which of the following?

options.text: Nonseductive confirmation of sexual identity by the opposite-sex parent and nonaggressive acceptance of competitive strivings by the same-sex parent
Complete abstinence from any parental admiration
Exclusive peer mirroring with no parental role
Only art and spirituality as selfobject sources
De-idealization of peers only

answer_text: Nonseductive confirmation of sexual identity by the opposite-sex parent and nonaggressive acceptance of competitive strivings by the same-sex parent
answer_raw: A. Nonseductive confirmation of sexual identity by the opposite-sex parent and nonaggressive acceptance of competitive strivings by the same-sex parent
explanation_text: A is the Oedipal-period selfobject need. B is wrong. C is more adolescent. D is middle age. E misplaces de-idealization. Teaching point: self psychology reinterprets Oedipal needs as selfobject functions, not only drive conflict.
clinical_application: Ask whether same-sex parent could tolerate competition without crushing the child, and whether opposite-sex parent confirmed identity without seduction.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: During latency, children often use teachers and sports figures as selfobjects primarily for which purpose?

options.text: Models for imitation outside the family circle
Targets for oedipal sexual aims
Sources of pharmacologic advice
Replacements for all peer relationships
Permanent idealized parental imagos that never change

answer_text: Models for imitation outside the family circle
answer_raw: A. Models for imitation outside the family circle
explanation_text: A is correct: “In the latency years, the child needs selfobjects as models for imitation outside the family circle; he or she often uses teachers and sports figures for this purpose.” (B) Targets for oedipal sexual aims belong to the Freudian Oedipal period, which Bienenfeld's account separately describes as needing nonseductive confirmation of sexual identity and nonaggressive acceptance of competitive strivings—not what latency teachers/sports figures are for. (C) Sources of pharmacologic advice name a medical role, not a latency selfobject function. (D) Replacements for all peer relationships overshoot: these figures are extrafamilial models for imitation, not a wipeout of peers (peers become central in the next, adolescent, sentence). (E) Permanent idealized parental imagos that never change contradict the next developmental move: adolescence de-idealizes early (parental) selfobjects. Teaching point: Latency selfobjects migrate outside the house—coaches and teachers as models, not as Oedipal objects.
clinical_application: A child’s intense coach idealization can be developmentally expectable selfobject use, not only pathology.

Permanently freezes idealization of parents without peer involvement
Abandons all selfobject needs forever
Returns exclusively to infantile oral needs only
Seeks only art and spirituality as selfobjects

answer_raw: A. De-idealizes them and turns to peers for more mature versions of these functions
explanation_text: A is the adolescent pattern. B freezes development. C is false. D is drive regression language. E is middle-age pattern. Teaching point: adolescent peer intensity can be selfobject reorganization, not only oppositionality.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: According to Bienenfeld’s lifespan sketch, middle-aged adults typically turn to more abstract and transcendent sources of selfobject fulfillment such as which of the following?

options.text: Art and spirituality
Only sports figures as in latency
Exclusive infantile mirroring without abstraction
Pharmacologic self-treatment alone
Complete isolation from all meaning systems

answer_text: Art and spirituality
answer_raw: A. Art and spirituality
explanation_text: A is correct: “In middle age, people typically turn to more abstract and transcendent sources of selfobject fulfillment such as art and spirituality.” (Late life then shifts to equanimity and acceptance of mortality.) (B) Only sports figures as in latency freezes the selfobject source at the school-age model-for-imitation stage Bienenfeld's account has already left behind. (C) Exclusive infantile mirroring without abstraction denies the midlife move toward abstract/transcendent sources. (D) Pharmacologic self-treatment alone is a medication/self-medication frame, not the art-and-spirituality turn named here. (E) Complete isolation from all meaning systems is the opposite of seeking transcendent sources of fulfillment. Teaching point: Midlife “I need something larger than praise” (art, faith, vocation) is a mature selfobject shift, not automatically emptiness or religiosity-as-defense.
clinical_application: In midlife depression workups, explore loss of art/spiritual selfobject sources, not only interpersonal ones.

bienenfeld.quote: In middle age, people typically turn to more abstract and transcendent sources of selfobject fulfillment such as art and spirituality. In late life, the task of acceptance of one's mortality comes to the fore and selfobject needs are focused on equanimity and acceptance.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: A cohesive self is defined as a self with a sense of constancy and internal reliability. Self-fragmentation, the opposite pole, is described as which of the following?

options.text: A sense of emptiness and a feeling that one’s self-experiences do not fit together
A permanent cure state
Only a DSM sleep disorder
Successful sublimation of all drives
The same as the healthy adult self

answer_text: A sense of emptiness and a feeling that one’s self-experiences do not fit together
answer_raw: A. A sense of emptiness and a feeling that one’s self-experiences do not fit together
explanation_text: A is correct: A cohesive self has “a sense of constancy and internal reliability.” “At the opposite pole from self-cohesion is self-fragmentation, a sense of emptiness, a feeling that one’s self-experiences do not fit together.” (B) A permanent cure state is not fragmentation; cohesion/fragmentation are poles on a continuum, never complete, not a finished “cured” condition. (C) Only a DSM sleep disorder shrinks fragmentation to a single Axis-I-style syndrome Bienenfeld's account does not use. (D) Successful sublimation of all drives is an ego-psychological defense ideal, not the definition of fragmentation. (E) Sameness with the healthy adult self is false: emptiness and disjointed self-experience are the opposite pole from cohesion, not Kohut’s healthy-adult list. Teaching point: “I feel empty and like the pieces of me don’t go together” is fragmentation language—use it in formulation when the complaint is incoherence, not only conflict.
clinical_application: Ask patients whether experiences ‘hold together’ or feel empty and discontinuous after slights or losses.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 95.

bienenfeld.quote: If all the ingredients are present and their integration is successful, the result is a cohesive self, i.e., a self with a sense of constancy and internal reliability. At the opposite pole from self-cohesion is self-fragmentation, a sense of emptiness, a feeling that one's self-experiences do not fit together.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: Cohesion and fragmentation form a continuum of states. Which clinical illustration does Bienenfeld give of a generally fragmented self cohering transiently?

options.text: An individual with a serious personality disorder managing an emergency successfully because there is no other option
A fully analyzed person with no residual needs
A child before any selfobject experience
Only patients with pure Oedipal neurosis in free association
Anyone who takes a stimulant medication

answer_text: An individual with a serious personality disorder managing an emergency successfully because there is no other option
answer_raw: A. An individual with a serious personality disorder managing an emergency successfully because there is no other option
explanation_text: A is correct: Cohesion and fragmentation are a continuum and also transient states. A generally cohesive self may fragment under extreme trauma; “less obviously, a generally fragmented self can cohere transiently, as when an individual with a serious personality disorder is able to manage an emergency successfully because there is no other option.” (B) A fully analyzed person with no residual needs contradicts both lifelong selfobject need and the claim that cohesion is never complete. (C) A child before any selfobject experience is not the illustration; the example is an adult with serious personality disorder under emergency demand. (D) Only patients with pure Oedipal neurosis in free association names a classical-neurotic treatment scene, not the PD-in-crisis example. (E) Anyone who takes a stimulant medication invents a pharmacologic cause of transient cohesiin Bienenfeld's account does not give. Teaching point: Cohesion is state as well as trait—a chaotic patient who organizes in a code or a trauma can look “suddenly well”; do not rewrite the baseline personality from one crisis hour.
clinical_application: Do not over-read crisis competence as cured personality structure; temporary cohesion under constraint is expected.

context: Continuum and transient states of cohesion/fragmentation.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 95.

bienenfeld.quote: Less obviously, a generally fragmented self can cohere transiently, as when an individual with a serious personality disorder is able to manage an emergency successfully because there is no other option.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: As previewed for Chapter 7, all psychopathology is seen as products of fragmentation of the self. How does Bienenfeld distinguish chronic versus strain-related clinical pictures, and what does therapy require?

options.text: Chronic fragmentation → personality disorders; cohesive self fragmenting under strain → neurotic symptoms/syndromes; therapy provides empathic attunement, attends to optimal frustration, interprets selfobject needs, enhances cohesiveness
Chronic fragmentation → only brief adjustment disorders; strain → only schizophrenia
All psychopathology is drive conflict; empathy is irrelevant
Personality disorders never involve the self
Therapy consists solely of behavioral activation

answer_text: Chronic fragmentation → personality disorders; cohesive self fragmenting under strain → neurotic symptoms/syndromes; therapy provides empathic attunement, attends to optimal frustration, interprets selfobject needs, enhances cohesiveness
answer_raw: A. Chronic fragmentation → personality disorders; cohesive self fragmenting under strain → neurotic symptoms/syndromes; therapy provides empathic attunement, attends to optimal frustration, interprets selfobject needs, enhances cohesiveness
explanation_text: A is correct: “All psychopathology is seen as products of the fragmentation of the self. A chronically fragmented self is manifest in one of the disorders of personality. A cohesive self that fragments under strain exhibits any of the range of specific psychopathological symptoms and syndromes previously characterized as neuroses.” Therapy “consists of providing empathic attunement, paying attention to the inevitable moments of optimal frustration, interpreting the selfobject needs, and thereby enhancing the cohesiveness of the self.” (B) Mapping chronic fragmentation only to brief adjustment disorders and strain only to schizophrenia scrambles both chronicity and syndrome type; Bienenfeld maps chronic → personality disorders, strain of a cohesive self → neurotic-range symptoms. (C) All psychopathology as drive conflict with empathy irrelevant is classical drive theory plus a denial of the treatment method this paragraph requires. (D) Personality disorders never involving the self contradicts the chronic-fragmentation = personality-disorder equation. (E) Therapy as solely behavioral activation is a CBT/behavioral depression technique, not empathic attunement plus interpretation of selfobject needs. Teaching point: Ask first whether the self is chronically in pieces (personality-level) or usually held together and now cracking (symptom-level)—then treat with attunement, bearable misses, and naming of selfobject needs.
clinical_application: For personality pathology, plan long-term work on self-cohesion; for symptomatic neuroses in a usually cohesive person, address strain-induced fragmentation.
video_query: psychodynamic self psychology psychopathology fragmentation treatment
context: Pathology and therapy summary at end of chapter theory.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 95.

bienenfeld.quote: As will be described in Chapter 7, all psychopathology is seen as products of the fragmentation of the self. A chronically fragmented self is manifest in one of the disorders of personality. A cohesive self that fragments under strain exhibits any of the range of specific psychopathological symptoms and syndromes previously characterized as neuroses. The therapy of these disorders, by necessity, consists of providing empathic attunement, paying attention to the inevitable moments of optimal frustration, interpreting the selfobject needs, and thereby enhancing the cohesiveness of the self.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: Which learning point correctly states Kohut’s stance on classical drive and structural theory?

options.text: He expanded the id–ego–superego model with a fourth agency, the selfobject
He rejected the drives and the structures of the earlier psychologies and described in detail the single structure of the self
He held that only the superego matters clinically
He restored the topographic model as the sole map of mind
He rejected any notion of structure, including the self

answer_text: He rejected the drives and the structures of the earlier psychologies and described in detail the single structure of the self
answer_raw: B. He rejected the drives and the structures of the earlier psychologies and described in detail the single structure of the self
explanation_text: B is correct: Learning point 1: “Heinz Kohut rejected the drives and the structures of the earlier psychologies and described in detail the single structure of the self.” (A) Expanding id–ego–superego with a fourth agency, the selfobject, invents a structural add-on; selfobjects are experiences, not a new agency, and Kohut rejected the earlier structures rather than extending them. (C) Only the superego matters clinically is a one-agency distortion of structural theory, not Kohut’s single-structure-of-the-self stance. (D) Restoring the topographic model (Ucs/Pcs/Cs) as the sole map revives Freud’s systems of consciousness, which this learning point does not do. (E) Rejecting any notion of structure, including the self, overshoots: he rejected earlier structures but kept and detailed the self as the one needed structure. Teaching point: Do not add “selfobject” as a fourth box beside id/ego/superego—Kohut replaced that apparatus with the self.
clinical_application: In formulation, lead with self cohesion and selfobject need rather than defaulting to id–ego–superego conflict when using this model.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: Between the self’s two poles of grandiosity and idealization lies which of the following, according to the learning points?

options.text: A repression barrier of forbidden wishes
A tension arc of innate talents and capacities
The death instinct
Only the Oedipus complex
The collective unconscious

answer_text: A tension arc of innate talents and capacities
answer_raw: B. A tension arc of innate talents and capacities
explanation_text: B is correct: Learning point 2: “Between the self’s two poles of grandiosity and idealization lies a tension arc of innate talents and capacities.” (A) A repression barrier of forbidden wishes is the topographic/structural barrier between unconscious wish and awareness, not the arc between grandiose and idealizing poles. (C) The death instinct is Freud’s later dual-drive (and Kleinian) aggressive/thanatic force, not what occupies the space between Kohut’s poles. (D) Only the Oedipus complex names the classical triangular conflict; the learning point’s in-between is talents/capacities in the tension arc. (E) The collective unconscious is Jung’s transpersonal psyche, not the bipolar-self arc. Teaching point: Talents live in the stretch between ambition and ideals—when either pole is missing, skills fail to refine.
clinical_application: Identify undeveloped talents when ambitions and ideals are both present but unexpressed.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 6  Self Psychology
stem: The self has a lifelong need for selfobject experiences that contribute to a sense of which of the following?

options.text: Permanence, identity, reliability, and self-esteem
Only instinctual discharge
Freedom from all relationships
Permanent pathological grandiosity
Elimination of ideals

answer_text: Permanence, identity, reliability, and self-esteem
answer_raw: A. Permanence, identity, reliability, and self-esteem
explanation_text: A is correct: Learning point 3: “The self has a lifelong need for selfobject experiences that contribute to a sense of permanence, identity, reliability, and self-esteem.” (B) Only instinctual discharge is Freudian drive economics (reduce tension), not the permanence/identity/reliability/esteem functions named. (C) Freedom from all relationships contradicts lifelong need for selfobject experiences, which are inherently relational. (D) Permanent pathological grandiosity is an unbalanced pole, not what healthy selfobject experiences are said to contribute. (E) Elimination of ideals would gut the idealizing pole; the learning point is about sustaining identity and esteem, not deleting ideals. Teaching point: Track whether relationships are actually lending the patient a felt “I persist, I am who I am, I can count on me, I am worth something.”
clinical_application: Assess whether current relationships supply permanence/identity/reliability/esteem functions or chronically fail them.
