stem: Psychopathology, in Bienenfeld’s self-psychology learning-point summary, is the manifestation of fragmentation of the self in which patterns?

options.text: Chronically in personality disorders or transiently in symptoms and syndromes
Only as conversion symptoms
Never in personality disorders
Only as medication side effects
Exclusively as Oedipal dreams

answer_text: Chronically in personality disorders or transiently in symptoms and syndromes
answer_raw: A. Chronically in personality disorders or transiently in symptoms and syndromes
explanation_text: A is correct: Learning point 4: “Psychopathology is the manifestation of fragmentation of the self, either chronically in personality disorders or transiently in symptoms and syndromes.” (B) Only as conversion symptoms narrows fragmentation to one classical hysterical form; the point is a general mechanism with two time courses. (C) Never in personality disorders reverses the chronic-arm mapping. (D) Only as medication side effects is a pharmacologic adverse-effect frame, not self-fragmentation. (E) Exclusively as Oedipal dreams confines pathology to a classical dream content, not chronic vs transient fragmentation. Teaching point: Same engine (fragmentation), two faces—enduring personality disorder versus time-limited symptoms when a cohesive self strains.
clinical_application: Separate trait-like chronic fragmentation (personality) from state fragmentation under stress (symptoms).

answer_raw: B. Each scheme describes a complicated system with multiple opportunities for processes to go awry
explanation_text:
B is correct: After noting that preceding chapters outlined the major philosophies of the structures and functions of the mind and their normal development, Bienenfeld emphasizes that “each scheme describes a complicated system with multiple opportunities for processes to go awry.”
(A) Claiming each scheme is so simple that pathology is rare reverses the sentence: complexity multiplies chances for derailment.
(C) The opening does not say schemes abandon developmental thinking; it just finished saying they describe normal development as well as structure and function.
(D) Restricting each scheme to psychosis only is not Bienenfeld's account’s claim; the learning objectives cover anxiety, emotional and behavioral pathology, and affective disorders across theories.
(E) The four schemes previewed (drive, ego psychology, object relations, self psychology) do not reject unconscious process; that rejection is not stated here.

Each school’s view of normal development and function is intimately linked to its view of how things go amiss
Pathology is explained only by genetics, independent of development

answer_raw: B. Each school’s view of normal development and function is intimately linked to its view of how things go amiss

B is correct: Because the major psychologies were derived from clinical practice, each school takes its own approach to the genesis and nature of psychopathology, and “each school’s view of normal development and function is intimately linked to its view of how things go amiss.”
(A) Treating normal development and pathology as unrelated contradicts the intimate-link sentence in Bienenfeld's account.
(C) Explaining pathology only by genetics, independent of development, is a biological-reduction claim this opening does not make; the link is developmental and functional within each school.
(D) Ignoring normal development once symptoms appear is the opposite of the stated intimate link between how things develop/function and how they go amiss.
(E) Restricting the development–pathology link to self psychology alone is false here: the claim is general for each school, not Kohut’s self psychology only (that school is one later objective, not the sole linker).

stem: In clinical practice and the theories that underlie it, how does Bienenfeld say emotions are considered relative to psychopathology?

options.text: Emotions are irrelevant to psychodynamic theory
Emotions are a special case of psychopathology, stemming from the same roots as disorders of thought, perception, and behavior
Emotions are purely biological and outside theory
Emotions exist only as conscious choices
Emotions are always secondary to cognitive schemas alone

answer_text: Emotions are a special case of psychopathology, stemming from the same roots as disorders of thought, perception, and behavior
answer_raw: B. Emotions are a special case of psychopathology, stemming from the same roots as disorders of thought, perception, and behavior
explanation_text:
B is correct: Emotions “color our individual worlds” as a vital part of normal mental life, but “in clinical practice, however, and in the theories that underlie it, emotions are considered a special case of psychopathology, stemming from the same roots as disorders of thought, perception, and behavior.”
(A) Calling emotions irrelevant to psychodynamic theory contradicts both their place in normal mental life and their inclusion in the psychopathology review.
(C) Treating emotions as purely biological and outside theory is not Bienenfeld's account’s stance; they are brought inside each theory’s view of emotional states.
(D) Emotions as only conscious choices deny the clinical-theory treatment of affect as sharing roots with thought, perception, and behavior disorders (including unconscious process in these schools).
(E) Making emotions always secondary to cognitive schemas alone is a cognitive-therapy frame (Beck-style), not Bienenfeld’s claim that affect shares the same roots as other psychopathologic domains.
Teaching point: Review affect inside each theory’s psychopathology, not as a separate nonpathological category in clinical theory.

Transference only
Working through

answer_raw: B. Mood, or emotion
explanation_text:
B is correct: Bienenfeld notes that “most of the literature uses the term ‘affect’ to describe what is more precisely identified as ‘mood,’ or, in everyday language, ‘emotion.’”
(A) Defense is an ego operation that manages impulse and affect; it is not the everyday referent the literature’s “affect” is said to name.
(C) Transference is the displacement of past object ties onto the clinician (a later clinical concept), not the mood/emotion “affect” is standing in for here.
(D) Working through is a treatment process of repeating and metabolizing conflict, not the everyday concept “affect” labels.
(E) Free association is Freud’s technical instruction to say whatever comes; it is method, not the mood/emotion named as “affect.”
Teaching point: In this literature, “affect” often means mood or emotion broadly—not a defense or a technique.

stem: From about 1885 to 1897, the topographic model of drive psychology focused on the so-called “actual neuroses.” Which pair does Bienenfeld name as the actual neuroses?

options.text: Hysteria and obsessional neurosis
Neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses
Paranoia and melancholia
Phobia and conversion disorder only
Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder

answer_text: Neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses
answer_raw: B. Neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses
explanation_text:
B is correct: From about 1885 to 1897 the topographic model focused on the so-called “actual neuroses,” “namely neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses.”
(A) Hysteria and obsessional neurosis belong with the later defense neuropsychoses / conflict model (page 99), not the 1885–1897 actual-neuroses pair.
(C) Paranoia and melancholia are later drive-structural applications on pages 101–103, not the actual-neuroses pair named here.
(D) Phobia and conversion are later symbolic/conflict presentations (defense neuropsychoses), not this early pair.
(E) Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are later descriptive psychiatric diagnoses; they are not the actual neuroses of this topographic scheme.
Teaching point: Early drive theory’s “actual neuroses” were neurasthenia and anxiety neurosis—direct products of sexual practice in predisposed persons—not later conflict neuroses.
clinical_application: Historically, actual neuroses were linked to sexual practices rather than repressed conflict—do not confuse with modern DSM categories.

stem: In the early “actual neuroses” model, excessive masturbation or nocturnal emissions were said to yield neurasthenia. Which symptom cluster does Bienenfeld attribute to neurasthenia?

options.text: Persistent anxiety punctuated by anxiety attacks only
Lassitude, fatigue, and somatic symptoms such as headache and dyspepsia
Fixed delusions of persecution
Manic elation and grandiosity
Selective mutism

answer_text: Lassitude, fatigue, and somatic symptoms such as headache and dyspepsia
answer_raw: B. Lassitude, fatigue, and somatic symptoms such as headache and dyspepsia
explanation_text:
B is correct: In individuals “tendered neuropathic by congenital or hereditary predisposition,” “excessive masturbation or nocturnal emissions yielded neurasthenia, a condition marked by lassitude, fatigue, and somatic symptoms such as headache and dyspepsia.”
(A) Persistent anxiety punctuated by anxiety attacks is Bienenfeld's account’s picture of anxiety neuroses, not neurasthenia.
(C) Fixed delusions of persecution belong to the later paranoia application (Daniel S., pages 101–102), not neurasthenia’s depletion-somatic cluster.
(D) Manic elation and grandiosity are not the lassitude/fatigue/headache/dyspepsia picture given for neurasthenia.
(E) Selective mutism is not among the somatic/fatigue signs listed for this actual neurosis.
Teaching point: In the actual-neuroses model, neurasthenia is a depletion-type somatic picture from excess discharge; do not confuse it with anxiety neurosis’s attacks.

stem: In the same early model, sexual frustration or sexual activity that did not result in gratification was said to produce anxiety neuroses. How were these neuroses marked?

By persistent anxiety punctuated by anxiety attacks

B is correct: “Sexual frustration or sexual activity that did not result in gratification produced anxiety neuroses, marked by persistent anxiety punctuated by anxiety attacks.”
(A) Conversion paralysis is hysteria/conversion territory in the later conflict formula (page 99), not this actual anxiety-neurosis marking.
(C) Euphoria and flight of ideas describe a manic picture, not persistent anxiety with attacks.
(D) Exclusive auditory hallucinations are a psychotic symptom cluster Bienenfeld's account does not assign to actual anxiety neuroses.

stem: The “dammed-up libido” model was modified as analysts attended more to the drives. In the second model (about 1897 to 1923), which statement is correct according to Bienenfeld?

options.text: Energy was the domain of the affect itself, not the drives
Emotions were considered drive derivatives, and psychopathology resulted from conflicts originating from the drives
Hysteria was abandoned as clinically irrelevant
Emotions were purely conscious and nonconflictual
Only hereditary predisposition explained all symptoms

answer_text: Emotions were considered drive derivatives, and psychopathology resulted from conflicts originating from the drives
answer_raw: B. Emotions were considered drive derivatives, and psychopathology resulted from conflicts originating from the drives
explanation_text:
B is correct: The “dammed-up libido” model lacked explanatory capacity; in the second model (about 1897 to 1923), “energy was the domain of the drives, not of the affect itself. Emotions were now considered to be drive derivatives, and psychopathology was the result of conflicts originating from the drives,” with the classical formulation of hysteria as bedrock.
(A) Reverses the energy claim: energy belonged to the drives, not to the affect itself.
(C) Hysteria was not abandoned; Bienenfeld says its classical formulation “formed the bedrock of psychoanalytic explanation of behavioral pathology.”
(D) Emotions as purely conscious and nonconflictual contradicts both drive-derivative status and conflict-origin pathology.
(E) Hereditary predisposition figured in the earlier actual-neuroses model; this second model centers drive conflict, not heredity alone as the explanation of all symptoms.
Teaching point: Affect shifts from a direct product of sexual practice (actual neuroses) to a derivative of conflicted drives (1897–1923).

stem: Freud and Josef Breuer examined patients with “hysteria.” How does Bienenfeld define those symptoms?

options.text: Delusions with clear neurologic lesions
Symptoms of muscular or sensory impairment not traceable to any somatic cause
Only primary process dream content
Manic flight without sensory change
Purely voluntary malingering

answer_text: Symptoms of muscular or sensory impairment not traceable to any somatic cause
answer_raw: B. Symptoms of muscular or sensory impairment not traceable to any somatic cause
explanation_text:
B is correct: Freud and Josef Breuer examined and treated patients with “hysteria,” defined as “symptoms of muscular or sensory impairment not traceable to any somatic cause.”
(A) Delusions plus clear neurologic lesions mix a psychotic sign with an organic lesion; hysteria here is impairment without a traceable somatic cause.
(C) Primary-process dream content is topographic dream language (Chapter 1), not the definition of hysterical muscular/sensory symptoms in Bienenfeld's account.
(D) Manic flight without sensory change is a mood-disorder picture, not muscular or sensory impairment without somatic cause.
(E) Purely voluntary malingering implies conscious faking; the formula that follows is unconscious suppression of conflicted emotion, not willful feigning.
Teaching point: Classical hysteria in Bienenfeld's account is conversion-type muscular or sensory impairment without an organic explanation.
clinical_application: In formulation, conversion-like symptoms invite inquiry into symbolic representation of conflicted emotion, as in the Breuer–Freud cases.

stem: Drawing on the work of which Paris clinicians did Freud and Breuer first hypnotize hysterical patients and discover emotional conflicts symbolically represented in symptoms?

Jean Martin Charcot and Pierre Janet

answer_raw: B. Jean Martin Charcot and Pierre Janet
explanation_text:
B is correct: “Drawing on the work of Jean Martin Charcot and Pierre Janet in Paris, they at first hypnotized their hysterical patients and discovered emotional conflicts that were being symbolically represented in the hysterical symptoms.”
(A) Eugen Bleuler and Emil Kraepelin are descriptive psychiatrists of dementia praecox/schizophrenia and the great nosology, not the Paris hypnosis sources named here.
(C) Alfred Adler and Carl Jung are later dissenters from Freud (Chapter 2); they are not the Paris clinicians who informed early hypnotic work with hysterics.
(D) Harry Stack Sullivan and Erich Fromm belong to interpersonal and cultural-revisionist traditions, not this Charcot–Janet historical note.
(E) Heinz Kohut and Otto Kernberg are self-psychological and object-relations theorists of later chapters; they are not the Paris sources for Freud and Breuer’s first hypnotic investigations.
Teaching point: Hypnosis, via Charcot and Janet, first showed emotional conflicts symbolically represented in hysterical symptoms.
clinical_application: Link conversion symptoms to conflict discovery historically via hypnosis, then free association—not to modern hypnosis as first-line treatment.

stem: In the case of Fraulein Elizabeth von R., after a walk with her sister’s husband she later awoke with unexplained pain and weakness in her legs. Under hypnosis it became evident that she desired her brother-in-law. In the topographic model, how was this formulated?

options.text: Desire was fully conscious and voluntarily suppressed by willpower alone
Desire was suppressed, and guilt was manifest as pain and weakness in the very legs that took her on the walk
Symptoms were due solely to organic neuropathy
Desire was projected onto the sister as hatred
Symptoms represented a manic defense against depression

answer_text: Desire was suppressed, and guilt was manifest as pain and weakness in the very legs that took her on the walk
answer_raw: B. Desire was suppressed, and guilt was manifest as pain and weakness in the very legs that took her on the walk
explanation_text:
B is correct: After a walk with her sister’s husband, Fraulein Elizabeth von R. awoke with unexplained pain and weakness in her legs; under hypnosis it was evident she desired her brother-in-law but could not acknowledge the forbidden attraction. In the topographic model, “her desire was suppressed, and her guilt was manifest as pain and weakness in the very legs that took her on the walk.”
(A) Fully conscious desire voluntarily suppressed by willpower alone contradicts suppression of an unacknowledgeable attraction into the unconscious topographic formula.
(C) Solely organic neuropathy is ruled out by the definition of hysteria (no traceable somatic cause) and by the hypnotic uncovering of forbidden desire.
(D) Projection of desire onto the sister as hatred is not the mechanism named; Bienenfeld gives suppression of her own desire and guilt in the walking legs.
(E) A manic defense against depression is a later/other affect-defense idea; this case is topographic suppression with symbolic somatic guilt, not mania.
Teaching point: The somatic symptom can be the symbolic stand-in for a conflicted, suppressed drive-derived emotion (legs that walked the forbidden walk).

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: In the topographic formula for hysteria in Bienenfeld's account, an unacceptable emotion stems from the drives and cannot be experienced in system Cs (conscious). Where is it relegated, and how is the drive energy then manifested?

options.text: It is relegated to system UCs (unconscious); energy is manifest in physical symptoms, usually symbolically representative of the conflict
It is discharged only through free association without symptoms
It remains fully in Cs and produces insight automatically
It is stored only in the superego as moral anxiety
It is eliminated by suggestion without residue

answer_text: It is relegated to system UCs (unconscious); energy is manifest in physical symptoms, usually symbolically representative of the conflict
answer_raw: A. It is relegated to system UCs (unconscious); energy is manifest in physical symptoms, usually symbolically representative of the conflict
explanation_text:
A is correct: “An unacceptable emotion stems from the drives. It cannot be experienced in the system Cs (conscious), so it is relegated to the system UCs (unconscious). Since there is no avenue for direct resolution of the conflicted emotional state, the energy deriving from the drive is manifest in physical symptoms, usually symbolically representative of the conflict itself.”
(B) Discharge only through free association without symptoms is the later talking-cure method, not this topographic formula of energy becoming symbolic physical symptoms.
(C) Remaining fully in Cs and producing insight automatically is the opposite of relegation to UCs with no direct resolution path.
(D) Storage only in the superego as moral anxiety is structural-model language (id/ego/superego, coming on page 100), not this topographic Cs/UCs formula.
(E) Elimination by suggestion without residue is closer to Bernheim-style hypnotic suggestion; Bienenfeld's account says hypnosis soon proved unnecessary and states a leftover-energy-as-symptom formula, not residue-free suggestion.
Teaching point: Without conscious processing, conflicted drive energy returns as symbolically meaningful somatic symptoms.
clinical_application: In conversion presentations, look for the forbidden affect and the symbolic fit of the symptom to the conflict.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Hysteria, obsessions, and phobias were classified together under which label in this formulation?

options.text: Actual neuroses
Defense neuropsychoses
Borderline personality organization
Narcissistic character disorders
Organic psychoses

answer_text: Defense neuropsychoses
answer_raw: B. Defense neuropsychoses
explanation_text:
B is correct: “Hysteria, obsessions, and phobias all shared the same formula and were classified together as the defense neuropsychoses.”
(A) Actual neuroses (neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses, page 98) were the earlier 1885–1897 pair produced directly by sexual practices, not this shared conflict formula.
(C) Borderline personality organization is Kernberg’s later object-relations diagnosis (later in Bienenfeld's discussion of affect and psychopathology), not the topographic label for hysteria/obsessions/phobias.
(D) Narcissistic character disorders belong to later self-psychological and object-relations nosology (Kohut/Kernberg), not this defense-neuropsychosis grouping.
(E) Organic psychoses imply brain disease; these three share a psychological conflict formula, not an organic-psychosis label.
Teaching point: Defense neuropsychoses share one formula—conflicted drive emotion relegated from Cs to UCs, then expressed as hysteria, obsession, or phobia.

stem: In this drive model, obsessions represented attachments to symbolic displacements of objects of earlier psychosexual stages. Phobias embodied which related process?

options.text: Purely conscious learning of danger cues without conflict
The overwhelming fear of such objects, similarly displaced into contemporary symbols
Only dopaminergic dysregulation
Failure of twinship selfobject needs alone
Altruistic surrender as the primary defense

answer_text: The overwhelming fear of such objects, similarly displaced into contemporary symbols
answer_raw: B. The overwhelming fear of such objects, similarly displaced into contemporary symbols
explanation_text:
B is correct: Obsessions “represented attachments to symbolic displacements of the objects of earlier psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic); phobias embodied the overwhelming fear of such objects, similarly displaced into contemporary symbols.”
(A) Purely conscious learning of danger cues without conflict is a conditioning/learning-theory account, not this drive-displacement formula.
(C) Only dopaminergic dysregulation is a neurochemical hypothesis; Bienenfeld's account’s phobia claim is displaced fear of psychosexual objects, not dopamine.
(D) Failure of twinship selfobject needs is Kohut’s self psychology (a later chapter objective), not the drive-model account of phobia in Bienenfeld's account.
(E) Altruistic surrender is Anna Freud’s later ego-psychological defense, not the mechanism named for phobias here.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: According to Bienenfeld, accumulation of clinical experience pushed the topographic model past its limits and forced another creative leap. What model did Freud produce that addressed those difficulties?

options.text: The interpersonal field model of Sullivan
The structural model
The selfobject matrix of Kohut exclusively
The behavioral chain analysis model
The attachment classifications of Ainsworth only

answer_text: The structural model
answer_raw: B. The structural model
explanation_text:
B is correct: Questions about the mechanism that diverts emotion from conscious to unconscious, how energy becomes symptoms, and where emotion is contained pushed the topographic model past its limits; “Freud produced the structural model, as described in Chapter 1, which addressed these difficulties and expanded the horizon of psychodynamic explanation of psychopathology.”
(A) Sullivan’s interpersonal field model is a neighboring interpersonal tradition, not the model Freud produced to solve these topographic difficulties.
(C) Kohut’s selfobject matrix is self psychology (a later objective of affect and psychopathology), not the 1923 structural solution named here.
(D) Behavioral chain analysis is a CBT/DBT method, not Freud’s next model of mind.
(E) Ainsworth’s attachment classifications are later developmental-attachment research, not the structural model produced to answer these questions.
Teaching point: Limits of topography—how emotion is diverted, converted, and contained—forced the structural model (id, ego, superego).
clinical_application: When topographic ideas (Cs/UCs) fail to locate the containing agency, shift to id–ego–superego structural formulation.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: The structural model, introduced in 1923, postulated the presence of id, ego, and superego. At its most basic, drive impulses originate in which structure?

options.text: Superego
Id
Ego ideal only
Conscious ego alone
External reality only

answer_text: Id
answer_raw: B. Id
explanation_text:
B is correct: The structural model, introduced in 1923, postulated id, ego, and superego; at its most basic, “drive impulses originate in the id.”
(A) The superego rejects some of those impulses as they press on awareness; it is not their origin.
(C) The ego ideal is a superego-related structure of valued aims, not the source of drive impulses.
(D) Conscious ego alone is the threatened, defending agency, not the origin of drives.
(E) External reality may stimulate or frustrate, but this formulation locates drive origin in the id, not in the outer world alone.
Teaching point: Structural psychopathology begins with id-origin drives pressing on awareness.
clinical_application: Locate unacceptable wishes as id-derived before mapping ego defenses and superego prohibitions.

stem: In the structural formulation, as affects and behavior deriving from id impulses press upon awareness, superego rejects some of them and ego is threatened by their power. What is the essence of psychological conflict?

options.text: The battle among the structures
Only conflict with external peers
Conflict solely between two conscious values
Absence of any internal structures
Conflict only between dream and waking thought

answer_text: The battle among the structures
answer_raw: A. The battle among the structures
explanation_text:
A is correct: As affects and behavior deriving from id impulses press upon awareness, “superego rejects some of them and ego is threatened by their power. The battle among the structures is the essence of psychological conflict.”
(B) Conflict only with external peers is interpersonal/social friction; Bienenfeld's account’s essence of conflict is intersystemic—among id, ego, and superego.
(C) Conflict solely between two conscious values is a conscious-moral dilemma, not the structural battle (much of which, the next bullet says, is unconscious).
(D) Absence of any internal structures denies the model just introduced (id, ego, superego).
(E) Conflict only between dream and waking thought is a topographic/dream issue, not the essence named here: battle among the structures.
Teaching point: In structural theory, conflict is intersystemic (id–ego–superego), not only person versus world.
clinical_application: Map symptoms to which structures are at war (wish vs conscience vs defense).

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Which statement about ego defensive strategies in the structural model is most accurate per Bienenfeld?

options.text: Defensive containment is always fully conscious and rational to the conscious ego
Most, if not all, of this defensive containment happens unconsciously; most mechanisms would be considered irrational by the conscious ego
Ego never uses defenses against id impulses
Only the id erects defenses
Defenses always eliminate drive energy completely

answer_text: Most, if not all, of this defensive containment happens unconsciously; most mechanisms would be considered irrational by the conscious ego
answer_raw: B. Most, if not all, of this defensive containment happens unconsciously; most mechanisms would be considered irrational by the conscious ego
explanation_text:
B is correct: Ego “erects various defensive strategies to contain or divert these undesirable impulses. Most, if not all, of this defensive containment happens unconsciously. Most of the mechanisms employed would be considered irrational by the conscious ego.”
(A) Fully conscious and rational defensive containment is the opposite of the unconscious, “irrational-to-conscious-ego” claim.
(C) Saying ego never uses defenses against id impulses contradicts the bullet that ego erects strategies to contain or divert those impulses.
(D) Only the id erects defenses misassigns the defensive function; defenses are ego strategies against undesirable impulses.
(E) Defenses always eliminating drive energy completely is not stated; the next sentence says the end result is a panoply of symptoms from defensive distortions of id impulses and drive derivatives—not clean erasure of energy.
Teaching point: Symptoms often reflect unconscious, irrational-seeming ego operations on drive derivatives.
clinical_application: Do not expect patients to report defenses as deliberate strategies; infer them from patterns of thought, affect, and behavior.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: In the structural re-explication of Fraulein von R., her desire for her brother-in-law originated in libidinal id impulses and was rejected by her superego before reaching consciousness. Ego first contained it by repression; as urges persisted, ego redirected libidinal energy how?

options.text: Through free association into insight without symptoms
Through symbolic representation in somatic symptoms
Through manic denial of all loss
Through deliberate behavioral experiments
Through only environmental change

answer_text: Through symbolic representation in somatic symptoms
answer_raw: B. Through symbolic representation in somatic symptoms
explanation_text:
B is correct: Fraulein von R.’s desire originated in libidinal id impulses and was rejected by her superego before reaching consciousness; ego first used repression (temporary), then, as urges persisted just beyond awareness, “ego was forced to redirect the libidinal energy through symbolic representation in somatic symptoms.”
(A) Free association into insight without symptoms is the treatment ideal, not this structural re-explication of how her symptoms formed.
(C) Manic denial of all loss is not the mechanism named for von R.; the path is repression then somatic symbolization of leftover libidinal energy.
(D) Deliberate behavioral experiments are CBT technique, not the ego’s unconscious redirection described here.
(E) Only environmental change omits the internal sequence: id wish → superego rejection → repression → residual energy as somatic symbol.
Teaching point: Conversion in the structural telling is leftover libidinal energy, after repression fails, expressed as a bodily symbol.
clinical_application: When repression fails to hold, expect substitute formations (somatic, phobic, obsessional) rather than pure absence of the wish.

stem: For Freud and his followers in this expansion of drive theory, which was the primary emotion, with all others as modifications, displacements, or substitutions?

options.text: Depression
Anxiety
Shame only
Envy only
Joy

answer_text: Anxiety
answer_raw: B. Anxiety
explanation_text:
B is correct: Expansion of drive theory to include a conflict model allowed psychoanalysis to address affect; “for Freud and his followers, the primary emotion was anxiety; all others were modifications, displacements, or substitutions.”
(A) Depression is treated later via “Mourning and Melancholia” (pages 102–103); it is not named as the primary emotion here.
(C) Shame is not the primary emotion of this drive-structural account; anxiety is, with others as modifications.
(D) Envy is a later Kleinian key affect (object relations, later in Bienenfeld), not the primary emotion for Freud and his followers in Bienenfeld's account.
(E) Joy is not listed as primary; anxiety is, and other emotions are modifications, displacements, or substitutions of it.
Teaching point: Drive-structural affect theory is anxiety-centered—other feelings are treated as variants or substitutes of anxiety.
clinical_application: Start affect formulations in classical drive theory with anxiety and ask how other affects may substitute or displace it.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: In structural theory, anxiety that is the inevitable result when the influx of energy from any stimulus is greater than what the individual can master is labeled what? What was the prototype stimulus?

options.text: Signal anxiety; prototype is a barking dog
Traumatic anxiety; birth was the prototype
Moral anxiety; prototype is the Oedipus complex only
Separation anxiety; prototype is school entry
Performance anxiety; prototype is examination

answer_text: Traumatic anxiety; birth was the prototype
answer_raw: B. Traumatic anxiety; birth was the prototype
explanation_text:
B is correct: Structural theory held that anxiety of one sort is the inevitable result “when the influx of energy from any stimulus is greater than what the individual can master. This type of anxiety was labeled traumatic anxiety; birth was the prototype for such a stimulus.”
(A) Signal anxiety with a barking-dog prototype is the next developmental step (page 101), not this unmasterable-influx type.
(C) Moral anxiety tied only to the Oedipus complex is a later structural refinement of superego threat, not the traumatic-anxiety/birth definition given here.
(D) Separation anxiety with school entry as prototype is a later developmental-clinical construct; Bienenfeld's account’s prototype is birth.
(E) Performance anxiety with an examination prototype is everyday situational language, not the traumatic-anxiety definition.
Teaching point: Traumatic (automatic) anxiety = overwhelm by an energy influx the person cannot master; birth is the prototype.
clinical_application: Distinguish traumatic (overwhelm) anxiety from later signal anxiety that warns and mobilizes defenses.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Because the infant’s ego is still immature, which form of anxiety is almost the only entity in the infant’s affective repertoire according to this model?

options.text: Signal anxiety prepared by mature memory
The reflex form of automatic anxiety (e.g., when hungry or in pain)
Only Oedipal guilt
Only existential dread
Only anticipatory castration anxiety

answer_text: The reflex form of automatic anxiety (e.g., when hungry or in pain)
answer_raw: B. The reflex form of automatic anxiety (e.g., when hungry or in pain)
explanation_text:
B is correct: The growing infant experiences similar automatic anxiety when hungry or in pain; “because the ego is still immature, this reflex form of anxiety is almost the only entity in the infant’s affective repertoire.”
(A) Signal anxiety prepared by mature memory is what Bienenfeld says comes later, once ego can connect traumatic events to their surroundings.
(C) Only Oedipal guilt belongs to a later psychosexual period, not the infant’s almost-only reflex anxiety.
(D) Only existential dread is a philosophical/existential register, not the hunger/pain automatic anxiety of the immature ego.
(E) Only anticipatory castration anxiety is a later Oedipal signal, not the infant’s reflex automatic anxiety.
Teaching point: The infant’s affective repertoire is almost only reflex/automatic anxiety; signal function waits on memory.
clinical_application: In infants and very regressed states, expect automatic overwhelm rather than nuanced signal affects.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: As the young ego associates mother’s departure or a dog’s presence with sensations of anxiety, it develops the capacity for which form of anxiety?

options.text: Only traumatic anxiety without anticipation
Signal anxiety
Only free-floating actual neurosis
Only moral masochism
Only primary process hallucination

answer_text: Signal anxiety
answer_raw: B. Signal anxiety
explanation_text:
B is correct: The infant notices hunger only in mother’s absence and that the dog’s bark causes fear; “the young ego associates the departure of mother or the presence of the dog with sensations of anxiety and develops the capacity for signal anxiety,” even though neither cue is inherently traumatic.
(A) Only traumatic anxiety without anticipation is the prior, unmasterable type; Bienenfeld's account is the step into anticipatory signal anxiety.
(C) Free-floating actual neurosis is the 1885–1897 dammed-up-libido picture (page 98), not this developmental acquisition of signal anxiety.
(D) Moral masochism is a later structural/character idea about unconscious guilt and suffering, not the dog/mother signal step.
(E) Primary-process hallucination is topographic wish-fulfillment language, not the association of cues with impending anxiety.
Teaching point: Signal anxiety anticipates danger from associated cues even when nothing inherently traumatic is happening now.
clinical_application: Use signal anxiety clinically as the ego’s early-warning system that mobilizes defenses before full overwhelm.

stem: Compared with the intolerable experience of unrestrained libidinal wishes toward a forbidden love object, the experience of signal anxiety as the person approaches is described as:

options.text: Stronger and less manageable than full traumatic overwhelm
Weaker and much more manageable, and it allows the ego to prepare defenses
Identical to birth trauma
Always fully conscious and planned
A product only of external conditioning

answer_text: Weaker and much more manageable, and it allows the ego to prepare defenses
answer_raw: B. Weaker and much more manageable, and it allows the ego to prepare defenses
explanation_text:
B is correct: Unrestrained libidinal wishes toward a forbidden love object would be intolerable; “the experience of signal anxiety when he or she approaches is weaker and much more manageable. Additionally, it allows the ego to prepare an array of defenses to contain and manage the drive derivatives.”
(A) Stronger and less manageable than traumatic overwhelm reverses the comparison: signal anxiety is weaker and more manageable.
(C) Identical to birth trauma collapses signal anxiety back into traumatic anxiety (page 100’s prototype), which this paragraph distinguishes.
(D) Always fully conscious and planned overstates awareness; signal anxiety is an ego capacity to anticipate and prepare defenses, not a fully conscious plan.
(E) A product only of external conditioning is a learning-theory reduction; here the mature ego also applies signal anxiety to internal stimuli—unacceptable id impulses.
Teaching point: Signal anxiety is adaptive anticipatory affect that lets ego mount defenses before full overwhelm.
clinical_application: When anxiety is mild and anticipatory before a conflicted situation, think signal function rather than only panic disorder biology.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: What does Bienenfeld call the first and most indispensable tool of the ego in managing anxiety?

options.text: Sublimation
The defense mechanism of repression
Humor
Intellectualization only
Acting out

answer_text: The defense mechanism of repression
answer_raw: B. The defense mechanism of repression
explanation_text:
B is correct: “The first and most indispensable tool of the ego in managing anxiety is the defense mechanism of repression. Unacceptable impulses are unconsciously extruded from the ego and returned to the id.”
(A) Sublimation is a later, more mature channeling of drive into valued activity; it is not named as the first, indispensable anxiety tool here.
(C) Humor is a mature defense in later ego-psychological lists (Anna Freud and after), not the first tool named in Bienenfeld's account.
(D) Intellectualization only is a higher-order isolation-of-thought defense, not the foundational extrusion of impulse from ego to id.
(E) Acting out discharges in behavior rather than unconsciously extruding impulse from ego; it is not the indispensable first tool given here.
Teaching point: Repression—unconscious return of unacceptable impulses from ego to id—is the foundational anxiety-management defense in this model.
clinical_application: When primary defense is repression, look for return of the repressed in symptoms rather than conscious reporting of the wish.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: When ego engages in repression, energy associated with the impulses is returned to the id. What consequence does Bienenfeld emphasize?

options.text: The id becomes permanently quiet
The id then presses its desires all the more powerfully; too much repression promotes emergence of emotional, cognitive, and/or behavioral pathology
All energy is lost to the environment
Superego dissolves
Signal anxiety becomes impossible forever

answer_text: The id then presses its desires all the more powerfully; too much repression promotes emergence of emotional, cognitive, and/or behavioral pathology
answer_raw: B. The id then presses its desires all the more powerfully; too much repression promotes emergence of emotional, cognitive, and/or behavioral pathology
explanation_text:
B is correct: With the repressed impulses goes their associated energy, so repression “feeds some of its energy to the id, which then presses its desires all the more powerfully. Too much repression, therefore, promotes the emergence of emotional, cognitive, and/or behavioral pathology. This constellation was named anxiety neurosis.”
(A) A permanently quieted id is the opposite of feeding energy to the id so it presses more powerfully.
(C) All energy lost to the environment is not the claim; energy associated with the impulses returns with them to the id.
(D) Superego dissolution is not a stated consequence of repression; the cost named is a stronger id press and possible anxiety neurosis.
(E) Signal anxiety becoming forever impossible is not stated; the pathology named is anxiety neurosis from too much repression, not loss of the signal function.
Teaching point: Repression is costly—it feeds the id’s pressure and, in excess, promotes symptoms (anxiety neurosis).
clinical_application: Chronic over-repression may present as anxiety neurosis and other psychoneurotic symptoms rather than “successful” forgetting.

context: Cost of repression: strengthened id pressure and pathology.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Collectively, the earlier-defined defense neuropsychoses (hysteria, obsessions, and phobias) and anxiety neurosis were now labeled as:

options.text: The actual neuroses
The psychoneuroses
The narcissistic neuroses only
The organic psychoses
The character disorders exclusively

answer_text: The psychoneuroses
answer_raw: B. The psychoneuroses
explanation_text:
B is correct: “Collectively, the earlier-defined defense neuropsychoses (hysteria, obsessions, and phobias) and anxiety neurosis were now labeled as the psychoneuroses.”
(A) The actual neuroses were the earlier 1885–1897 pair (neurasthenia and anxiety neuroses as direct sexual-practice products), not this collective structural-era label.
(C) Narcissistic neuroses only is a narrower classical contrast (often psychosis/narcissistic transferences), not the collective label given for these four pictures.
(D) Organic psychoses imply brain disease; this grouping is psychological—defense neuropsychoses plus anxiety neurosis.
(E) Character disorders exclusively belong to the later Abraham character-types discussion (page 103–104); they are not this psychoneuroses label.
Teaching point: Psychoneuroses = defense neuropsychoses (hysteria, obsessions, phobias) + anxiety neurosis in this structural expansion.
clinical_application: On historical PRITE items, psychoneurosis groups conversion/obsessional/phobic pictures with anxiety neurosis under conflict models.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Mr. Brown acts out a typical “success neurosis.” Just on the brink of interpersonal or business success that would echo the original Oedipal situation, what emerges and what does his superego do?

options.text: Pride emerges and ego freely achieves the goal
Oedipal guilt emerges with castration anxiety; his superego must defeat his id aims rather than allow ego to achieve the goal and risk retribution
Only separation anxiety from mother appears
Only twinship longing appears
He experiences pure joy without conflict

answer_text: Oedipal guilt emerges with castration anxiety; his superego must defeat his id aims rather than allow ego to achieve the goal and risk retribution
answer_raw: B. Oedipal guilt emerges with castration anxiety; his superego must defeat his id aims rather than allow ego to achieve the goal and risk retribution
explanation_text:
B is correct: Mr. Brown first identifies with father and attempts interpersonal sexual and external business success; either would echo the original Oedipal situation, and “just on the brink of this success, Oedipal guilt emerges, and he fears the consequence in the form of castration anxiety. As a result, his superego must defeat his id aims rather than allow ego to achieve his goal and put him at risk for retribution.”
(A) Pride with free ego achievement is the success the neurosis prevents; the box is about guilt, castration fear, and superego defeat of id aims.
(C) Only separation anxiety from mother is a different developmental danger (signaled in Bienenfeld's account by mother’s departure); the box specifies Oedipal guilt and castration anxiety.
(D) Twinship longing is a Kohutian selfobject need (self psychology, later in Bienenfeld), not Mr. Brown’s success-neurosis dynamic.
(E) Pure joy without conflict denies the Oedipal echo, guilt, and castration fear that halt him at the brink.
Teaching point: Success can be sabotaged when achievement symbolically reenacts forbidden Oedipal victory—superego defeats the aim to avoid retribution.
clinical_application: When patients self-sabotage at the brink of achievement, consider Oedipal success neurosis (guilt/castration anxiety) in the differential of formulation.

stem: An early example of applying the structural/drive model to paranoia is drawn from Freud’s view of a patient, Daniel S., who maintained a fixed belief that his prior psychiatrist was engaged in a plot to do what?

options.text: Cure him with free association
Change him into a woman and abuse him
Promote him at work
Only abandon him for vacation
Teach him self psychology

answer_text: Change him into a woman and abuse him
answer_raw: B. Change him into a woman and abuse him
explanation_text:
B is correct: An early application of this model is Freud’s view of paranoia in Daniel S., who “maintained a fixed and unshakable belief that his prior psychiatrist was engaged in a plot to change him into [a] woman and abuse him.” Associations pointed to a sadistic father and unusual discipline; later in Bienenfeld continues with castration fear.
(A) A plot to cure him with free association invents a treatment method as the delusion; the belief named is feminization and abuse.
(C) A plot to promote him at work is unrelated to the feminization/abuse delusion and the sadistic-father material.
(D) Only abandonment for vacation is a later object-relations/separation theme (Ms. Gray on page 106), not Daniel’s stated belief.
(E) A plot to teach him self psychology imports Kohut’s school; this is Freud’s drive/structural paranoia case, not a self-psychology vignette.
Teaching point: Daniel S.’s feminization-and-abuse delusion, grounded in a sadistic father and castration fear, sets up the defensive sequence on page 102.

stem: Figure 7-1 (drive model of paranoia) sequences defenses from “I love my mother.” After castration anxiety leads to “I love my father,” which mechanism leads to “I love my doctor”?

options.text: Projection
Displacement
Sublimation
Undoing
Isolation of affect

answer_text: Displacement
answer_raw: B. Displacement
explanation_text:
B is correct: Figure 7-1 sequences the drive model of paranoia from “I love my mother” through castration anxiety to “I love my father”; the next labeled mechanism is displacement, producing “I love my doctor.”
(A) Projection is the last step in the figure (“I hate my doctor” → “My doctor hates me”), not the step from father-love to doctor-love.
(C) Sublimation (channeling drive into socially valued activity) is not a labeled step in Figure 7-1.
(D) Undoing (a typical obsessional defense) is not in this paranoia sequence.

stem: Freud defined mourning as the state in which a person has lost a significant love object (or abstract representation) and feels sadness about the loss. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The emotion is entirely unconscious and the loss is unknown
The emotion is entirely conscious, as is awareness of the loss, although its meaning may be hidden in the unconscious
Mourning never involves sadness
Mourning is identical to melancholia
Mourning requires delusional guilt

answer_text: The emotion is entirely conscious, as is awareness of the loss, although its meaning may be hidden in the unconscious
answer_raw: B. The emotion is entirely conscious, as is awareness of the loss, although its meaning may be hidden in the unconscious
explanation_text:
B is correct: Freud defined mourning as the state in which a person has lost a significant love object or abstract representation of such an object and feels sadness about the loss. “The emotion is entirely conscious, as is the awareness of the loss, although its meaning may be hidden in the unconscious.”
(A) Entirely unconscious emotion with an unknown loss reverses the definition: both the sadness and the awareness of loss are conscious.
(C) Mourning never involving sadness contradicts “feels sadness about the loss.”
(D) Identity with melancholia is denied by the contrast that follows: melancholia is deeper despair, often with an unavailable or insufficient object.
(E) Delusional guilt is not required for mourning; that more pathogenic self-attack belongs with melancholia’s self-reproach, not this conscious-sadness definition.
Teaching point: Mourning (grief/bereavement) links conscious sadness to a known external loss, even if deeper meaning stays unconscious.
clinical_application: If a patient can name the loss and connect sadness to it, think mourning/grief even if symbolic meanings remain unconscious.

stem: A person loses a job and consciously feels sad about the job loss, though may not recognize that the job represented potency or parental approval. In Freud’s terms this best illustrates:

options.text: Melancholia with loss only inside the self
Mourning, with conscious sadness linked to a specific external loss
Only paranoid projection
Only actual neurasthenia
Only Don Juan syndrome

answer_text: Mourning, with conscious sadness linked to a specific external loss
answer_raw: B. Mourning, with conscious sadness linked to a specific external loss
explanation_text:
B is correct: The job-loss example is mourning: the person “may not immediately recognize that the job represents a feeling of potency in the world or a potential source of parental approval. But he or she is consciously aware of feeling sad and consciously connects the sadness to the job loss.”
(A) Melancholia with loss only inside the self is the contrasting state (unconscious or insufficient object; loss perceived within the self).
(C) Only paranoid projection is the Daniel S. solution on the prior discussions, not this conscious sadness-to-job-loss link.
(D) Actual neurasthenia is the 1885–1897 lassitude/somatic picture from excess discharge (page 98), not job-loss mourning.
(E) Don Juan syndrome is Anna Freud’s incompatible-urges example on page 105, not this mourning illustration.
Teaching point: Conscious sadness tied to a known external loss is mourning even when potency or parental-approval meanings remain hidden.

Within the self

answer_raw: B. Within the self
explanation_text:
B is correct: Melancholia is a much more deep-seated despair, often marked by apathy and pessimism; the object of sadness may be unavailable to awareness or the identified loss utterly insufficient to justify the distress. “In such cases, Freud usually found that there was an unconscious perception of loss of something within the self.”
(A) Locating the essential loss only in the external economy may name a precipitant (as in the fired-employee example) but not Freud’s usual finding of unconscious loss within the self.
(C) Loss only in the therapist is a transference localizatiin Bienenfeld's account does not make the essence of melancholia.
(D) Only conscious sibling rivalry misplaces both the object (within the self) and the awareness (unconscious perception).
(E) Only cultural status with full awareness contradicts both “within the self” and the suppressed link between stimulus and response.
Teaching point: In melancholia the felt loss is inside the self, and the object or the link may be unconscious or too small to explain the despair.

stem: Which patients does Bienenfeld say may be more vulnerable to this type of depression (melancholia) when other losses occur in adult life?

options.text: Only those without any early losses
People who have suffered repeated or intense early losses; those with particularly harsh superegos are more susceptible to self-criticism
Only those with weak superegos and no early loss
Only those with pure traumatic anxiety and no object loss

answer_raw: B. People who have suffered repeated or intense early losses; those with particularly harsh superegos are more susceptible to self-criticism
explanation_text:
B is correct: “People who have suffered repeated or intense early losses may be more vulnerable to experiencing this type of depression when other losses occur in adult life. Those with particularly harsh superegos are more susceptible to self-criticism.”
(A) Only those without any early losses reverses the vulnerability claim.
(C) Only those with weak superegos and no early loss reverses both modifiers: early loss increases melancholic vulnerability; harsh—not weak—superegos increase self-criticism.
(D) Only those with pure traumatic anxiety and no object loss mixes page 100’s automatic anxiety with this object-loss model and denies the loss history that raises risk.
(E) Only those with oral-character optimism (overgratified infants on page 104) is the opposite valence of melancholic vulnerability and is a later character typology, not this risk pair.
Teaching point: Early repeated or intense loss plus a harsh superego raise melancholic risk when adult losses hit.

stem: Even after a century, Bienenfeld says the formulation retains validity. Melancholia (depression proper in contemporary terminology) is best summarized as:

options.text: A conscious state of sadness linked by the patient to a specific external loss
A more profound state of despair in which the loss is perceived as being within the self, and the links are mostly unconscious
Identical to uncomplicated bereavement

answer_text: A more profound state of despair in which the loss is perceived as being within the self, and the links are mostly unconscious
answer_raw: B. A more profound state of despair in which the loss is perceived as being within the self, and the links are mostly unconscious
explanation_text:
B is correct: Even after a century the formulation “retains validity”: mourning (grief/bereavement) is conscious sadness linked by the patient to a specific external loss; “melancholia (depression proper in contemporary terminology) is a more profound state of despair in which the loss is perceived as being within the self, and the links are mostly unconscious.”
(A) Conscious sadness linked to a specific external loss is the summary of mourning, not melancholia.
(C) Identity with uncomplicated bereavement collapses the distinction Bienenfeld says still holds.
(D) Only a personality style without affective change denies the “more profound state of despair.”
(E) Only a medical thyroid disorder is a somatic differential; Bienenfeld's account’s melancholia is the psychodynamic depression-proper formulation, not an endocrine diagnosis.

stem: While drive psychology never addressed what are now defined as personality disorders, Freud’s followers—particularly which theorist (1877–1925)—elucidated character types as a persistent, background form of psychopathology?

options.text: Heinz Hartmann
Karl Abraham
Heinz Kohut

answer_text: Karl Abraham
answer_raw: B. Karl Abraham
explanation_text:
B is correct: Drive psychology “never addressed what are now defined as personality disorders,” but Freud’s followers, “particularly Karl Abraham (1877–1925), elucidated character types that represented a persistent, background form of psychopathology.”
(A) Heinz Hartmann is the ego psychologist of adaptation and “fitting together” (page 105), not the 1877–1925 character-type theorist named here.
(C) Heinz Kohut is the self-psychology founder (a later chapter objective), not Abraham.
(D) Melanie Klein founds a later object-relations model of positions and innate aggression (page 107), not this Abraham character-type note.
(E) Harry Stack Sullivan is the interpersonal theorist, not the Freudian follower who elucidated psychosexual character types in Bienenfeld's account.
Teaching point: Abraham’s psychosexual character types are drive theory’s stand-in for what later nosology calls personality disorders—persistent background psychopathology.

stem: Failure to cope with the demands of any psychosexual phase can result in fixation. Stress or stimulus beyond ego’s capacity later in life can lead to:

options.text: Only progressive maturation
Regression, a return to an earlier developmental level
Only permanent psychosis
Only selfobject transference

answer_raw: B. Regression, a return to an earlier developmental level
explanation_text:
B is correct: Normal psychosexual development proceeds through oral, anal, and phallic stages, each with its demands. “Failure to cope with the demands of any phase can result in fixation, an inability to move beyond the characteristics of that stage; stress or stimulus beyond ego’s capacity to cope at later points in life can lead to regression, a return to an earlier developmental level.”
(A) Only progressive maturation is the opposite of regression under later overload.
(C) Only permanent psychosis overstates the definition: regression is return to an earlier developmental level, not necessarily lasting psychosis.
(D) Only selfobject transference is Kohutian self psychology, not the drive-theory definition of regression given here.
(E) Only extinction of all drives is not regression; drives remain, expressed at an earlier level.
Teaching point: Fixation = stuck at a stage’s characteristics; regression = return to an earlier level when later stress exceeds ego’s capacity.

stem: According to Bienenfeld’s drive-character account, overgratified infants become optimistic, contented adults, whereas frustrated infants become:

answer_raw: B. Pessimistic grown-ups
explanation_text:
B is correct: Oral behavior focuses on eating and smoking—indulging excess or obsessively limiting, depending on whether parents were overindulgent or withholding. “Overgratified infants become optimistic, contented adults; frustrated infants become pessimistic grown-ups.”
(A) Only manic is not the adult outcome named for frustrated infants; the valence given is pessimism.
(C) Only obsessional without mood valence is closer to anal character (order, control) and denies the optimistic/pessimistic mood stamp of oral history.
(D) Only paranoid is the drive-model paranoia sequence (pages 101–102), not the oral frustration → pessimism claim.
(E) Without any character stamp contradicts the point of Bienenfeld’s account: early oral excess or deprivation leaves an outlook and oral-behavior pattern.
Teaching point: Parental overindulgence versus withholding shapes oral-character outlook (optimism vs pessimism) and oral behaviors (excess vs restriction).
clinical_application: Link lifelong pessimistic expectancy and oral self-soothing/restriction to early oral frustration when clinically fitting.

stem: Anal character types grow from difficulties around toilet training and related tasks. Children’s attempts to restrain natural anal impulses yield overconcern with self-control. They grow up to be excessively orderly and interpersonally inflexible. Because feces equates to both dirt and money in drive symbolism, anal characters are also:

options.text: Only generous and messy always
Parsimonious and obsessively neat, with islands of messiness or indulgence when impulses break through
Without any orderliness
Only orally dependent
Only phallically exhibitionistic

answer_text: Parsimonious and obsessively neat, with islands of messiness or indulgence when impulses break through
answer_raw: B. Parsimonious and obsessively neat, with islands of messiness or indulgence when impulses break through
explanation_text:
B is correct: Anal characters, products of parents who cannot help through toilet training and related tasks, grow “excessively orderly and interpersonally inflexible.” Because feces “equates to both dirt and money,” they are “parsimonious and obsessively neat.” “Because this restraint is born of conflict, the underlying impulses frequently break through the repression barrier in episodes or islands of messiness or indulgence.”
(A) Only generous and messy always reverses the baseline (parsimony and obsessive neatness), though islands of messiness do break through.
(C) Without any orderliness contradicts “excessively orderly” and “obsessively neat.”
(D) Only orally dependent is the prior oral-character concern (nurture/dependency), not anal control, money/dirt, and neatness.
(E) Only phallically exhibitionistic is a later psychosexual style, not this toilet-training/self-control character.
Teaching point: Anal character is conflict-born control—thrift and neatness with breakthrough islands of mess or indulgence—not a seamless trait.
clinical_application: Expect neat/stingy presentation with occasional messy or indulgent breakthroughs in anal-character conflict.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: As structural theory unfolded affect and pathology, it became clear that id impulses drive these phenomena and superego often counterbalances at a cost of internal conflict. The production of symptoms and their specific relationship to underlying conflicts was the work of:

options.text: Only the id
The ego
Only external reality
Only the therapist
Only the drives without ego mediation

answer_text: The ego
answer_raw: B. The ego
explanation_text:
B is correct: As the structural model unfolded affect and pathology, id impulses were the driving force and superego often counterbalanced them at the cost of internal conflict. “It also became clear that the production of symptoms and their specific relationship to the underlying conflicts was the work of the ego.” Anna Freud’s The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense then “put flesh on the bones of the earlier formulations.”
(A) Only the id names the driving force behind the phenomena, not the agency that produces symptoms and links them to conflict.
(C) Only external reality omits the internal ego work that shapes how conflict becomes a particular symptom.
(D) Only the therapist misattributes symptom production to the clinician; Bienenfeld assigns it to the patient’s ego.
(E) Only the drives without ego mediation is the force side of the story; mediation—how this conflict becomes that symptom—is ego’s work and the bridge into ego psychology.
Teaching point: Symptom choice and its specific tie to conflict are ego work—the hinge from drive theory into ego psychology.
clinical_application: Analyze not only the wish and prohibition but how the ego constructs the particular symptom form.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Anna Freud examined reasons a person might fear direct expression of drives. Critical words from a supervisor may trigger murderous derivatives of the aggressive drive, requiring extra ego energy and producing paralyzing anxiety. This illustrates fear of drive expression because:

options.text: The very strength of the drive threatens to upset internal harmony
Only the environment lacks resources
Only selfobject failure occurs
Drives do not exist
Only conscious preference for calm

answer_text: The very strength of the drive threatens to upset internal harmony
answer_raw: A. The very strength of the drive threatens to upset internal harmony
explanation_text:
A is correct: Anna Freud examined reasons a person might fear direct expression of drives. First: “in some instances, the very strength of the drive threatens to upset the internal harmony of the individual.” Critical words from a supervisor may trigger murderous derivatives of the aggressive drive, requiring extra ego energy and creativity and producing paralyzing anxiety.
(B) Only the environment lacks resources is a later Hartmann adaptation problem (deficiencies in the environment); this vignette is internal drive strength vs harmony.
(C) Only selfobject failure is Kohut’s self psychology, not Anna Freud’s first motive for fearing drive expression.
(D) Drives do not exist denies the whole drive-psychology frame she is elaborating.
(E) Only conscious preference for calm understates the claim: it is the strength of (often unconscious) drive derivatives that threatens internal harmony and forces costly ego work.
Teaching point: One motive for defense is sheer intensity of drive derivatives—strong enough to wreck inner harmony (supervisor → murderous rage → paralysis).
clinical_application: When minor criticism yields disproportionate rage/anxiety, consider threatening intensity of aggressive derivatives and ego’s costly containment.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: A meek, constrained man taken to a strip show on a business trip becomes anxious and poorly concentrated after aroused libido triggers massive superego countermeasures. This illustrates fear of drive expression because:

options.text: The values and standards of the superego are so rigorous that they are threatened by id impulses
He lacks any id
Only twinship needs failed
Only oral fixation explains all anxiety
Anxiety is always traumatic birth reenactment only

answer_text: The values and standards of the superego are so rigorous that they are threatened by id impulses
answer_raw: A. The values and standards of the superego are so rigorous that they are threatened by id impulses
explanation_text:
A is correct: Second reason: “sometimes the values and standards of the superego are so rigorous that they are threatened by id impulses.” The meek, constrained man at a strip show has aroused libido that “triggers massive countermeasures from superego,” leaving heart-in-throat anxiety and impaired concentration.
(B) He lacks any id contradicts the example: aroused libido (id) is exactly what the harsh superego counters.
(C) Only twinship needs failed is Kohutian selfobject language, not this superego-versus-id illustration.
(D) Only oral fixation explains all anxiety reduces the trip anxiety to page 104’s oral character; the mechanism named is a rigorous superego threatened by libidinal arousal.
(E) Anxiety always as traumatic birth reenactment only is page 100’s traumatic-anxiety prototype generalized too far; this vignette is moral/superego threat, not birth overwhelm.
Teaching point: A second motive for defense is a harsh superego that treats ordinary libidinal arousal as an emergency.
clinical_application: Moral panic after sexual stimulation may reflect rigorous superego countermeasures rather than only external danger.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: A man with intense homosexual and heterosexual desires exhibits obsessive pursuit of multiple women to submerge homosexual impulses beneath volume of heterosexual behavior. Bienenfeld calls this the:

options.text: Success neurosis
Don Juan syndrome
Actual neurasthenia
Paranoid-schizoid position
Mirror-hungry personality

answer_text: Don Juan syndrome
answer_raw: B. Don Juan syndrome
explanation_text:
B is correct: Third reason: drives may yield mutually incompatible urges. The man with intense homosexual and heterosexual desires—each threatening the other—“exhibits the ‘Don Juan syndrome’ of obsessive pursuit of multiple women, with the unconscious aim of submerging the homosexual impulses beneath the volume of heterosexual behavior.”
(A) Success neurosis is Mr. Brown’s Oedipal pattern on page 101 (guilt and castration fear at the brink of achievement), not this incompatible-urges picture.
(C) Actual neurasthenia is the 1885–1897 lassitude/somatic product of excess discharge (page 98), not Anna Freud’s Don Juan example.
(D) The paranoid-schizoid position is Melanie Klein’s later object-relations constellation (page 107), not Bienenfeld's account’s incompatible-drive syndrome.
(E) Mirror-hungry personality is a Kohutian/self-psychological character style, not the Don Juan label given here.
Teaching point: A third motive for defense is incompatible drive aims—here, volume of heterosexual pursuit used to drown a threatening homosexual impulse.
clinical_application: Compulsive heterosexual conquest may defend against unconscious same-sex wishes in classical formulation (Don Juan).

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Heinz Hartmann extended Anna Freud’s formulations and specified which function as the pre-eminent role of the ego?

options.text: Only repression
Adaptation; “fitting together” with the environment is the optimal outcome of successful adaptation
Only dream censorship
Only generation of id impulses
Only creation of the superego

answer_text: Adaptation; “fitting together” with the environment is the optimal outcome of successful adaptation
answer_raw: B. Adaptation; “fitting together” with the environment is the optimal outcome of successful adaptation
explanation_text:
B is correct: “Heinz Hartmann extended Anna Freud’s formulations and specified the function of adaptation as the pre-eminent role of the ego. ‘Fitting together’ with the environment is the optimal outcome of successful adaptation.” He aimed at a general psychology focused almost exclusively on normal development.
(A) Only repression is Anna Freud/Freud’s first anxiety tool (page 101), not Hartmann’s pre-eminent ego function.
(C) Only dream censorship is the early topographic “dream censor” (Chapter 1), not Hartmann’s adaptation/fitting-together role.
(D) Only generation of id impulses is an id function in the structural model, not the ego’s pre-eminent role.
(E) Only creation of the superego is not Hartmann’s specification; he elevates adaptation, not superego-making, as ego’s chief job.
Teaching point: Ego psychology as general psychology centers adaptation—“fitting together”—not only conflict pathology.
clinical_application: Assess how the patient’s ego “fits together” with environment, not only intrapsychic conflict, when using Hartmann.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Failure to adapt and inability to fit together does not necessarily produce pathological affects and behaviors. The inability to adapt may be a product of which of the following per Bienenfeld?

options.text: Only hereditary id strength
Deficiencies in the environment, abnormalities within the person, or disorders of equilibrium between the two
Only unconscious homosexuality
Only birth trauma alone
Only free association failure

answer_text: Deficiencies in the environment, abnormalities within the person, or disorders of equilibrium between the two
answer_raw: B. Deficiencies in the environment, abnormalities within the person, or disorders of equilibrium between the two
explanation_text:
B is correct: Failure to adapt and inability to fit together “does not necessarily produce pathological affects and behaviors. The inability to adapt may be a product of deficiencies in the environment, abnormalities within the person, or disorders of equilibrium between the two.”
(A) Only hereditary id strength is a one-factor drive claim; Hartmann’s followers allow environment, person, or the fit between them.
(C) Only unconscious homosexuality is the Daniel S. repressed-wish theme (page 102), not this three-source account of failed adaptation.
(D) Only birth trauma alone is page 100’s prototype of traumatic anxiety, not the exclusive source of inability to adapt.
(E) Only free-association failure is a technical/treatment problem, not a stated origin of failed adaptation.
Teaching point: Ego-psychological sources of failed adaptation are multi-factorial—environment, person, or their equilibrium—not drive conflict alone.
clinical_application: Formulate adaptation failure as person, environment, and/or person–environment fit—not only internal conflict.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Just as in the original Freudian model, which is the first and most important affect experienced by the ego in this ego-psychological account?

options.text: Shame only
Anxiety
Only boredom
Only elation
Only envy

answer_text: Anxiety
answer_raw: B. Anxiety
explanation_text:
B is correct: “Just as in the original Freudian model, anxiety is the first and most important affect experienced by the ego. It appears when id impulses threaten to overwhelm the defenses or as a signal of threat or loss from the environment.”
(A) Shame only is not named as first and most important here; anxiety is (shame is not Bienenfeld's account’s primary ego affect).
(C) Only boredom is not the primary ego affect in this continuity with Freud.
(D) Only elation is not listed; anxiety remains first, whether from inner id threat or outer danger/loss.
(E) Only envy is Klein’s later key affect in object relations (page 107+), not the ego-psychological primary named here.
Teaching point: Ego psychology keeps Freud’s anxiety primacy—now as overwhelm of defenses or as a signal of environmental threat or loss.
clinical_application: Keep anxiety central when assessing ego’s response to internal impulse pressure or external threat/loss.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Transformation of anxiety into a different, less threatening affect is a tool for ego mastery. Commonly, if a person is put into a helpless situation, anxiety may be transformed into anger because anger:

options.text: Eliminates the id permanently
Gives the ego more of a sense of potential mastery
Always produces depression immediately
Is always more dangerous than anxiety
Only increases traumatic anxiety

answer_text: Gives the ego more of a sense of potential mastery
answer_raw: B. Gives the ego more of a sense of potential mastery
explanation_text:
B is correct: Transformation of anxiety into a different, less threatening affect is among ego’s tools for mastering it. “If a person is put into a helpless situation, anxiety may be transformed into anger, which gives the ego more of a sense of potential mastery.”
(A) Permanently eliminating the id is not what anger-transformation does; it changes the affect to restore a sense of possible mastery.
(C) Always producing depression immediately is the next, “widely discredited” inward-aggression path that begins at Bienenfeld’s end—not the common helpless-anxiety → anger route.
(D) Anger always more dangerous than anxiety contradicts the point of the transformation: anger is the less threatening, more mastery-affording affect in helplessness.
(E) Only increasing traumatic anxiety reverses the aim: the shift is toward a more manageable affect, not toward unmasterable traumatic anxiety.
Teaching point: Affect transformation can be a defensive mastery strategy—helpless anxiety turned into anger to feel some potential control.
clinical_application: Helpless patients who shift into anger may be recruiting a mastery-conferring affect—explore before only suppressing anger.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: In the classic (though now widely discredited) formulation of depression, when pressure of aggressive urges threatens to produce anxiety, the ego may turn the aggression inward on the self. The ego then becomes:

options.text: The anxious purveyor of aggression only
Its depressed victim
Free of all affect
Only manic
Only paranoid without depression

answer_text: Its depressed victim
answer_raw: B. Its depressed victim
explanation_text:
B is correct: In the classic (now widely discredited) formulation continued from page 105, when pressure of aggressive urges threatens to produce anxiety, “the ego may turn the aggression inward on the self. Instead of being the anxious purveyor of aggression, the ego is now its depressed victim.”
(A) The anxious purveyor of aggression is the state this maneuver leaves behind, not the end-state named.
(C) Free of all affect contradicts becoming the depressed victim of inward-turned aggression.
(D) Only manic is the opposite pole of mood; the formulation is depression via aggression-against-self.
(E) Only paranoid without depression is Bienenfeld 102 projection-of-hate solution, not this inward turn that yields a depressed victim-ego.
Teaching point: Know the classic aggression-turned-against-self model of depression—and that Bienenfeld flags it as now widely discredited.
clinical_application: Even if discredited as universal, the aggression-inward model still helps some patients who experience self-attack as redirected rage.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Ego psychology’s elaboration of mechanisms yields ambiguity because the very mechanisms that drive development and support ego structure are also:

options.text: Irrelevant to adult life
The same ones that produce symptoms
Only conscious learning strategies
Only id functions
Only cultural rituals

answer_text: The same ones that produce symptoms
answer_raw: B. The same ones that produce symptoms
explanation_text:
B is correct: Elaboration of ego mechanisms “yields some ambiguity. The very mechanisms that drive development and support the structure of the ego are the same ones that produce symptoms.” In building a general psychology, ego psychologists “blurred the line between normality and psychopathology.”
(A) Irrelevant to adult life contradicts both their role in supporting adult ego structure and their capacity to produce adult symptoms.
(C) Only conscious learning strategies understates the model: these are ego mechanisms of development and defense, not merely conscious study skills.
(D) Only id functions misassigns them; they are ego mechanisms that both build structure and make symptoms.
(E) Only cultural rituals is an anthropological reductiin Bienenfeld's account does not make; the ambiguity is inside ego psychology’s own mechanisms.
Teaching point: The same ego operations that build a mind can make symptoms—normality and pathology share machinery.
clinical_application: Do not pathologize every defense; ask whether the mechanism fits the developmental task and adult context.
