deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Using the ego-psychological model, it becomes more useful to think of the relevance of adaptive mechanisms to the tasks at hand. Defensive operations that serve to build the ego at age 4, if they do not evolve over time, usually:

options.text: Remain optimally adaptive for all adult tasks
Turn out to be maladaptive to living among others as an adult
Disappear without residue
Become id impulses
Only improve with aging automatically

answer_text: Turn out to be maladaptive to living among others as an adult
answer_raw: B. Turn out to be maladaptive to living among others as an adult
explanation_text:
B is correct: It becomes more useful to think of the relevance of adaptive mechanisms to the tasks at hand. “The defensive operations that serve to build the ego at age 4, if they do not evolve over time, usually turn out to be maladaptive to living among others as an adult.”
(A) Remaining optimally adaptive for all adult tasks is the opposite of the usual fate of unevolved age-4 defenses.
(C) Disappearing without residue denies persistence: they remain and typically become maladaptive in adult social life.
(D) Becoming id impulses misidentifies them; they stay defensive operations, now poorly fitted to adult tasks.
(E) Only improving with aging automatically contradicts the need that they “evolve over time” or else turn maladaptive.
Teaching point: Judge defenses by developmental fit to current tasks, not by a permanent “defense vs non-defense” label.
clinical_application: Ask whether a defense still fits adult relational and occupational tasks or is a childhood solution out of context.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: A defense such as compulsive attention to detail may prevent a father from playing with his children but may be very adaptive in his work as a surgeon. This example best illustrates that:

options.text: All defenses are always pathological
Adaptiveness of a defense depends on the tasks and context
Compulsiveness is never useful
Only family life defines mental health
Surgeons cannot have ego defenses

answer_text: Adaptiveness of a defense depends on the tasks and context
answer_raw: B. Adaptiveness of a defense depends on the tasks and context
explanation_text:
B is correct: “A defense such as compulsive attention to detail may prevent a father from playing with his children, but may be very adaptive in his work as a surgeon”—so adaptiveness depends on the tasks and context, not on the defense name alone.
(A) All defenses are always pathological is what this ego-psychological stance rejects: the same operation can help in one role and hurt in another.
(C) Compulsiveness is never useful is denied by the surgical example, where meticulous attention is “very adaptive.”
(D) Only family life defines mental health ignores the work context in which the same defense helps.
(E) Surgeons cannot have ego defenses is absurd in Bienenfeld's account: the surgeon’s useful meticulousness is explicitly a defense in another setting.
Teaching point: Context-relative adaptiveness is central to ego psychology’s clinical stance—ask where the defense fits the task.
clinical_application: Evaluate defenses by role-specific costs/benefits rather than labeling them globally good or bad.

context: Context-dependent adaptiveness of defenses.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: When defenses, or even symptoms, are integrated with and acceptable to the entire personality, they are considered ego syntonic. When elements of the personality regard the defense as a source of problems and wish to be rid of it, it is:

options.text: Ego syntonic
Ego dystonic
Only primary process
Only secondary process
Only conflict-free

answer_text: Ego dystonic
answer_raw: B. Ego dystonic
explanation_text:
B is correct: When defenses, or even symptoms, “are integrated with, and acceptable to, the entire personality, they are considered ego syntonic. When elements of the personality regard the defense as a source of problems, and wish to be rid of it, it is ego dystonic.”
(A) Ego syntonic is the integrated, acceptable state—the opposite of wishing to be rid of the defense.
(C) Only primary process is the id’s mode of thought (Chapter 1), not the personality’s stance toward a defense.
(D) Only secondary process is waking rational thought style, not the syntonic/dystonic distinction.
(E) Only conflict-free names Hartmann’s autonomous ego sphere, not the wish-to-be-rid-of-it relation that defines dystonicity.
Teaching point: Ego-dystonic means parts of the personality experience the defense as a problem and want it gone.
clinical_application: Motivation for treatment often tracks ego-dystonicity; syntonic traits may not present as complaints.

context: Ego syntonic vs dystonic.

sources: Bienenfeld D. Psychodynamic Theory for Clinicians. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2006. p. 106.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: According to Bienenfeld, which group of defenses may be defined as symptoms?

options.text: Only ego-syntonic defenses
The ego-dystonic group of defenses
Only conflict-free autonomous functions
Only mature altruism always
Only adaptive surgical meticulousness without complaint

answer_text: The ego-dystonic group of defenses
answer_raw: B. The ego-dystonic group of defenses
explanation_text:
B is correct: After defining syntonic versus dystonic, Bienenfeld states, “It is the latter group of defenses that may be defined as symptoms.”
(A) Only ego-syntonic defenses are the integrated, acceptable ones—not the group defined as symptoms.
(C) Only conflict-free autonomous functions are Hartmann’s nonconflictual ego equipment, not the dystonic defenses called symptoms.
(D) Only mature altruism always is a mature mechanism later said to be unavailable to Ms. Gray; altruism is not the definitional criterion for “symptom.”
(E) Only adaptive surgical meticulousness without complaint is the syntonic/adaptive-in-context example, not the dystonic group defined as symptoms.
Teaching point: Symptom status hinges on the personality’s relation to the defense (dystonicity), not only on the defense’s name.
clinical_application: A trait becomes a “symptom” for treatment purposes when the patient experiences it as alien and problematic.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Ms. Gray has a limited range of defenses, uses splitting of others as idealized saviors or malicious failures, and when angered by the therapist’s upcoming absence regresses and turns aggression against herself, threatening suicide. Mature mechanisms such as altruism and sublimation appear unavailable. This vignette introduces which major theory section?

options.text: Drive psychology only
Object relations
Only self psychology without OR
Only actual neuroses
Only behavioral activation

answer_text: Object relations
answer_raw: B. Object relations
explanation_text:
B is correct: The Ms. Gray vignette sits under the heading OBJECT RELATIONS: limited range of defenses from developmental deficits; repressed traumatic memories; splitting of others (including the therapist) into idealized saviors or malicious failures; regression with aggression turned against herself and a suicide threat when angered by the therapist’s upcoming absence; mature mechanisms such as altruism and sublimation unavailable. The text then says object-relations theory, having clarified the role of others (or their internal representations) in normal development, “also undertook to explain psychopathology in similar terms.”
(A) Drive psychology only is the prior major section (actual neuroses through Abraham’s character types); this vignette opens the object-relations section.
(C) Only self psychology without object relations is Bienenfeld’s later fourth objective (Kohut), not the heading and theory named here.
(D) Only actual neuroses are the 1885–1897 neurasthenia/anxiety-neurosis pair (page 98), not Ms. Gray’s splitting and separation-rage picture.
(E) Only behavioral activation is a CBT/behavioral depression technique, not the theory section this vignette introduces.

answer_text: Rage
answer_raw: C. Rage
explanation_text:
C is correct: Bienenfeld states that even in the depressive position, splitting may be mobilized as the child constructs good objects to contain gratification and bad objects to contain rage.
(A) Curiosity is not the content assigned to bad objects; the pair in Bienenfeld's account is gratification in good objects versus rage in bad ones.
(B) Empathy is not what bad objects are said to contain; depressive-position work holds love with hate, it does not store empathy in a bad object.
(D) Idealization is a way of overvaluing a good object, not the rage this sentence parks in bad objects.
(E) Libido belongs with the good-object/gratification side (and with the aggression–libido conflict that can foster ego growth), not with what bad objects contain here.
Teaching point: Residual splitting can still park gratification in “good” objects and rage in “bad” ones after the child reaches the depressive position.

stem: A child who gets vegetative satisfaction from a nervous or dissatisfied mother but does not connect it with emotional-need gratification will, in Mahler’s terms in Bienenfeld's account, grow up with “affect hunger” and later pursue relationships with:

options.text: Classical oedipal triangulation without residue
Stable whole-object ambivalence
Unfulfillable expectations and predictable disappointment
Intact continuous self free of false-self accommodation
Secure idealizable selfobjects only

answer_text: Unfulfillable expectations and predictable disappointment
answer_raw: C. Unfulfillable expectations and predictable disappointment
explanation_text:
C is correct: A nervous or dissatisfied mother may give vegetative satisfaction without linking it to emotional-need gratification; such a child grows up with “affect hunger” and later pursues relationships with unfulfillable expectations and predictable disappointment.
(A) Classical oedipal triangulation without residue is a later, healthier structural picture; this Mahler sentence predicts chronic hunger and letdown, not a clean oedipal resolution.
(B) Stable whole-object ambivalence is an integrated/depressive-position capacity; affect hunger here yields disappointed pursuit, not stable ambivalence.
(D) An intact continuous self free of false-self accommodation is Winnicott’s health criterion later in Bienenfeld, not Mahler’s affect-hunger outcome.
(E) Secure idealizable selfobjects only is later self-psychological language; the Mahler line names unfulfillable expectations and predictable disappointment.
Teaching point: Vegetative care without emotional partnership breeds later love that is chased hungrily and then predictably let down.
clinical_application: Patients who chronically expect partners to fill an unfillable emotional void may be living out Mahlerian affect hunger from failed emotional symbiosis.

stem: Mental health for Winnicott is defined by the integrity and spontaneity of the self; psychopathology reflects distortion and constraint in self expression. Because the false self relies heavily on cognitive operations to comply with an inadequate mother, ascendancy of the false self is manifest in:

options.text: Primary process dominance without secondary process
An overactive mind in which cognition is separated from genuine emotion
Purely somatic conversion without ideation
Absence of any cognitive activity
Only manic flight of ideas

answer_text: An overactive mind in which cognition is separated from genuine emotion
answer_raw: B. An overactive mind in which cognition is separated from genuine emotion
explanation_text:
B is correct: Because the false self must rely heavily on cognitive operations to comply with an inadequate mother, its ascendancy is manifest in an overactive mind in which cognition is separated from genuine emotion.
(A) Primary-process dominance without secondary process is a drive/topographic contrast; Winnicott’s false-self picture here is compliant overactive cognition split from feeling, not raw primary process.
(C) Purely somatic conversion without ideation is a classical hysterical pattern; Bienenfeld describes cognitive overactivity, not conversion emptied of thought.
(D) Absence of any cognitive activity reverses the claim: the false self leans on cognition to figure out how to comply.
(E) Only manic flight of ideas is a mood-disorder form of racing thought; the overactive mind here is compliant intellect cut off from genuine emotion, not mania.
Teaching point: Intellectualized compliance without authentic feeling is the clinical flag of false-self ascendancy.
clinical_application: Patients who “think their way” through relationships without feeling may be living from a Winnicottian false self.

stem: Winnicott’s original three-type diagnostic scheme included pre-self disorders, depressive disorders, and neuroses. Pre-self disorders, characterized by breakdown within the most primitive sets of object relations, included which group?

options.text: Only classical hysteria and obsessional neurosis
Psychosis, schizoid conditions, and borderline states
Only narcissistic behavior disorders
Only psychoneuroses as special variants of narcissistic disorder
Only oedipal-stage selfobject deficits

answer_text: Psychosis, schizoid conditions, and borderline states
answer_raw: B. Psychosis, schizoid conditions, and borderline states
explanation_text:
B is correct: Winnicott’s pre-self disorders are breakdowns within the most primitive sets of object relations and include psychosis, schizoid conditions, and borderline states.
(A) Only classical hysteria and obsessional neurosis are the Freudian neuroses in his original three-type scheme—manifestations of classical conflict, not pre-self disorders.
(C) Only narcissistic behavior disorders is later self-psychology nosology (a milder rank than borderline), not his pre-self list.
(D) Only psychoneuroses as special variants of narcissistic disorder is likewise Kohutian ranking, not Winnicott’s primitive pre-self category.
(E) Only oedipal-stage selfobject deficits is the self-psychological account of psychoneuroses (ages 4–6), not pre-self breakdown of primitive object relations.
Teaching point: Winnicott’s most primitive pathology is pre-self: psychosis, schizoid conditions, and borderline states.
clinical_application: Reserve “pre-self” language for severe primitive pathology with early object-relations breakdown, not ordinary neurosis.

stem: Over time, Winnicott reclassified Freudian neurotics as belonging to a small class of very healthy individuals because classical neurosis requires:

options.text: Exclusive reliance on expulsion as defense
Absence of any self structure
Presence of an intact and continuous self reflecting healthy parenting
Complete lack of depressive-position capacity
Permanent weakness of the nuclear self

answer_text: Presence of an intact and continuous self reflecting healthy parenting
answer_raw: C. Presence of an intact and continuous self reflecting healthy parenting
explanation_text:
C is correct: Over time Winnicott reclassified Freudian neurotics as a small class of very healthy individuals because a classical neurosis requires the presence of an intact and continuous self, which in turn reflects healthy parenting.
(A) Exclusive reliance on expulsion as defense is Klein’s earliest (paranoid-schizoid) defense, not the intact-self prerequisite for classical neurosis.
(B) Absence of any self structure is the opposite of what he required; neurosis presupposes a present, continuous self.
(D) Complete lack of depressive-position capacity points toward more primitive organization; he recoded Kleinian depressive problems as ordinary, not as the requirement for neurosis.
(E) Permanent weakness of the nuclear self is self psychology’s borderline/narcissistic language, not Winnicott’s intact-self criterion for neurosis.
Teaching point: For late Winnicott, a classical neurosis is a high-health achievement—it means the self held together under good-enough parenting.
clinical_application: Do not treat classical neurotic structure as the most severe pathology; Winnicott saw it as evidence of a relatively intact self.

stem: After reclassifying Freudian neurotics as very healthy and Kleinian depressive disorders as characteristic of most normal people, Winnicott was left maintaining that all psychopathology fell into which category?

options.text: Oedipal psychoneuroses
Narcissistic behavior disorders only
Pre-self disorders, all resulting from parental failings
Drive-based actual neuroses
Selfobject psychoneuroses of ages 4–6 only

answer_text: Pre-self disorders, all resulting from parental failings
answer_raw: C. Pre-self disorders, all resulting from parental failings
explanation_text:
C is correct: After moving Freudian neurotics into a small very-healthy class and Kleinian depressive disorders into the majority of ordinary people, he was left maintaining that all psychopathology fell into the category of pre-self disorders, and all resulted from parental failings.
(A) Oedipal psychoneuroses are what he recoded as that small healthy class requiring an intact continuous self—not remaining pathology.
(B) Narcissistic behavior disorders only is a later self-psychological rank, not the leftover category he named.
(D) Drive-based actual neuroses belong to classical drive theory, not Winnicott’s residual of parental-failure pre-self disorders.
(E) Selfobject psychoneuroses of ages 4–6 only is Kohut’s least-severe rank; Winnicott’s remaining pathology is pre-self, not oedipal-stage selfobject deficit.
Teaching point: Late Winnicott radicalizes all pathology as pre-self consequences of parental failure.
clinical_application: A Winnicottian extreme view attributes clinical pathology to early parental failings disrupting continuous self, not only to adult conflict.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: In Kernberg’s model, if early emotional experience is perceived as much more unpleasant than pleasant, “good” object representations cannot outweigh and master “bad” ones. The result is that the primitive split is never overcome and:

options.text: Signal anxiety fully replaces traumatic anxiety
Depressive-position mourning is automatic
Oedipal triangulation is achieved early
The false self dissolves spontaneously
The merger necessary for a robust ego is never complete

answer_text: The merger necessary for a robust ego is never complete
answer_raw: E. The merger necessary for a robust ego is never complete
explanation_text:
E is correct: If early emotional experience is perceived as much more unpleasant than pleasant, “good” object representations cannot outweigh and master “bad” ones; the primitive split is never overcome, and the merger necessary for a robust ego is never complete.
(A) Signal anxiety fully replacing traumatic anxiety is an ego-psychological developmental claim, not the consequence Kernberg names for unmastered bad objects.
(B) Depressive-position mourning is not automatic here; failed good-over-bad mastery leaves early splitting in place rather than depressive integration.
(C) Early oedipal triangulation is a later structural achievement; Bienenfeld's account is about incomplete pre-Oedipal merger of good and bad.
(D) The false self dissolving spontaneously is Winnicott’s language, and the opposite of what follows from persistent splitting.
Teaching point: When bad outweighs good, the merger that builds a robust ego never finishes—and infantile splitting remains.
clinical_application: Severe early negative affective environments predict persistent splitting and incomplete ego integration on a Kernbergian model.

stem: Rapid alternation of overvaluation and depreciation in borderline organization leads, according to Bienenfeld, to corollary vacillations of emotional state and attitude:

options.text: From true self to false self exclusively
From boredom to curiosity only
From signal anxiety to sublimation
From excited to euphoric, and from love to hate
From guilt to reparation only

answer_text: From excited to euphoric, and from love to hate
answer_raw: D. From excited to euphoric, and from love to hate
explanation_text:
D is correct: Rapid, extreme alternation of overvaluation and depreciation leads to corollary vacillations of emotional state from excited to euphoric, and of attitude from love to hate.
(A) True self versus false self is Winnicott’s polarity, not the affect/attitude swing Kernberg names for borderline splitting.
(B) Boredom to curiosity only is not the pair given; Bienenfeld specifies excited–euphoric affect and love–hate attitude.
(C) Signal anxiety to sublimation is ego-psychological language (a warning affect and a mature defense), not these idealization/devaluation storms.
(E) Guilt to reparation only is Kleinian depressive-position work, not the love/hate and excited/euphoric vacillations of unintegrated splitting.
Teaching point: Extreme idealization/devaluation travels with love/hate attitude swings and excited-to-euphoric affect.
clinical_application: Track session-to-session idealization and devaluation as linked love/hate vacillations of borderline splitting.

stem: Under ideal circumstances in Kernberg’s model in Bienenfeld's account, the nature of the object and the quality of the affect lead to:

options.text: Absence of any need for mourning
A false self without true-self residue
Smooth development of properly functioning mental structures
Permanent reliance on expulsion as sole defense
Elimination of all aggressive drive

answer_text: Smooth development of properly functioning mental structures
answer_raw: C. Smooth development of properly functioning mental structures
explanation_text:
C is correct: Under ideal circumstances in Kernberg’s model, the nature of the object and the quality of the affect lead to a smooth development of properly functioning mental structures.
(A) Absence of any need for mourning is not claimed; good-enough early coloring builds structure—it does not abolish mourning.
(B) A false self without true-self residue is a Winnicottian pathogenic outcome, not Kernberg’s ideal developmental result.
(D) Permanent reliance on expulsion as sole defense is Klein’s earliest defense, not the product of ideal affective coloring.
(E) Elimination of all aggressive drive is not stated; the ideal is well-functioning structure from predominantly good-enough affective experience, not drive erasure.
Teaching point: Early affective coloring of object relations builds mental structure when it is good enough.
clinical_application: Emphasize quality of early emotional environments when teaching how structure formation succeeds or fails.

stem: Kernberg noted that borderline patients act on impulse with no evident awareness of the emotion and ideation associated with the behavior. When the correlation was pointed out, patients typically blandly acknowledged cognitive validity but could not:

options.text: Incorporate it in a meaningful or emotional way
Use repression as a defense
Form any words in response
Experience signal anxiety thereafter
Deny the observation entirely

answer_text: Incorporate it in a meaningful or emotional way
answer_raw: A. Incorporate it in a meaningful or emotional way
explanation_text:
A is correct: Kernberg noted that borderline patients act on impulse with no evident awareness of the associated emotion and ideation; when he pointed out the correlation, they typically blandly acknowledged the cognitive validity of the observation but were unable to incorporate it in a meaningful or emotional way.
(B) Using repression as a defense is not the observation; repression would hide the idea, whereas they could think the link but not feel it.
(C) Forming any words in response contradicts “blandly acknowledge”; they did speak agreement.
(D) Experiencing signal anxiety thereafter is not what he recorded after pointing out the impulse–affect split.
(E) Denying the observation entirely is the opposite of bland cognitive acknowledgment.
Teaching point: Knowing the interpretation without being able to feel it is this split’s signature—and it blocks learning from experience.
clinical_application: Do not equate intellectual agreement with integration; borderline patients may acknowledge interpretations without emotional uptake.

stem: Further complicating borderline pathology, splitting is not only between good and bad experiences but also between:

options.text: Mental functions (experience vs structure)
Primary and secondary process only
Id and libido only
Symbiotic and separation phases only

answer_text: Mental functions (experience vs structure)
answer_raw: A. Mental functions (experience vs structure)
explanation_text:
A is correct: Further complicating matters, the splitting is not just between good and bad experiences and impressions but also between mental functions; this splitting of experience from structure impairs the capacity to learn from experience.
(B) Primary versus secondary process only is a drive-psychology thought-mode contrast, not the functional split Kernberg adds here.
(C) Id and libido only mixes structural and drive terms; the added split is among mental functions (experience versus structure).
(D) Symbiotic and separation phases only is Mahler’s developmental sequence, not this functional splitting.
(E) Mirroring and idealizing poles exclusively is self psychology’s bipolar self, not Kernberg’s good/bad plus function split.
Teaching point: Watch for splitting of mental functions (knowing versus feeling/structure), not only good-versus-bad content.
clinical_application: When affect, idea, and action don’t cohere, consider Kernbergian splitting of mental functions as well as object images.

stem: Disordered borderline behavior, in Kernberg’s summary here, is a consequence of reactivity to environmental events unbuffered by internal affective constancy, and by a complementary search for:

options.text: Quiescent states for true-self formation only
Perfect selfobject twinship exclusively
Depressive-position guilt without action
Stability and fulfillment in the wrong places
Only oedipal rivals

answer_text: Stability and fulfillment in the wrong places
answer_raw: D. Stability and fulfillment in the wrong places
explanation_text:
D is correct: Disordered borderline behavior is a consequence of reactivity to environmental events, unbuffered by internal affective constancy, and of a complementary search for stability and fulfillment in the wrong places.
(A) Quiescent states for true-self formation only is Winnicott’s early need (and one form of pathogenic maternal failure), not the complementary search named here.
(B) Perfect selfobject twinship exclusively is Kohutian; this sentence names a misplaced search for stability and fulfillment.
(C) Depressive-position guilt without action is Kleinian; Bienenfeld describes impulsive, environmentally reactive behavior, not guilt-only depressive work.
(E) Only oedipal rivals is classical drive language, not the “wrong places” pursuit of stability Kernberg summarizes.
Teaching point: Unbuffered environmental reactivity plus chasing stability in the wrong places organizes much borderline chaos.
clinical_application: Frame impulsive attachments and crises as attempts to find stability externally when internal affective constancy is missing.

stem: From the self-psychological perspective, disorders are characterized not by their phenomenology but by their etiology. Symptoms are manifestations of a particular deficit of selfobject function filtered through temperament and contemporary experience. In this model, “selfobject” refers to:

options.text: A person who is fused with the self permanently
A selfobject function or experience (not a person)
Only the bad internal object of Klein
The false self of Winnicott
The ego’s observing function

answer_text: A selfobject function or experience (not a person)
answer_raw: B. A selfobject function or experience (not a person)
explanation_text:
B is correct: From the self-psychological perspective, disorders are characterized by etiology rather than phenomenology, and Bienenfeld reminds the reader that “selfobject” refers not to a person but to a selfobject function or experience.
(A) A person fused with the self permanently reifies the term as a human being; Bienenfeld forbids that equation.
(C) Only the bad internal object of Klein is an object-relations internal image, not a selfobject function or experience.
(D) The false self of Winnicott is a compliant self-organization, not the definition of selfobject.
(E) The ego’s observing function is a structural-ego capacity, not what “selfobject” names here.
Teaching point: Keep “selfobject” as a function or experience—not a synonym for “important person.”
clinical_application: When teaching residents, define selfobject as a function/experience that completes the self, not merely as “a supportive person.”

stem: Bienenfeld states that the single biggest difference between the self-psychological model of pathology and all others is the distinction between:

options.text: True self and false self
Primary and secondary process
Conflict and deficit
Love and hate
Signal and traumatic anxiety

answer_text: Conflict and deficit
answer_raw: C. Conflict and deficit
explanation_text:
C is correct: Because there is no ego, id, or superego and there are no drives, the word “conflict” has no place in the self-psychology lexicon; instead all problems are selfobject deficits, and this distinction between conflict and deficit is probably the single biggest difference from all other models.
(A) True self and false self is Winnicott’s core polarity, not the contrast Bienenfeld crowns here.
(B) Primary and secondary process is drive psychology’s thought-mode pair, not the self-psychological differentiator.
(D) Love and hate is Klein’s internal conflict, which this model explicitly sets aside.
(E) Signal and traumatic anxiety is an ego-psychological anxiety distinction, not conflict versus deficit.
Teaching point: Self psychology is a deficit model; do not smuggle structural “conflict” into a Kohutian formulation.
clinical_application: Ask whether the case is better organized as structural conflict or as selfobject deficit before choosing interpretive strategy.

answer_text: Instability of mood, apathy, and a narrow, self-centered outlook
answer_raw: D. Instability of mood, apathy, and a narrow, self-centered outlook
explanation_text:
D is correct: The idealizable selfobject supports the idealized parental imago (self-soothing, regulation of feelings, enthusiasm, devotion to ideals); inadequate objects of idealization predispose to instability of mood, apathy, and a narrow, self-centered outlook.
(A) Automatic achievement of twinship is another selfobject function, not the outcome of failed idealization.
(B) Only weak ambitions without mood effects confuses the mirroring pole (self-esteem, pleasure, ambitions and goals) with idealization; this sentence names mood instability, apathy, and self-centeredness.
(C) Exclusive true-self spontaneity is Winnicottian health, the opposite of this deficit picture.
(E) Purely obsessional neurosis without self meaning is classical nosology; Bienenfeld specifies mood instability, apathy, and a narrow outlook.
Teaching point: Failed idealizable selfobjects hit soothing, ideals, and mood—not primarily ambition (that is the mirroring pole).
clinical_application: Apathetic, mood-labile, self-preoccupied patients may lack idealizable selfobject experiences more than mirroring alone.

stem: Mr. Brown had an idealizable selfobject in his father but little mirroring from either parent; his mother was deficient in providing idealizable experiences. His bipolar self is thus skewed toward narcissistic needs. His pattern of pursuing paternal ideals yet tripping himself up before success is attributed primarily to:

options.text: Unconscious castration anxiety alone
Failure to receive the mirroring in adulthood that he has lacked since childhood
Successful twinship with peers only
Innate Kleinian aggression without self meaning
Complete absence of any ideals

answer_text: Failure to receive the mirroring in adulthood that he has lacked since childhood
answer_raw: B. Failure to receive the mirroring in adulthood that he has lacked since childhood
explanation_text:
B is correct: Mr. Brown had an idealizable father but little mirroring from either parent, so his bipolar self is skewed toward narcissistic needs; he pursues internalized paternal ideals yet, failing to receive the mirroring in adulthood that he has lacked since childhood, repeatedly trips himself up before achieving success.
(A) Unconscious castration anxiety alone is a classical oedipal explanation; the vignette attributes the self-sabotage to lifelong missing mirroring, not castration fear.
(C) Successful twinship with peers only is not described; neither parent offered much mirroring, and the sabotage is from that lack, not from achieved twinship.
(D) Innate Kleinian aggression without self meaning imports Klein’s drive; the box is a bipolar-self, mirroring-deficit story.
(E) Complete absence of any ideals is false: he had an idealizable father and pursues those paternal ideals—the gap is mirroring, not ideals.
Teaching point: An idealizable pole with a mirroring deficit yields a skewed bipolar self and self-defeating ambition.
clinical_application: High ideals with self-sabotage before achievement may reflect mirroring deficit despite retained idealized ideals.

clinical_application: Chronic empathy failures in narcissistically organized patients may reflect bipolar-self imbalance, not only willful selfishness.

(B) Convert traumatic into signal anxiety is an ego-psychological developmental task, not the function named for addictions or perversions here.
(C) Eliminate all need for selfobjects contradicts the model: selfobjects remain necessary; addictions try to patch the deficit, not abolish the need.
(D) Complete oedipal triangulation is a structural/drive achievement, not what addictions are recruited to do in Bienenfeld's account.
(E) Achieve depressive-position reparation only is Kleinian; the function here is shoring up missing selfobject experience.

answer_raw: E. Keep contemporary relationships shallow to avoid repetition of early noxious harm
explanation_text:
E is correct: Borderline states result from severe, early, and ongoing selfobject deficits, usually at both poles, and require constant complex defenses for psychic survival; schizoid attitudes or histrionic style may keep contemporary relationships shallow to avoid repetition of the harm from the early noxious ones.
(A) Dissolve the nuclear self deliberately is the opposite of psychic-survival defenses; these styles protect a fragile self, they do not aim to dissolve it.
(B) Guarantee twinship experiences is not the function named; the aim is distance from repetition of early harm, not securing twinship.
(C) Deepen intimacy rapidly is the opposite of keeping relationships shallow.
(D) Establish classical free association is a technical method of drive/ego analysis, not a borderline survival style in Bienenfeld's account.
Teaching point: Schizoid or histrionic style can be distance regulation after toxic early selfobjects.
clinical_application: Schizoid distance or histrionic shallowness may be self-protective against retraumatizing intimacy.

C is correct: In the same self-psychological account of borderline defenses, paranoid strategies may allow the person to disown blame for intolerable feeling states.

(B) Increase empathy for the aggressor is not the function named; the move is disowning blame, not empathic identification.
(D) Achieve permanent nuclear-self cohesion is a health outcome; these borderline states still show instability of mood and self-esteem and chaos of self-image.
(E) Abandon all selfobject needs is impossible in this model; paranoia redistributes blame, it does not cancel selfobject need.

deck: Psychotherapy: Psychodynamic · Bienenfeld — 7  Affect and Psychopathology
stem: Object relations theories, constituting a more divergent group than the other schools, are said in the learning points to offer:

options.text: A single unified explanation identical to drive theory
A range of explanations of affect and pathology
No account of adult conditions
Only a ranking of selfobject severity
Exclusive focus on oedipal conflict

answer_text: A range of explanations of affect and pathology
answer_raw: B. A range of explanations of affect and pathology
explanation_text:
B is correct: The learning points state that object relations theories, constituting a more divergent group than the other schools, offer a range of explanations of affect and pathology (Klein: aggression and the struggle between love and hate; Mahler: adult conditions as early separation-individuation problems; Winnicott: true self versus false self; Kernberg: persistence of infantile splitting).
(A) A single unified explanation identical to drive theory contradicts both “more divergent” and the separate drive-psychology learning point (defenses mounted to keep id drives out of awareness in classical neuroses).
(C) No account of adult conditions is false: the bullets explicitly map adult problems (Mahler’s adult conditions, Winnicott’s adult true/false-self struggle, Kernberg’s borderline psychopathology).
(D) Only a ranking of selfobject severity is the self-psychology nosology from earlier pages (psychosis–borderline–narcissistic–psychoneurosis), not this object-relations learning point.
(E) Exclusive focus on oedipal conflict is drive/ego territory; the object-relations bullets stress aggression/love-hate, separation-individuation, true/false self, and infantile splitting.
Teaching point: Expect heterogeneity inside object-relations models of affect and pathology—do not collapse them into one story.
clinical_application: Do not treat “object relations” as one theory; Klein, Mahler, Winnicott, and Kernberg diverge.

stem: Early Freud, flush with success treating hysteria, initially assumed symptom relief would come primarily from which process?

options.text: Awareness of the unconscious origins of the symptoms
Pharmacologic blockade of libidinal drive
Behavioral exposure hierarchies alone
Family structural realignment without individual insight

answer_raw: A. Awareness of the unconscious origins of the symptoms
explanation_text: A is correct: “Sigmund Freud, flush with his early successes in treating hysteria, assumed that alleviation from symptoms would come directly and simply from awareness of their unconscious origins.” B (pharmacologic blockade of libidinal drive) is a biological-reduction treatment, not early topographic talking-cure theory. C (behavioral exposure hierarchies alone) is later CBT/exposure method, not Freud’s awareness assumption. D (family structural realignment without individual insight) is Minuchin-style family-systems work, not this one-person drive opening. E (strengthening the observing ego before any recall) anticipates a later technical requirement of the structural/drive model (p. 123), not this earliest assumption that awareness itself would relieve. Teaching point: earliest topographic therapy assumed making the unconscious conscious would itself lift hysterical symptoms.
clinical_application: If a resident equates insight with cure, teach Freud’s own later discovery that pure awareness is often insufficient without interpretation and working through.

stem: In early drive therapy, “abreaction” referred to which clinical process?

options.text: The reawakening and release of memories and emotions in the present
The permanent abolition of all defense mechanisms
The analyst’s disclosure of countertransference feelings
Systematic desensitization of phobic stimuli
Pharmacologic sedation of traumatic memories

answer_text: The reawakening and release of memories and emotions in the present
answer_raw: A. The reawakening and release of memories and emotions in the present
explanation_text: A is correct: therapy required “abreaction,” defined as “the reawakening and release of memories and emotions in the present”; met with the analyst’s verbal responses, it released “strangulated” affect and supplied a conscious, rational framework for pathogenic memories. B (permanent abolition of all defenses) is not claimed; defenses remain ego tools that later become objects of analysis. C (analyst disclosure of countertransference) is a later two-person/relational technical issue (Chapter 9), not the definition of abreaction. D (systematic desensitization of phobic stimuli) is Wolpe-style behavior therapy, not revived memory-plus-affect. E (pharmacologic sedation of traumatic memories) would suppress rather than reawaken and release the strangulated affect Bienenfeld's account names. Teaching point: early-drive abreaction = revived memory + affect discharge + rational reworking with the analyst.
clinical_application: When a patient re-experiences a traumatic memory with affect in session, name abreaction historically—and still attend to meaning, defenses, and safety rather than catharsis alone.

stem: Bienenfeld lists four achievements of self-awareness that can change symptoms, behavior, emotion, and personality. Which of the following is included?

options.text: Able to organize thought, feeling, and action to satisfy drives in a manner appropriate to reality
Able to eliminate all unconscious mental activity permanently
Able to make the analyst into a permanent real parent
Able to avoid any experience of anxiety during treatment
Able to rely solely on suggestion without ego work

answer_text: Able to organize thought, feeling, and action to satisfy drives in a manner appropriate to reality
answer_raw: A. Able to organize thought, feeling, and action to satisfy drives in a manner appropriate to reality
explanation_text: A is correct: the fourth listed fruit of self-awareness is being “able to organize thought, feeling, and action to satisfy drives in a manner appropriate to reality” (with awareness of conflicts/defenses, of their origin, and conscious overcoming of them). B (eliminate all unconscious mental activity permanently) contradicts the dynamic-unconscious premise of the model; the aim is conscious mastery, not abolition of unconscious process. C (make the analyst a permanent real parent) is closer to Alexander’s “corrective emotional experience” or later good-object/reparenting talk, not one of the four self-awareness achievements listed. D (avoid any experience of anxiety during treatment) is not listed; later Bienenfeld passages treat post-interpretation anxiety as expectable and technically useful. E (rely solely on suggestion without ego work) is Bernheim-style suggestion, the opposite of organizing ego functions to satisfy drives under reality. Teaching point: classical cure includes adaptive drive satisfaction under reality’s constraints, not erasure of the unconscious or suggestion alone.
clinical_application: Outcome measures for insight work include not only “understanding” but more adaptive action and affect regulation in real relationships.

stem: When a repressed conflict is mobilized by an interpretation and enters consciousness, the immediate affective consequence described by Bienenfeld is:

options.text: Anxiety, which both mobilizes further defenses and drives pursuit of change
Immediate and permanent calm without further work
Abolition of all transference feelings
Psychotic disintegration in every case
Loss of the capacity for free association forever

answer_text: Anxiety, which both mobilizes further defenses and drives pursuit of change
answer_raw: A. Anxiety, which both mobilizes further defenses and drives pursuit of change
explanation_text: A is correct: when interpretation mobilizes a repressed conflict into (partial) consciousness, “this revelation induces anxiety, which both mobilizes further defenses and also drives the pursuit of change through the analytic process.” B (immediate and permanent calm without further work) is the opposite of the induced anxiety that both defends and motivates further work. C (abolition of all transference feelings) contradicts the surrounding discussion of transference-object vs original-object differences that enable structural change. D (psychotic disintegration in every case) is not the stated consequence; the affect named is anxiety in a neurotic process, not universal psychosis. E (permanent loss of free-association capacity) is not claimed; anxiety fuels the process, it does not abolish the method. Teaching point: post-interpretation anxiety is expectable and technically useful—it tightens defenses and also drives change.
clinical_application: After a mutative interpretation, monitor anxiety and new defenses; work with them rather than assuming the interpretation “didn’t land.”

stem: According to Bienenfeld, patients most suitable for therapy in the drive model include those with classic “neurotic” symptoms such as conversion disorders and performance anxiety, as well as moderate levels of affective distress such as:

options.text: Dysthymic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder
Acute mania with psychosis only
Severe schizophrenia without observing ego
Delirium tremens exclusively
Comatose patients

answer_text: Dysthymic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder
answer_raw: A. Dysthymic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder
explanation_text: A is correct: patients most suitable for drive-model therapy have classic “neurotic” symptoms (conversion, performance anxiety) “as well as those with moderate levels of affective distress such as dysthymic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder”—because the model needs a strong observing ego to separate from and modify the experiencing ego. B (acute mania with psychosis only) lacks the observing-ego distance Bienenfeld requires. C (severe schizophrenia without observing ego) is exactly the population this model does not select; treatment assumes fully formed structures and ability to observe irrational products. D (delirium tremens exclusively) is an acute medical/withdrawal state, not a neurotic/moderate-affective indication. E (comatose patients) cannot associate or observe at all. Teaching point: classical drive analysis suits higher-functioning neurotic or moderate affective distress, not acute psychosis, delirium, or absent observing ego.
clinical_application: For conversion, performance anxiety, dysthymia, or GAD with good observing ego, consider insight-oriented drive/ego work; for psychosis, choose other modalities first.

stem: The fundamental rule of psychoanalysis, as Bienenfeld states, is to:

options.text: “Say what comes to mind,” without editing, revision, or refinement

explanation_text: A is correct: “The fundamental rule of psychoanalysis is to ‘say what comes to mind,’ without editing, revision, or refinement.” B (only discuss dreams, never waking thoughts) censors waking material and violates unedited saying-what-comes. C (obey the analyst’s every advice without question) is authoritarian suggestion, opposite free association and later abstinence from advice. D (avoid all mention of sexual or aggressive wishes) reinstalls the censorship the rule is designed to overcome. Teaching point: free association—“say what comes to mind” without editing—is the fundamental rule of classical analysis.
clinical_application: Teach patients the fundamental rule explicitly; then treat systematic violations (editing, politeness, intellectualization) as resistance to analyze.

stem: Hartmann's conflict-free sphere of development, applied to therapy in Bienenfeld's account, primarily expands opportunities by allowing the therapist to:

options.text: Treat all mechanisms only as pathological residues of early anxiety
See mechanisms previously viewed only as defenses as positive products of development available for adaptive use
Ignore mental capabilities that work well
Focus exclusively on id content
Eliminate the need to investigate strengths

answer_text: See mechanisms previously viewed only as defenses as positive products of development available for adaptive use
answer_raw: B. See mechanisms previously viewed only as defenses as positive products of development available for adaptive use
explanation_text: B is correct: Hartmann’s conflict-free sphere “expands the available opportunities. Mechanisms that were previously seen only as defenses can now be seen as positive products of development,” and the therapist is obliged to investigate these capabilities for use where automatic mechanisms are maladaptive. A (treat all mechanisms only as pathological residues of early anxiety) is exactly the narrower view this idea revises (the weakling-turned-verbal example is not “only” a residue). C (ignore mental capabilities that work well) contradicts the obligation to investigate those capabilities. D (focus exclusively on id content) is drive-theory aim, not Hartmannian use of conflict-free strengths. E (eliminate the need to investigate strengths) again contradicts the stated obligation to investigate these mental capabilities. Teaching point: conflict-free strengths are therapeutic tools, not only defenses to dismantle.
clinical_application: Inventory skills that work (intellect, humor, organization) and intentionally recruit them when automatic defenses fail.

stem: How does Bienenfeld contrast drive and ego psychologies with the relational theories according to Bienenfeld?

options.text: Drive and ego psychologies are essentially one-person systems repairing a self-contained system; relational theories view development and psychopathology as creations of an interpersonal environment
Both families are identical two-person systems with no differences
Relational theories ignore interpersonal environment entirely
Drive and ego psychologies are primarily two-person field theories
Only drive psychology conceptualizes therapy as interpersonal creation

answer_text: Drive and ego psychologies are essentially one-person systems repairing a self-contained system; relational theories view development and psychopathology as creations of an interpersonal environment
answer_raw: A. Drive and ego psychologies are essentially one-person systems repairing a self-contained system; relational theories view development and psychopathology as creations of an interpersonal environment
explanation_text: A is correct: “Drive and ego psychologies are essentially one-person systems and conceptualize therapy as the correction of errors or the repair of injuries within that self-contained system. The relational theories, i.e., the object relations schools and self psychology, view development and psychopathology as creations of an interpersonal environment.” B (both families identical two-person systems) denies the one-person vs interpersonal contrast just drawn. C (relational theories ignore interpersonal environment entirely) is the opposite of their defining view. D (drive and ego are primarily two-person field theories) assigns Sullivan-style field theory to the one-person systems Bienenfeld's account contrasts. E (only drive psychology conceptualizes therapy as interpersonal creation) reverses the attribution: interpersonal creation is the relational claim. Teaching point: one-person repair vs interpersonal etiology is what mandates different philosophies of cure.
clinical_application: If you formulate only internal drive/ego error, you are in a one-person model; if you formulate co-created interpersonal patterns, you are in the relational family.

answer_raw: A. A corrective emotional experience framed as simply replacing bad past others with a better present other
explanation_text: A is correct: “The self-psychological therapist does not provide a corrective emotional experience to replace the harmful ones in the patient’s past”; because the therapist is human and will disappoint some selfobject need, those junctures become disruption–restoration rather than simple replacement of bad past others. C (interpretation of disruptions) is exactly what follows a disappointment in Bienenfeld's account. D (a nonjudgmental setting) is one of the two vital ingredients of the self-psychological environment (pp. 144–145). E (analysis of selfobject needs) is the model’s focus once needs are mobilized in the regressed transference. stem: Which of the following therapist events can disrupt the selfobject matrix according to Bienenfeld?

options.text: Only major ethical violations, never ordinary human limits
An incompletely empathic interpretation; failure to live up to desire for constant immediate availability; or human failings that resonate with archaic need or fear

explanation_text: B is correct: the matrix is disrupted “when the therapist provides an incompletely empathic interpretation; when he or she fails to live up to the patient’s desire for constant and immediate availability; when any of the therapist’s human failings resonate with an archaic need or fear.” A (only major ethical violations, never ordinary human limits) is too narrow; the listed disruptors are ordinary limits (imperfect empathy, availability, human failings). E (only when insurance changes occur) is an administrative stressor not listed among the selfobject-matrix disruptors here. Teaching point: ordinary human limits—not only scandals—are clinically usable disruptions.

explanation_text: A is correct: against critics who say self psychology counts on cure by kindness and empathy, “Ernest Wolf (1999, p. 117) has countered, ‘Neither empathy nor love cures.’” Therapeutic empathy includes understanding and explaining. B (“Only empathy and love cure”) reverses Wolf’s sentence. C (“Interpretation is never useful”) is not Wolf’s claim; explaining is part of therapeutic empathy here. D (“Patients must never be frustrated”) contradicts the next sentence: empathy often illuminates the necessity of frustration. E (“Drive theory is obsolete in all cases”) is not Wolf’s counter in Bienenfeld's account. Teaching point: neither empathy nor love by itself cures—empathy includes explaining, and needed frustration.
clinical_application: When accused of being “just nice,” articulate that therapeutic empathy includes explanation and workable frustration in disruption–restoration.

stem: Therapeutic empathy, per Bienenfeld’s summary of Wolf’s position, includes both understanding and explaining. Empathy often illuminates the necessity of which experience for growth via disruption and restoration?

options.text: Frustration
Permanent gratification without limit
Moral condemnation
Therapist self-disclosure of all personal problems
Avoidance of any affective experience

answer_text: Frustration
answer_raw: A. Frustration
explanation_text: A is correct: “Empathy often illuminates the necessity of frustration in order for the patient to grow from the process of disruption and restoration.” B (permanent gratification without limit) is not growth-promoting in this model; frustration is necessary to the disruption–restoration cycle. C (moral condemnation) is a judgmental attitude the nonjudgmental setting forbids. D (therapist self-disclosure of all personal problems) is not the experience named; the necessity illuminated is frustration. E (avoidance of any affective experience) contradicts mutative work centering on emotional experience. Teaching point: optimal frustration is part of empathic treatment, not its opposite.
clinical_application: Help patients see that some frustration in the matrix is the raw material of restoration, not proof you do not care.

stem: Object relations theories, per the learning points, identify splitting (as defined by the respective models) and aim to do which of the following through therapy?

options.text: Rectify pathogenic splitting
Intensify splitting as a permanent adaptation
Ignore splitting in favor of only dream work
Define splitting as a purely medical symptom
Treat splitting only with antipsychotics by definition

answer_text: Rectify pathogenic splitting
answer_raw: A. Rectify pathogenic splitting
explanation_text: A is correct: “Object relations theories identify splitting (as defined by the respective models) and aim to rectify pathogenic splitting through the therapy.” B (intensify splitting as a permanent adaptation) is the opposite of rectifying pathogenic splitting. C (ignore splitting in favor of only dream work) substitutes topographic dream technique for the OR aim named. D (define splitting as a purely medical symptom) medicalizes a psychodynamic process the models define theoretically. E (treat splitting only with antipsychotics by definition) is a pharmacologic-only plan, not psychotherapy aimed at rectifying splitting. Teaching point: model-specific definitions of splitting guide different technical paths to integration.
clinical_application: Specify which theory’s “splitting” you mean (Klein, Kernberg, etc.) before planning how you will try to heal it.

explanation_text: A is correct: “Self psychology emphasizes the importance of empathy as both a diagnostic tool and an instrument of healing.” B (only diagnostic, never healing) drops the instrument-of-healing half. stem: Self psychology anticipates disruptions in the selfobject matrix of the transference and uses which process as a central element of therapeutic change?

options.text: Restoration of the matrix
Permanent elimination of all selfobject needs
Avoidance of any further sessions after disruption
Only medication changes without relational work
Deliberate intensification of shame

answer_text: Restoration of the matrix
answer_raw: A. Restoration of the matrix
explanation_text: A is correct: “Self psychology anticipates disruptions in the selfobject matrix of the transference and uses restoration of the matrix as a central element of therapeutic change.” B (permanent elimination of all selfobject needs) contradicts the model: needs mature; they are not abolished. C (avoidance of any further sessions after disruption) treats expected disruption as a reason to stop rather than to restore. D (only medication changes without relational work) is a biological response, not restoration of the selfobject matrix. E (deliberate intensification of shame) is not the central element; restoration after disruption is. Teaching point: disruption is expected; restoration of the matrix is mutative.
clinical_application: Schedule time to complete restoration after known disruptions (vacations, missed sessions, clumsy comments).
